statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{4x-3}$, for $x\ge\dfrac34$. (a) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$, and state its domain. [4] (c) Solve $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)\ge0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $x=\sqrt{4y-3}$ (interchange $x$ and $y$) [M1] $x^2=4y-3$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x^2+3}{4}$ [A1] domain $x\ge0$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $f$ is increasing, so the graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ can only meet on the line $y=x$ [R1] $\sqrt{4x-3}=x$, so $4x-3=x^2$ [M1] $x=1$ or $x=3$ [A1] (both satisfy $\sqrt{4x-3}=x$) [3 marks]
tips: The domain of an inverse is the range of the original function, so state it explicitly. For an increasing function, $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ is equivalent to $f(x)=x$, which is much easier to solve.

subtopic: Odd periodic function
statement: The function $f$ is odd and periodic with period $6$. For $0\le x\le3$, $f(x)=x(3-x)$. (a) Find $f(-1)$. [2] (b) Find $f(10)$. [2] (c) Find $f(-7.5)$. [2] (d) Solve $f(x)=2$ for $0\le x\le6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f(-1)=-f(1)$ [M1] $=-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(10)=f(4)=f(-2)$ [M1] $=-f(2)=-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f(-7.5)=f(-1.5)$ [M1] $=-f(1.5)=-\dfrac94=-2.25$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) For $0\le x\le3$: $x(3-x)=2$ gives $x=1$ or $x=2$ [A1] For $3<x<6$: $f(x)=f(x-6)=-f(6-x)<0$ because $f>0$ on $(0,3)$, so there are no further solutions [R1] Solutions: $x=1$ and $x=2$ [2 marks]
tips: Reduce the argument into the interval where the function is defined by adding or subtracting multiples of the period, and use oddness to move to a positive argument. Check that $f$ is not positive on the rest of the interval before declaring that a solution list is complete.

subtopic: Restricted domain and inverse of a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-6x+11$, for $x\ge a$. (a) Find the smallest value of $a$ for which $f$ has an inverse function. [2] Let $a$ take the value found in part (a). (b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-3)^2+2$ [M1] smallest $a=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=(y-3)^2+2$ (interchange $x$ and $y$) [M1] $y-3=\sqrt{x-2}$ (positive root since $y\ge3$) [A1] $f^{-1}(x)=3+\sqrt{x-2}$, domain $x\ge2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f$ is increasing on $x\ge3$, so solutions lie on $y=x$ [R1] $x^2-6x+11=x$, so $x^2-7x+11=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] reject $x=\dfrac{7-\sqrt5}{2}\ (\approx2.38)$ since it is less than $3$; so $x=\dfrac{7+\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The inverse of a restricted quadratic needs the correct sign for the square root: the sign is fixed by the restriction on the domain of $f$. When solving $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ by setting $f(x)=x$, check each root against the domain.

subtopic: Stationary point, range and inverse of x e^(-x/2)
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x/2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the coordinates of the local maximum of the graph of $f$. [3] (b) Write down the range of $f$. [2] (c) Explain why $f$ has no inverse function. [1] Let $g$ be the function $f$ restricted to the domain $x\ge2$. (d) Solve $g(x)=0.3$. [2] (e) Write down the domain and the range of $g^{-1}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=e^{-x/2}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ [A1] $f'(x)=0$ [M1] local maximum at $(2,\,0.736)$ (exact $\left(2,\,\dfrac2e\right)$) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)\le0.736$ [A1] since $f(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ there is no lower bound, so the range is $\left]-\infty,\ \dfrac2e\right]$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $f$ is not one-to-one: for example the line $y=0.3$ meets the graph twice [R1] [1 mark] (d) Solve $xe^{-x/2}=0.3$ for $x\ge2$ [M1] $x=5.99$ ($5.9871\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (e) Domain of $g^{-1}$: $0<x\le0.736$ [A1] range of $g^{-1}$: $y\ge2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a restricted function, the domain of the inverse is the range of the function on that restricted domain, so look at the behavior of the graph as $x\to\infty$ as well as at the turning point. Use the GDC to solve equations of this form.

subtopic: Composite functions of linear and quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=3x-2$ and $g(x)=x^2+1$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$. [1] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [2] (c) Solve the equation $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answers in exact form. [3]
tips: $(f\circ g)(x)$ means $f(g(x))$: the inner function is applied first. In general $f\circ g\ne g\circ f$, which is why the equation in (c) is not an identity.

subtopic: Odd log function: domain, symmetry and inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)$, for $x$ in the largest possible real domain. (a) Find the domain of $f$. [2] (b) Show that $f$ is an odd function. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (d) State the domain of $f^{-1}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}>0$ [M1] $x<-1$ or $x>1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(-x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{-x+1}{-x-1}\right)=\ln\left(\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\right)$ [M1] $=-\ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)=-f(x)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=\ln\left(\dfrac{y+1}{y-1}\right)$, so $e^x=\dfrac{y+1}{y-1}$ [M1] $ye^x-e^x=y+1$, so $y(e^x-1)=e^x+1$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}=1+\dfrac{2}{x-1}$ never equals $1$, so $f(x)\ne0$; domain of $f^{-1}$ is $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\ne0$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the domain of a logarithm of a fraction, solve a sign inequality for the fraction. The domain of the inverse is the range of $f$, so look for any value that $f$ can never take.

subtopic: Factor theorem and remainder theorem with two unknowns
statement: Let $p(x)=2x^3+ax^2-7x+b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. The polynomial $p(x)$ has a factor $(x-2)$, and the remainder when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x+1)$ is $12$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [5] (b) Factorize $p(x)$ completely into linear factors over $\mathbb{R}$, and hence solve $p(x)=0$. [3]
tips: The factor theorem gives $p(c)=0$ and the remainder theorem gives $p(c)=r$ for division by $(x-c)$; each condition produces one linear equation in the unknowns. After finding a root, divide to reduce to a quadratic, then use the formula if it does not factorize.

subtopic: Roots of a cubic: symmetric functions and reciprocal roots
statement: The roots of the equation $2x^3-6x^2+3x+5=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [3] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. [2] (c) Find a cubic equation, with integer coefficients, that has roots $\dfrac1\alpha$, $\dfrac1\beta$ and $\dfrac1\gamma$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=3$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\dfrac32$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=-\dfrac52$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)$ [M1] $=9-3=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sum of the new roots: $\dfrac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\dfrac{3/2}{-5/2}=-\dfrac35$ [M1] [A1] Sum of products in pairs: $\dfrac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\dfrac65$ [A1] Product: $\dfrac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\dfrac25$ [A1] Equation: $t^3+\dfrac35t^2-\dfrac65t+\dfrac25=0$, i.e. $5t^3+3t^2-6t+2=0$ [A1] [5 marks] Alternative: substitute $x=\dfrac1t$ into $2x^3-6x^2+3x+5=0$ and multiply by $t^3$ to get $2-6t+3t^2+5t^3=0$ (M1 for substitution, A1 for the equation, then A1 A1 A1 as the working shown).
tips: For a cubic $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, the sums of roots are $-b/a$, $c/a$ and $-d/a$. For reciprocal roots, substituting $x=1/t$ is usually the quickest method.

subtopic: Complex roots of a real cubic
statement: The cubic equation $z^3-5z^2+pz-q=0$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{R}$, has a root $z=1+2i$. (a) Write down a second root of the equation, with a reason. [1] (b) Find the third root. [2] (c) Find the values of $p$ and $q$. [3] (d) Write the cubic polynomial as a product of three linear factors. [1]
markscheme: (a) $1-2i$, because the non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs [A1] [1 mark] (b) Sum of roots $=5$: $(1+2i)+(1-2i)+r=5$ [M1] $r=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $p=(1+2i)(1-2i)+3(1+2i)+3(1-2i)$ [M1] $=5+6=11$ [A1] $q=3(1+2i)(1-2i)=15$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $(z-3)(z-1-2i)(z-1+2i)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Non-real roots of real-coefficient polynomials always come in conjugate pairs, which gives the third root from the sum of the roots. Use $z^3-(\text{sum})z^2+(\text{pair sums})z-(\text{product})$ to match coefficients.

subtopic: Open box volume as a cubic
statement: A rectangular sheet of cardboard measures $30$ cm by $20$ cm. A square of side $x$ cm is cut from each corner and the sides are folded up to form an open box of volume $V\ \text{cm}^3$. (a) Show that $V=4x^3-100x^2+600x$. [2] (b) State the set of possible values of $x$. [1] (c) Find the maximum volume of the box, and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [3] (d) The box must hold at least $900\ \text{cm}^3$. Find the possible values of $x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Base dimensions $(30-2x)$ and $(20-2x)$, height $x$ [M1] $V=x(30-2x)(20-2x)=x(600-100x+4x^2)=4x^3-100x^2+600x$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $0<x<10$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Maximum using the GDC (or $V'(x)=12x^2-200x+600=0$) [M1] $x=3.92$ ($3.9237\ldots$) [A1] $V=1060\ \text{cm}^3$ ($1056.3\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $4x^3-100x^2+600x=900$ [M1] $x=2.30$ and $x=5.78$ (the third root $16.9$ is outside the domain) [A1] $2.30\le x\le5.78$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In 'show that' questions write every algebraic step. State the domain from the physical constraints: both $30-2x>0$ and $20-2x>0$, so the second condition is the binding one.

subtopic: Repeated root, sign of a cubic and number of solutions
statement: Let $p(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+27$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $p(x)=(x-3)^2(x+3)$. [3] (b) Solve the inequality $p(x)\le0$. [3] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $p(x)=k$ has exactly two distinct real solutions. [3]
markscheme: (a) $p(3)=27-27-27+27=0$, or grouping: $x^2(x-3)-9(x-3)$ [M1] $=(x-3)(x^2-9)$ [A1] $=(x-3)(x-3)(x+3)=(x-3)^2(x+3)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Critical values $x=-3$ and $x=3$ [A1] $(x-3)^2\ge0$, so the sign of $p$ is that of $(x+3)$ except at $x=3$ where $p=0$ [M1] $x\le-3$ or $x=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $p'(x)=3x^2-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1)$ [M1] local maximum $(-1,\,32)$ and local minimum $(3,\,0)$ [A1] $k=0$ or $k=32$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A repeated factor means the graph touches the axis without crossing, so the sign of the polynomial does not change there but the value zero still satisfies $\le0$. Exactly two solutions occurs when the horizontal line touches one turning point.

subtopic: Polynomial identity and remainder on division by a quadratic
statement: (a) Find the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $2x^2+5x-1\equiv A(x-1)^2+B(x-1)+C$. [4] (b) Hence find the remainder when $2x^2+5x-1$ is divided by $(x-1)^2$. [2]
tips: To match an identity, expand the right-hand side and equate coefficients of each power of $x$. The remainder after division by a quadratic has degree less than $2$, so it is the leftover linear part.

subtopic: Laws of logarithms and a logarithmic equation
statement: (a) Given that $\log_2 a=p$ and $\log_2 b=q$, express $\log_2\left(\dfrac{8a^2}{\sqrt b}\right)$ in terms of $p$ and $q$. [3] (b) Solve the equation $\log_3(x+2)+\log_3(x-4)=3$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\log_2 8+2\log_2 a-\dfrac12\log_2 b$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] $=3+2p-\dfrac{q}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\log_3\big((x+2)(x-4)\big)=3$ [M1] $(x+2)(x-4)=27$ [A1] $x^2-2x-35=0$, so $x=7$ or $x=-5$ [A1] $x=-5$ is rejected because the arguments of the logarithms must be positive; $x=7$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Combine logarithms into a single logarithm before converting to exponential form, and always check the answers against the domain of the original equation.

subtopic: Exponential equations: quadratic in 2^x and different bases
statement: (a) Solve the equation $4^x-5\cdot2^x+4=0$. [4] (b) Solve the equation $3^{2x+1}=5^x$, giving your answer in the form $\dfrac{\ln a}{\ln b}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{Q}$. [3]
tips: Recognize $4^x=(2^x)^2$ so that the equation becomes a quadratic. When the bases cannot be matched, take logarithms of both sides and collect the terms in $x$.

subtopic: Exponential decay model for caffeine
statement: The amount of caffeine in Rosa's body, $A$ mg, $t$ hours after she drinks a cup of coffee, is modeled by $A(t)=180e^{-kt}$, where $k>0$. After $3$ hours there are $126$ mg of caffeine in her body. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the half-life of caffeine in her body, in hours. [2] (c) Find the time until the amount of caffeine first falls below $20$ mg. [2] Rosa drinks a second cup of coffee $6$ hours after the first, which adds $100$ mg of caffeine to her body. Assume that after the second cup the total amount decays at the same rate as before. (d) Find the amount of caffeine in her body $8$ hours after the first cup. [3]
markscheme: (a) $126=180e^{-3k}$ [M1] $e^{-3k}=0.7$ [A1] $k=\dfrac{\ln(10/7)}{3}=0.119$ ($0.118891\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $e^{-kt}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}=5.83$ hours ($5.8300\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $180e^{-kt}=20$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln9}{k}=18.5$ hours ($18.4809\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (d) Just before the second cup: $A(6)=180\times0.7^2=88.2$ mg [M1] after the second cup: $188.2$ mg [A1] two hours later: $188.2\,e^{-2k}=148$ mg ($148.37\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use unrounded values of $k$ in later parts to avoid accumulating rounding error. For the second dose, treat the new total as a fresh starting amount that decays for the remaining time.

subtopic: Log-linear and log-log linearization
statement: (a) The variables $x$ and $y$ are such that the graph of $\ln y$ against $x$ is a straight line. When $x=0$, $\ln y=2$, and when $x=3$, $\ln y=8$. Express $y$ in terms of $x$ in the form $y=e^{mx+c}$. [3] (b) The variables $u$ and $v$ are such that the graph of $\ln v$ against $\ln u$ is a straight line. When $\ln u=1$, $\ln v=5$, and when $\ln u=2$, $\ln v=8$. Express $v$ in the form $v=au^n$, where $a$ is given in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) Gradient $=\dfrac{8-2}{3-0}=2$ [M1] $\ln y=2x+2$ [A1] $y=e^{2x+2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{8-5}{2-1}=3$ [M1] $\ln v=3\ln u+2$ [A1] $v=e^2u^3$, so $a=e^2$ and $n=3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A straight line in $\ln y$ against $x$ indicates an exponential relationship; in $\ln v$ against $\ln u$ it indicates a power relationship. Find the gradient and the intercept, then convert back with the exponential function.

subtopic: Equation involving log base x and an inequality
statement: (a) Show that $\log_x2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}$, for $x>0,\ x\ne1$. [1] (b) Hence solve the equation $\log_2x+6\log_x2=5$. [4] (c) Solve the inequality $\log_2x+6\log_x2<5$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\log_x2=\dfrac{\log_22}{\log_2x}=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (b) Let $u=\log_2x$ [M1] $u+\dfrac6u=5$ [A1] $u^2-5u+6=0$, so $u=2$ or $u=3$ [A1] $x=4$ or $x=8$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $u+\dfrac6u-5<0\iff\dfrac{(u-2)(u-3)}{u}<0$ [M1] $u<0$ or $2<u<3$ [A1] $0<x<1$ or $4<x<8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Do not multiply an inequality by $u=\log_2x$ without considering its sign; combine into one fraction instead. Convert back to $x$ at the end, remembering that $u<0$ corresponds to $0<x<1$.

subtopic: Logarithmic scale: earthquake magnitude and energy
statement: The magnitude $M$ of an earthquake that releases energy $E$ joules is given by $M=\dfrac23\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{E}{E_0}\right)$, where $E_0$ is a positive constant. (a) Show that $E=E_0\times10^{1.5M}$. [2] (b) Find the ratio of the energy released by an earthquake of magnitude $7.1$ to the energy released by one of magnitude $6.4$. [2] (c) An earthquake releases $50$ times as much energy as one of magnitude $5.2$. Find its magnitude. [3] (d) Two earthquakes, of magnitudes $6.0$ and $6.5$, occur. The total energy released is equal to the energy released by a single earthquake of magnitude $M^*$. Find $M^*$. [4]
tips: Energies add, magnitudes do not: convert each magnitude to energy, add, and convert back. On a logarithmic scale, equal differences in magnitude correspond to equal ratios of energy.

subtopic: Sector perimeter and area equations
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians, where $0<\theta<2\pi$. The perimeter of the sector is $20$ cm and its area is $24\text{ cm}^2$. (a) Show that $r^2-10r+24=0$. [3] (b) Find the two possible pairs of values of $r$ and $\theta$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Arc length $=r\theta$, so perimeter $2r+r\theta=20$, giving $r\theta=20-2r$ [M1] Area $=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12r(r\theta)=\tfrac12r(20-2r)$ [M1] $=10r-r^2=24$, so $r^2-10r+24=0$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(r-4)(r-6)=0$ [M1] $r=4,\ \theta=\dfrac{20-8}{4}=3$ [A1] $r=6,\ \theta=\dfrac{20-12}{6}=\dfrac43$ [A1] Both satisfy $0<\theta<2\pi$. [3 marks]
tips: Express the arc length as $r\theta$ and eliminate $\theta$ using the perimeter condition. Always check that each solution satisfies the stated restriction on $\theta$.

subtopic: Cosine rule with exact values
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=4$ cm, $AC=2\sqrt3$ cm and angle $BAC=30^\circ$. (a) Use the cosine rule to find the length of $BC$. [3] (b) Find the area of triangle $ABC$. [2] (c) Hence show that angle $ACB=90^\circ$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $BC^2=4^2+(2\sqrt3)^2-2(4)(2\sqrt3)\cos30^\circ$ [M1] $=16+12-16\sqrt3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] $=28-24=4$, so $BC=2$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(4)(2\sqrt3)\sin30^\circ$ [M1] $=2\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $BC^2+AC^2=4+12=16$ [M1] $=AB^2$, so by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem angle $ACB=90^\circ$ [A1] Accept $\sin C=1$ from the area formula in (b). [2 marks]
tips: Know the exact values of $\sin$ and $\cos$ at $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Simplify surds fully and check your answer by looking for special triangles.

subtopic: Area and perimeter of a segment
statement: $O$ is the centre of a circle of radius $4$ cm. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on the circle such that angle $AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. The minor segment is the region bounded by the chord $AB$ and the minor arc $AB$. (a) Write down the length of the minor arc $AB$. [1] (b) Find the exact area of the segment. [3] (c) Find the exact perimeter of the segment. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s=4\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) Sector area $=\tfrac12(4^2)\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}$ [M1] Triangle area $=\tfrac12(4^2)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=4\sqrt3$ [M1] Segment area $=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}-4\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles with apex angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, hence equilateral, so $AB=4$ (or cosine rule) [M1] Perimeter $=4+\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Segment area is sector area minus triangle area. The chord is not the arc: do not forget it when you are asked for a perimeter.

subtopic: Cosine rule with bearings
statement: Two ships leave port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ travels on a bearing of $060^\circ$ at $40\text{ km h}^{-1}$ and ship $B$ travels on a bearing of $140^\circ$ at $30\text{ km h}^{-1}$. After $2$ hours the ships are at points $A$ and $B$ respectively. (a) Write down the size of angle $APB$. [1] (b) Find the distance $AB$ in km. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $B$ from $A$, giving your answer to the nearest degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $140^\circ-60^\circ=80^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $PA=80$ km, $PB=60$ km [A1] $AB^2=80^2+60^2-2(80)(60)\cos80^\circ$ [M1] $AB=91.3$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) Sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin\angle PAB}{60}=\dfrac{\sin80^\circ}{91.285}$ [M1] $\angle PAB=40.3^\circ$ [A1] The bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $240^\circ$ [M1] Bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $240^\circ-40.3^\circ=199.7^\circ\approx200^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Draw a quick sketch with a north line at each point. For the bearing from $A$ to $B$, start from the back bearing $A\to P$ and adjust by the angle at $A$.

subtopic: Ambiguous case of the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $BAC=35^\circ$, $BC=6$ cm and $AC=9$ cm. (a) Find the two possible sizes of angle $ABC$. [3] (b) Find the two possible lengths of $AB$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin B}{9}=\dfrac{\sin35^\circ}{6}$ [M1] $\sin B=0.8604$ [A1] $B=59.4^\circ$ or $B=120.6^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Case 1: $C=180^\circ-35^\circ-59.36^\circ=85.6^\circ$ [M1] $AB=\dfrac{6\sin85.6^\circ}{\sin35^\circ}=10.4$ cm [A1] Case 2: $C=180^\circ-35^\circ-120.64^\circ=24.4^\circ$ [M1] $AB=\dfrac{6\sin24.4^\circ}{\sin35^\circ}=4.31$ cm [A1] [4 marks]
tips: When the given angle is not between the two given sides and the side opposite it is the shorter one, always test for the obtuse alternative $180^\circ-B$.

subtopic: Right pyramid: edges and face angles
statement: A right pyramid $VABCD$ has a horizontal square base $ABCD$ of side $8$ cm. The vertex $V$ is vertically above the centre $O$ of the base and $VO=6$ cm. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. (a) Find the length of $VA$. [2] (b) Find the angle between $VA$ and the base $ABCD$. [2] (c) Find the angle between the face $VBC$ and the base $ABCD$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{8^2+8^2}=8\sqrt2$, so $AO=4\sqrt2$ [A1] $VA=\sqrt{(4\sqrt2)^2+6^2}=\sqrt{68}=8.25$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Required angle is $\angle VAO$ [M1] $\tan\angle VAO=\dfrac{6}{4\sqrt2}$, so $\angle VAO=46.7^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Required angle is $\angle VMO$ (since $OM\perp BC$ and $VM\perp BC$) [M1] $OM=4$ [A1] $\tan\angle VMO=\dfrac64$, so $\angle VMO=56.3^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Identify the right-angled triangle that contains the required angle, and state it. The angle between a plane face and the base is measured along a line perpendicular to their line of intersection.

subtopic: Angles of elevation from two points
statement: A vertical tower $PQ$ stands on level ground with $Q$ at its base and $P$ at its top. Points $A$ and $B$ are on the ground with $AB=120$ m, angle $QAB=64^\circ$ and angle $QBA=48^\circ$. The angle of elevation of $P$ from $A$ is $26^\circ$. (a) Find the length $AQ$. [3] (b) Find the height of the tower. [2] (c) Find the angle of elevation of $P$ from $B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Angle $AQB=180^\circ-64^\circ-48^\circ=68^\circ$ [A1] $\dfrac{AQ}{\sin48^\circ}=\dfrac{120}{\sin68^\circ}$ [M1] $AQ=96.2$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) $PQ=AQ\tan26^\circ$ [M1] $=96.18\times0.4877=46.9$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $BQ=\dfrac{120\sin64^\circ}{\sin68^\circ}=116.3$ m [A1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{46.91}{116.33}$ [M1] $\theta=22.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Keep unrounded values in your calculator between parts. The ground triangle is not right-angled, so use the sine rule there and ordinary trigonometry in the vertical triangles.

subtopic: Segment area equal to triangle area
statement: The sector $OAB$ of a circle has centre $O$, radius $10$ cm and angle $AOB=\theta$ radians, where $0<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that the area of the segment bounded by chord $AB$ and arc $AB$ is $50(\theta-\sin\theta)\text{ cm}^2$. [2] (b) The area of the segment equals the area of triangle $OAB$. Show that $\theta=2\sin\theta$. [2] (c) Solve $\theta=2\sin\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. [2] (d) Hence find the length of arc $AB$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $OAB$ [M1] $=\tfrac12(10^2)\theta-\tfrac12(10^2)\sin\theta=50(\theta-\sin\theta)$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) Triangle area $=50\sin\theta$ [M1] $50(\theta-\sin\theta)=50\sin\theta\Rightarrow\theta=2\sin\theta$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) Attempt to solve graphically or with GDC (note $\theta=0$ is excluded) [M1] $\theta=1.90$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $10\times1.8955=19.0$ cm [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $\theta$ from your calculator in later parts. The equation has no algebraic solution, so a GDC intersection is expected.

subtopic: Space diagonals of a cube
statement: $ABCDEFGH$ is a cube of side $2$, where $ABCD$ is the horizontal base, $E,F,G,H$ lie directly above $A,B,C,D$ respectively, so $G$ is opposite to $A$ and $H$ is opposite to $B$. The diagonals $AG$ and $BH$ intersect at the centre $O$ of the cube. (a) Find the exact length of $AG$. [2] (b) Find the exact value of $\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [3] (c) Show that $\cos\angle AOB=\dfrac13$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $AG=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+2^2}$ [M1] $=2\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Required angle is $\angle GAC$, where $C$ is directly below $G$ [M1] $CG=2$ [A1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2}{2\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\ \left(=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $AO=BO=\tfrac12(2\sqrt3)=\sqrt3$ [A1] Cosine rule in triangle $AOB$ with $AB=2$: $\cos\angle AOB=\dfrac{3+3-4}{2\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2}{6}$ [A1] $=\dfrac13$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Draw a sketch of the cube and mark the relevant right angles. For part (c), $O$ is the midpoint of both diagonals, so $AO=BO$.

subtopic: Triangle sides to angle and area
statement: Triangle $PQR$ has $PQ=9$ cm, $QR=11$ cm and $PR=16$ cm. (a) Find the size of the largest angle of the triangle. [3] (b) Find the area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the shortest distance from $Q$ to the line $PR$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Largest angle is $Q$, opposite the longest side [M1] $\cos Q=\dfrac{9^2+11^2-16^2}{2(9)(11)}=-\dfrac{3}{11}$ [A1] $Q=106^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(9)(11)\sin Q$ [M1] $=47.6\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tfrac12(16)h=47.62$ [M1] $h=5.95$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The largest angle is opposite the longest side. Use unrounded values from earlier parts and remember that the shortest distance is the perpendicular height.

subtopic: Cone formed from a sector
statement: A sector of a circle of radius $12$ cm and angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ radians is cut out of paper. The two straight edges are joined together to form a cone (with no overlap). (a) Find the arc length of the sector. [1] (b) Find the radius of the base of the cone. [2] (c) Show that the height of the cone is $\sqrt{119}$ cm. [2] (d) Find the exact volume of the cone. [2]
markscheme: (a) $12\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=10\pi$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) Arc length equals base circumference: $2\pi r=10\pi$ [M1] $r=5$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Slant height $=12$ cm [M1] $h=\sqrt{12^2-5^2}=\sqrt{119}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (d) $V=\tfrac13\pi(5^2)\sqrt{119}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{25\pi\sqrt{119}}{3}\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The arc length of the sector becomes the circumference of the base, and the radius of the sector becomes the slant height of the cone.

subtopic: Triangle area gives two possible angles
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$ cm, $AC=11$ cm and the area of the triangle is $30\text{ cm}^2$. Angle $BAC$ may be acute or obtuse. (a) Show that $\sin\angle BAC=\dfrac{15}{22}$. [2] (b) Find the two possible lengths of $BC$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $30=\tfrac12(8)(11)\sin A$ [M1] $\sin A=\dfrac{30}{44}=\dfrac{15}{22}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=43.0^\circ$ or $A=137.0^\circ$ [A1] Cosine rule: $BC^2=8^2+11^2-2(8)(11)\cos A$ [M1] Acute: $BC=7.50$ cm [A1] Obtuse: $BC=17.7$ cm [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Both $A$ and $180^\circ-A$ have the same sine, so there are two triangles. Use the cosine rule for each, keeping unrounded angles.

subtopic: Overlap of two circles
statement: Two circles have centres $C_1$ and $C_2$ with $C_1C_2=7$ cm. The first circle has radius $5$ cm and the second has radius $3$ cm. The circles intersect at points $X$ and $Y$. Let $\alpha=\angle XC_1C_2$ and $\beta=\angle XC_2C_1$. (a) Show that $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{13}{14}$ and find $\alpha$ in radians. [3] (b) Find $\beta$ in radians. [2] (c) Find the area of the region common to both circles. [4]
markscheme: (a) Cosine rule in triangle $XC_1C_2$: $3^2=5^2+7^2-2(5)(7)\cos\alpha$ [M1] $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{65}{70}=\dfrac{13}{14}$ [AG] [A1] $\alpha=0.380$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $5^2=3^2+7^2-2(3)(7)\cos\beta$ [M1] $\cos\beta=\dfrac{33}{42}=\dfrac{11}{14}$, $\beta=0.667$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Common area $=$ segment of circle 1 (angle $2\alpha$) $+$ segment of circle 2 (angle $2\beta$) [M1] $\left(\tfrac12\cdot25(2\alpha-\sin2\alpha)\right)+\left(\tfrac12\cdot9(2\beta-\sin2\beta)\right)$ [M1] Substituting $\alpha=0.38025$, $\beta=0.66695$ [A1] $=2.52\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The common region is the union of two circular segments, one from each circle, sharing the chord $XY$. Use the double angle $2\alpha$ at each centre.

subtopic: Radian measure, arc length and sector area
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $3$ cm and angle $210^\circ$. (a) Convert $210^\circ$ to radians, giving your answer as a multiple of $\pi$. [1] (b) Find the arc length of the sector. [2] (c) Find the area of the sector. [2]
markscheme: (a) $210\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $s=3\times\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{7\pi}{2}$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A=\tfrac12(3^2)\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{21\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The formulas $s=r\theta$ and $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$ require $\theta$ in radians, so convert first.

subtopic: Cross product and area of a triangle
statement: The points $A(1,2,0)$, $B(3,-1,2)$ and $C(0,4,5)$ form a triangle. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Attempt at cross product [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}(-3)(5)-(2)(2)\\(2)(-1)-(2)(5)\\(2)(2)-(-3)(-1)\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-19\\-12\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area $=\tfrac12\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|$ [M1] $=\tfrac12\sqrt{361+144+1}=\dfrac{\sqrt{506}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Check your cross product by taking its scalar product with each original vector; both must give zero. The area of the triangle is half the magnitude of the cross product.

subtopic: Intersection of lines and angle between lines
statement: Two lines have equations $l_1:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\5\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the lines intersect and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the cosine of the acute angle between the lines. [3]
markscheme: (a) Equating components: $1+2s=4-t$, $2-s=t$, $3+s=-1+5t$ [M1] From the first two: $1+2s=4-(2-s)\Rightarrow s=1,\ t=1$ [A1] Third equation: $3+1=4$ and $-1+5=4$, so consistent [R1] Intersection $(3,1,4)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2=-2-1+5=2$ [A1] Use of $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}$ with $|\mathbf d_1|=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf d_2|=\sqrt{27}$ [M1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{162}}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{9}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Solve two of the three component equations and then test the third; a failed check means the lines are skew. Use the direction vectors, not the position vectors, for the angle.

subtopic: Shortest distance between skew lines
statement: Consider the lines $l_1:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $l_1$ and $l_2$ are skew. [3] (b) Find a vector perpendicular to both lines. [2] (c) Hence find the shortest distance between the two lines. [3]
markscheme: (a) Directions are not parallel, since $(1,1,0)$ is not a multiple of $(2,0,1)$ [R1] Equating: $1+s=2t$, $s=1$, $2=2+t$ [M1] gives $s=1$, $t=0$, but then $1+s=2\neq 2t=0$, so no intersection [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{A_1A_2}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $d=\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{A_1A_2}\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\dfrac{|-1-1+0|}{\sqrt6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt6}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To show lines are skew you need both non-parallel directions and no common point. The shortest distance is the projection of the vector between the lines onto the common perpendicular.

subtopic: Plane through three points
statement: The points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(2,1,0)$ and $C(0,3,1)$ lie in the plane $\Pi$. (a) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $\Pi$ meets the $z$-axis. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Cross product [M1] $\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $5x+3y+4z=5(1)+3(0)+4(2)$ [M1] $5x+3y+4z=13$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Set $x=y=0$: $4z=13$ [M1] $\left(0,0,\dfrac{13}{4}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Verify your Cartesian equation by substituting all three given points. Points on a coordinate axis have the other two coordinates equal to zero.

subtopic: Line meets plane; angle between line and plane
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $x+2y+2z=11$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l$ meets $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of the sine of the acute angle between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(1+2t)+2(-2+t)+2(3-t)=11$ [M1] $3+2t=11$, $t=4$ [A1] Point $(9,2,-1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2+2-2=2$ [A1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$ with $|\mathbf d|=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf n|=3$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt6}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{9}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane uses $\sin$ with the normal vector (the angle with the normal is the complement). Substitute the line's parametric coordinates into the plane equation.

subtopic: Distance, foot and reflection in a plane
statement: The plane $\Pi$ has equation $2x-3y+6z=5$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(3,-1,4)$. (a) Find the perpendicular distance from $P$ to $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\Pi$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the reflection of $P$ in $\Pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d=\dfrac{|2(3)-3(-1)+6(4)-5|}{\sqrt{2^2+3^2+6^2}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{28}{7}$ [A1] $=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Line through $P$ perpendicular to $\Pi$: $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\6\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Substituting: $33+49\lambda=5$, $\lambda=-\dfrac47$ [A1] $F=\left(\dfrac{13}{7},\dfrac57,\dfrac47\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{OP'}=2\overrightarrow{OF}-\overrightarrow{OP}$ [M1] $P'=\left(\dfrac57,\dfrac{17}{7},-\dfrac{20}{7}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The foot of the perpendicular is the intersection of $\Pi$ with the line through $P$ parallel to the normal. The reflection lies the same distance beyond the plane, so use the midpoint relation.

subtopic: Line of intersection of two planes
statement: Two planes have equations $\Pi_1:\ x+2y-z=4$ and $\Pi_2:\ 2x-y+3z=3$. (a) Find a direction vector for the line of intersection of $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_2$. [3] (b) Show that the point $(2,1,0)$ lies on both planes, and hence write down a vector equation of the line of intersection. [3] (c) Find the exact value of the cosine of the acute angle between the planes. [3]
markscheme: (a) Normals $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Cross product [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}5\\-5\\-5\end{pmatrix}$, so direction $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\Pi_1$: $2+2-0=4$ [A1] $\Pi_2$: $4-1+0=3$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2=2-2-3=-3$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2|}{|\mathbf n_1||\mathbf n_2|}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6\sqrt{14}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{21}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{14}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The line of intersection is perpendicular to both normals. Any direction vector can be scaled, so simplify it before writing the line.

subtopic: Three planes: parameter and geometry
statement: Consider the planes $\Pi_1:\ x+y+z=3$, $\Pi_2:\ 2x+y-z=1$ and $\Pi_3:\ 3x+2y+kz=m$, where $k,m\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the three planes do not meet at a single point. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the three planes intersect in a line. [2] (c) For this value of $k$ and $m\neq4$, describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes. [2] (d) For $m=4$, find a vector equation of the line of intersection. [3]
markscheme: (a) Determinant of coefficient matrix [M1] $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\2&1&-1\\3&2&k\end{vmatrix}=1(k+2)-1(2k+3)+1(4-3)=-k$ [A1] No unique intersection when $k=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) With $k=0$ the left side of $\Pi_3$ is $\Pi_1+\Pi_2$ [M1] Consistent when $m=3+1=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) No common point, but no two planes are parallel (normals not multiples) [R1] The planes form a triangular prism [A1] [2 marks] (d) Let $z=\lambda$: $x+y=3-\lambda$, $2x+y=1+\lambda$ [M1] $x=-2+2\lambda$, $y=5-3\lambda$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For three planes, zero determinant means either a common line or a triangular prism (or parallel planes); consistency decides which. Check that no two normal vectors are parallel before naming the arrangement.

subtopic: Closest approach of moving objects
statement: Two drones move so that, $t$ seconds after take-off, their position vectors (in metres) relative to an origin $O$ are $\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix}14\\5\\-6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the distance between the drones when $t=0$. [2] (b) Show that the square of the distance between the drones at time $t$ is $D(t)=61t^2-240t+280$. [3] (c) Find the minimum distance between the drones, and the time at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}-12\\-6\\10\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\sqrt{144+36+100}=\sqrt{280}=16.7$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf r_A-\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix}-12+5t\\-6\\10-6t\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $D=(5t-12)^2+36+(10-6t)^2$ [M1] $=25t^2-120t+144+36+100-120t+36t^2=61t^2-240t+280$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (c) Use of $D'(t)=0$ or GDC minimum [M1] $t=1.97$ s [A1] Minimum distance $=\sqrt{43.93}=6.63$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Minimising the squared distance is easier than the distance itself and gives the same time. Keep unrounded values until the final square root.

subtopic: Scalar product: angle, perpendicularity, unit vector
statement: Let $\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$. [3] (b) The vector $\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}3\\k\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf u$. Find $k$. [2] (c) Find a unit vector in the direction opposite to $\mathbf u$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=2-2+4=4$ [M1] $|\mathbf u|=|\mathbf v|=3$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac49$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf w=0$: $6-k-2=0$ [M1] $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac23\\ \frac13\\ -\frac23\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. A unit vector is a vector divided by its own magnitude.

subtopic: Closest point on a line and area of triangle
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(5,4,3)$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $Q$ on $l$ that is closest to $P$. [4] (b) Find the shortest distance from $P$ to $l$. [2] (c) The points $R$ and $S$ lie on $l$ with $s=-1$ and $s=2$ respectively. Find the area of triangle $PRS$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2s-4\\s-2\\-2s-3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}=0$ [M1] $4s-8+s-2+4s+6=9s-4=0$ [A1] $s=\dfrac49$, $Q=\left(\dfrac{17}{9},\dfrac{22}{9},-\dfrac89\right)=(1.89,\,2.44,\,-0.889)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|$ [M1] $=\dfrac{7\sqrt5}{3}=5.22$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $RS=3\left|\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\right|=9$ [A1] Area $=\tfrac12\times9\times5.217$ [M1] $=23.5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular, so set the scalar product of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ with the direction vector to zero. The perpendicular distance is also the height of the triangle.

subtopic: Collinearity and ratio; line meets coordinate plane
statement: The points $A(2,1,-1)$ and $B(5,4,2)$ lie on a line $L$. The point $C$ has coordinates $(11,p,q)$ and also lies on $L$. (a) Find the values of $p$ and $q$. [3] (b) Find the ratio $AB:BC$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $L$ meets the $xy$-plane. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}9\\p-1\\q+1\end{pmatrix}=\lambda\overrightarrow{AB}$ [M1] $\lambda=3$ [A1] $p=10$, $q=8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\\6\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $AB:BC=1:2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $z=0\Rightarrow\mu=1$ [M1] $(3,2,0)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Three points are collinear when one displacement vector is a scalar multiple of another. The $xy$-plane is $z=0$.

subtopic: Plane from vector form to Cartesian equation
statement: The plane $\Pi$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [2] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$ in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. [2] (c) Determine whether each of the points $A(4,5,1)$ and $B(2,1,3)$ lies on $\Pi$. [2] (d) Find the distance from the origin to $\Pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $-x+y+2z=-1+0+4$ [M1] $-x+y+2z=3$ (accept $x-y-2z=-3$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A$: $-4+5+2=3$, so $A$ lies on $\Pi$ [A1] $B$: $-2+1+6=5\neq3$, so $B$ does not lie on $\Pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $d=\dfrac{|3|}{\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2+2^2}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6}=1.22$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A normal vector comes from the cross product of the two direction vectors. Always test points by substituting into the Cartesian equation.

subtopic: Line parallel to a plane and distance
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\a\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $3x-y+2z=b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb R$. (a) Given that $l$ is parallel to $\Pi$, find $a$. [3] (b) Given also that $l$ lies in $\Pi$, find $b$. [2] (c) Given instead that $b=6$, find the distance between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Direction vector perpendicular to normal [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}2\\a\\1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}=6-a+2=0$ [A1] $a=8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Substitute a point of $l$, e.g. $(1,2,-1)$ [M1] $b=3-2-2=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The distance is that of any point of $l$ to $\Pi$, e.g. $(1,2,-1)$ [M1] $\dfrac{|3-2-2-6|}{\sqrt{14}}=\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{14}}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A line parallel to a plane has a direction vector perpendicular to the plane's normal, and every point on it is the same distance from the plane.

subtopic: Compound angle formula with exact values
statement: (a) By writing $\dfrac{\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, show that $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$. [3] (b) Write down the exact value of $\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$. [1] (c) Given that $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}$, find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$, giving your answer in the form $a+\sqrt b$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\left(\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi4\right)=\cos\dfrac\pi3\cos\dfrac\pi4+\sin\dfrac\pi3\sin\dfrac\pi4$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt2+\sqrt6}{4}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)=\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}$ [M1] Multiply by $\sqrt6+\sqrt2$: $\dfrac{(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)^2}{4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{8+4\sqrt3}{4}=2+\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\cos(A-B)=\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B$ with angles whose exact values you know. Rationalize the denominator to reach the requested form.

subtopic: Double angle formulae with a given sine
statement: The angle $\theta$ satisfies $\sin\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}$ and $\dfrac\pi2<\theta<\pi$. (a) Find the value of $\cos\theta$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\sin2\theta$. [2] (c) Find the value of $\cos2\theta$. [2] (d) Hence find the value of $\tan2\theta$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\cos^2\theta=1-\dfrac{25}{169}=\dfrac{144}{169}$ [M1] $\theta$ is obtuse so $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ [M1] $=2\cdot\dfrac{5}{13}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{12}{13}\right)=-\dfrac{120}{169}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$ [M1] $=1-\dfrac{50}{169}=\dfrac{119}{169}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\tan2\theta=\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{\cos2\theta}=-\dfrac{120}{119}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the quadrant to decide the sign of $\cos\theta$. Choose the form of $\cos2\theta$ that uses information you already have.

subtopic: Quadratic equation in sine using the Pythagorean identity
statement: Solve the equation $2\cos^2x+3\sin x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [6]
markscheme: Use $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $2(1-\sin^2x)+3\sin x=3$ [M1] $2\sin^2x-3\sin x+1=0$ [A1] $(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-1)=0$ [M1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$ or $\sin x=1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Convert to a single trigonometric function, treat the result as a quadratic and factorize. Remember that sine takes each positive value twice in $[0,2\pi]$.

subtopic: Equation involving tan of a double angle
statement: Solve the equation $\tan2x=3\tan x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [6]
markscheme: $\dfrac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2x}=3\tan x$ [M1] Let $t=\tan x$: $2t=3t(1-t^2)$ [A1] $t(3t^2-1)=0$ [M1] $t=0$ gives $x=0,\ \pi$ [A1] $t=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] ($x=\dfrac\pi2$ is not a solution since $\tan x$ is undefined) [6 marks]
tips: Never divide by $\tan x$: factorize instead, so you do not lose the solution $\tan x=0$. Check the end points of the interval.

subtopic: Proving an identity and using it
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}\equiv\tan x$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}=\sqrt3$ for $0<x<\pi$. [2] (c) Hence find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac\pi8$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$ [M1] $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$ [M1] $\dfrac{2\sin^2x}{2\sin x\cos x}=\tan x$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan x=\sqrt3$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Let $x=\dfrac\pi8$: $\tan\dfrac\pi8=\dfrac{1-\cos\frac\pi4}{\sin\frac\pi4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}=\dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt2-1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Start from the more complicated side and use $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$. For part (c) choose $x$ so that $2x$ is a standard angle.

subtopic: Harmonic form R sin(x + alpha)
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt3\sin x+\cos x$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $R\sin(x+\alpha)$, where $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. [3] (b) Hence solve $f(x)=\sqrt2$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [3] (c) Write down the greatest value of $f(x)$ and the smallest positive value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) $R\sin x\cos\alpha+R\cos x\sin\alpha$, so $R\cos\alpha=\sqrt3$ and $R\sin\alpha=1$ [M1] $R=2$ [A1] $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi6\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [M1] $x+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi4$ or $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ or $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Greatest value $2$ [A1] $x+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi2$, so $x=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Compare coefficients of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ to find $R$ and $\alpha$. When solving, convert the range for $x$ to the range for $x+\alpha$.

subtopic: Inverse trigonometric functions
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\arccos\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)$. [2] (b) Solve the equation $\arcsin x=\arccos(2x)$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [M1] $\arccos\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ (the principal value lies in $[0,\pi]$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $\theta=\arcsin x=\arccos2x$, so $\sin\theta=x$, $\cos\theta=2x$ [M1] $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$: $5x^2=1$ [M1] $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ [A1] $\theta=\arcsin x\in\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ and $\theta=\arccos2x\in[0,\pi]$, so $\theta\in\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ and $x\ge0$ [R1] $x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Remember the ranges: $\arcsin\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ and $\arccos\in[0,\pi]$. Squaring can introduce extra solutions, so always check the sign against the ranges.

subtopic: Reciprocal trigonometric ratios
statement: The angle $\theta$ satisfies $\sec\theta=-3$ and $\dfrac\pi2<\theta<\pi$. (a) Find the exact value of $\sin\theta$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\cot\theta$. [2] (c) Solve $\operatorname{cosec}x=2$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\theta=-\dfrac13$ [A1] $\sin^2\theta=1-\dfrac19=\dfrac89$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cot\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{-1/3}{2\sqrt2/3}=-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite every reciprocal function in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$ first. In the second quadrant sine is positive and cosine is negative.

subtopic: Tidal depth model
statement: The depth of water in a harbor, $d$ meters, is modeled by $d(t)=6+2.5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6.2}\right)$, where $t$ is the time in hours after a high tide. (a) Write down the maximum depth, the minimum depth and the period of the model. [3] (b) Boats can enter the harbor when $d\ge7.5$. Find the values of $t$ in the interval $0\le t\le12.4$ for which $d=7.5$. [3] (c) Find the total length of time in one cycle, beginning at a high tide, for which the depth is at least $7.5$ m. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $8.5$ m [A1] Minimum $3.5$ m [A1] Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6.2}=12.4$ hours [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6.2}\right)=0.6$ [M1] $t=1.83$ [A1] $t=12.4-1.83=10.6$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The depth is at least $7.5$ for $0\le t\le1.83$ and $10.57\le t\le12.4$ [M1] Total $=2\times1.83=3.66$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the GDC or exact inverse cosine, in radian mode. By the symmetry of the cosine curve, the second crossing in a cycle is $12.4-t_1$.

subtopic: Determining a cosine model from its graph features
statement: The function $f(x)=p\cos(qx)+r$, where $p,q>0$, has maximum value $9$ at $x=0$, minimum value $-1$ and period $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. (a) Find the values of $p$, $q$ and $r$. [4] (b) Solve $f(x)=4$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Attempt to use $\dfrac{\max-\min}{2}$ [M1] $p=5$ [A1] $r=4$ [A1] $q=\dfrac{2\pi}{2\pi/3}=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $5\cos3x=0$ [M1] $3x=\dfrac\pi2$ or $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6$ or $\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum, and the midline value is their mean. Convert the interval for $x$ to the interval for $3x$.

subtopic: Mixed trigonometric equation solved on a calculator
statement: (a) Solve $3\cos x=2\sin2x+1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [4] (b) Hence write down the solutions of the equation in the interval $2\pi\le x\le4\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Attempt to solve graphically or with GDC, e.g. intersection of $y=3\cos x$ and $y=2\sin2x+1$ [M1] Both intersections found in the interval [A1] $x=0.486$ [A1] $x=4.86$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Add $2\pi$ to each solution [M1] $x=6.77$, $x=11.1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch both sides on your GDC over the whole interval so that no intersections are missed. Solutions repeat every period of $2\pi$.

subtopic: Compound angle: tan(A+B) and sin(A+B)
statement: The angles $A$ and $B$ are both acute with $\tan A=2$ and $\tan B=3$. (a) Find the exact value of $\tan(A+B)$. [2] (b) Find the exact value of $\sin(A+B)$. [3] (c) Hence find the value of $A+B$ in radians, giving your answer as a multiple of $\pi$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{5}{1-6}=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sin A=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$, $\cos A=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ [A1] $\sin B=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$, $\cos B=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$ [A1] $\sin(A+B)=\dfrac{2\cdot1+1\cdot3}{\sqrt{50}}=\dfrac{5}{5\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0<A+B<\pi$ and $\tan(A+B)=-1$ gives $A+B=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Build right-angled triangles from $\tan A$ and $\tan B$ to read off the sine and cosine. The sign of $\tan(A+B)$ and the range for the sum determine the angle.

subtopic: Triple angle identity and its consequences
statement: (a) Show that $\cos3x\equiv4\cos^3x-3\cos x$. [3] (b) Solve $\cos3x=\dfrac12$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [3] (c) Hence show that $\cos\dfrac\pi9$, $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{9}$ and $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{9}$ are the roots of the equation $8c^3-6c-1=0$. [2] (d) Hence find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac\pi9\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{9}\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{9}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos3x=\cos(2x+x)=\cos2x\cos x-\sin2x\sin x$ [M1] $=(2\cos^2x-1)\cos x-2\sin^2x\cos x$ [M1] $=2\cos^3x-\cos x-2\cos x(1-\cos^2x)=4\cos^3x-3\cos x$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0\le3x\le3\pi$, so $3x=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3}$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi9$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{9}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{9}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) From (a), $\cos3x=\dfrac12$ becomes $4c^3-3c=\dfrac12$ where $c=\cos x$ [M1] $8c^3-6c-1=0$; the three values of $x$ in (b) have distinct cosines on $[0,\pi]$, so they give three distinct roots of this cubic [A1] [2 marks] (d) Product of roots of $8c^3-6c-1=0$ is $-\dfrac{-1}{8}$ [M1] $=\dfrac18$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expand $\cos(2x+x)$ and use double angle formulae to write everything in terms of $\cos x$. Part (d) uses the relationship between the roots and coefficients of a cubic.

subtopic: Identity with sec squared
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta}\equiv2\sec^2\theta$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta}=8$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Common denominator: $\dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)+(1-\sin\theta)}{(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2\theta}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta}=2\sec^2\theta$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2\sec^2\theta=8$, so $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac14$ [M1] $\theta=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1] $\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The product $(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)$ is a difference of two squares. Remember that $\cos^2\theta=\tfrac14$ gives both $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$ and $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$.

subtopic: Equation with cot and cosec
statement: Solve $3\cot^2x-5\operatorname{cosec}x+1=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [7]
markscheme: Use $\cot^2x=\operatorname{cosec}^2x-1$ [M1] $3\operatorname{cosec}^2x-5\operatorname{cosec}x-2=0$ [A1] $(3\operatorname{cosec}x+1)(\operatorname{cosec}x-2)=0$ [M1] $\operatorname{cosec}x=2$ or $-\dfrac13$ [A1] Reject $-\dfrac13$ since $|\operatorname{cosec}x|\ge1$ [R1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$, so $x=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [7 marks]
tips: Use $1+\cot^2x=\operatorname{cosec}^2x$ to make an equation in one function. Check that each root lies in the range of the function.

subtopic: Harmonic form with radians on a calculator
statement: Let $f(t)=5\sin t+12\cos t$. (a) Write $f(t)$ in the form $R\sin(t+\alpha)$, where $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$, giving $\alpha$ in radians to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Solve $f(t)=8$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$. [3] (c) Find the greatest value of $f(t)$ and the smallest non-negative value of $t$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) $R\cos\alpha=5$, $R\sin\alpha=12$ [M1] $R=13$ [A1] $\alpha=\arctan\dfrac{12}{5}=1.18$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sin(t+1.176)=\dfrac{8}{13}$ [M1] $t=1.30$ [A1] $t=5.77$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Greatest value $13$ [A1] $t+1.176=\dfrac\pi2$, $t=0.395$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use radian mode. For part (b) the range for $t+\alpha$ is $[\alpha,2\pi+\alpha]$, so look for a second solution using $\pi-\arcsin\frac{8}{13}$ and one in the next cycle.

subtopic: Completing the square and exact roots
statement: Let $f(x)=2x^2-12x+7$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $a(x-h)^2+k$. [2] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)=0$, giving your answers in exact form. [2]
tips: When completing the square, take the factor $a$ out of the $x^2$ and $x$ terms only. Check by expanding your vertex form.

subtopic: Discriminant: tangent line and intersections
statement: Consider the curve $C:\ y=x^2-4x+7$. (a) The line $y=2x+k$ is a tangent to $C$. Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the set of values of $m$ for which the line $y=mx$ intersects $C$ at two distinct points. [4]
tips: A tangent corresponds to a repeated root, that is a zero discriminant. Two distinct intersections need a positive discriminant, which for a squared expression gives two separate inequalities.

subtopic: Sum and product of roots
statement: The roots of the equation $2x^2-7x+4=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$. [2] (c) Find the value of $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta$. [2] (d) Find a quadratic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=\dfrac72$ [A1] $\alpha\beta=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=\dfrac{49}{4}-4=\dfrac{33}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{7}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Sum $\dfrac{33}{4}$ [A1] Product $(\alpha\beta)^2=4$ [A1] $x^2-\dfrac{33}{4}x+4=0$, so $4x^2-33x+16=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Express each required quantity in terms of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ without solving the quadratic.

subtopic: Projectile height model
statement: A ball is thrown upward from a point above the ground. Its height $h$ meters above the ground, $t$ seconds after it is thrown, is modeled by $h(t)=-4.9t^2+12t+1.5$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Write down the height from which the ball is thrown. [1] (b) Find the maximum height of the ball and the time at which it is reached. [3] (c) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2] (d) Find the length of time for which the ball is higher than $6$ m above the ground. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1.5$ m [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of vertex formula or GDC maximum [M1] $t=\dfrac{-12}{2(-4.9)}=1.22$ s [A1] $h=8.85$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $h(t)=0$ [M1] $t=2.57$ s [A1] [2 marks] (d) $-4.9t^2+12t+1.5=6$ [M1] $t=0.462$ and $t=1.99$ [A1] Duration $=1.52$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Reject the negative root of $h(t)=0$ because $t\ge0$. For heights above a given level, find both crossing times and subtract.

subtopic: Quadratic from roots and a point; inequality
statement: The graph of the quadratic function $f$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-1$ and $x=4$, and passes through the point $(2,12)$. (a) Find $f(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)>6$. [3]
tips: With known roots, use the factored form $a(x-p)(x-q)$. The axis of symmetry lies midway between the roots.

subtopic: Roots in a given ratio
statement: The equation $2x^2-kx+9=0$, where $k\in\mathbb R$, has two real roots, one of which is twice the other. (a) Find the possible values of $k$. [6] (b) For the positive value of $k$, solve the equation. [2]
markscheme: (a) Roots $\alpha$ and $2\alpha$ [M1] Sum: $3\alpha=\dfrac k2$ [A1] Product: $2\alpha^2=\dfrac92$ [A1] $\alpha=\pm\dfrac32$ [M1] $k=6\alpha$, so $k=9$ [A1] or $k=-9$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $2x^2-9x+9=(2x-3)(x-3)=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac32$ or $x=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $2\alpha$ and use both the sum and product of roots. Do not forget the negative case.

subtopic: Pearson correlation and regression line
statement: A gardener measures the height, $y$ cm, of a seedling at $x$ weeks after planting. The results are given in the table. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 2 & 4 & 5 & 7 & 8 & 10 \\ \hline y & 14 & 19 & 23 & 27 & 33 & 36 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Use your graphic display calculator to find the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient of the regression line in this context. [1] (d) Use your regression line to estimate the height of the seedling after 9 weeks. [1] (e) The gardener uses the regression line to predict the height after 40 weeks. Give one reason why this prediction is unreliable. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC to find $r$ [M1] $r=0.991$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC for linear regression of $y$ on $x$ [M1] $y=2.86x+8.19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) On average the height increases by $2.86$ cm each week [A1] [1 mark] (d) $y=2.857\times 9+8.190=33.9$ cm [A1] Follow through from their equation. [1 mark] (e) $x=40$ lies far outside the range of the data ($2\le x\le 10$), so this is extrapolation and the linear model may not hold [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Give the gradient a units-and-context interpretation (cm per week), not just a number. Any prediction outside the range of the data is extrapolation and should be flagged as unreliable.

subtopic: Regression line from summary statistics
statement: For a set of paired data $(x,y)$, the following summary statistics are known: $\bar x=12$, $\bar y=30$, $s_x=4$, $s_y=10$ and the covariance $s_{xy}=24$. (a) Find the value of the product-moment correlation coefficient $r$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, giving your answer in the form $y=ax+b$. [3] (c) Use your equation to estimate the value of $y$ when $x=16$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=\dfrac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{24}{4\times10}=0.6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}=\dfrac{24}{16}$ [M1] $=1.5$ [A1] Line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $y-30=1.5(x-12)$, so $y=1.5x+12$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=1.5(16)+12=36$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ always passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so you only need the gradient $s_{xy}/s_x^2$. Be careful to use the variance $s_x^2$, not $s_x$, in the denominator.

subtopic: Effect of linear transformations on regression and r
statement: For a set of paired data $(x,y)$, the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=2.5x-3$ and the correlation coefficient is $r=0.8$. A new variable is defined by $w=4y+1$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $w$ on $x$. [2] (b) Write down the correlation coefficient between $w$ and $x$. [1] (c) A third variable is defined by $v=-y$. Write down the correlation coefficient between $v$ and $x$. [1] (d) Write down the equation of the regression line of $v$ on $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Substitute $y=2.5x-3$ into $w=4y+1$ [M1] $w=4(2.5x-3)+1=10x-11$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $r=0.8$ (a positive linear transformation does not change $r$) [A1] [1 mark] (c) $r=-0.8$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $v=-(2.5x-3)=-2.5x+3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Linear changes of variable can be applied directly to the regression equation. Multiplying one variable by a negative number reverses the sign of $r$ but not its magnitude.

subtopic: Effect of an outlier on r and regression
statement: The following table gives the number of hours, $x$, a student spent revising and the score, $y$, on a short quiz for eight students. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline y & 3.1 & 4.2 & 5.8 & 6.1 & 8.3 & 9.2 & 10.1 & 2.0 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient for all eight students. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for all eight students. [2] The student with $x=8$ was ill during the quiz. This point is removed from the data. (c) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient for the remaining seven students. [2] (d) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for the remaining seven students. [2] (e) State, with a reason, which of the two regression lines is more suitable for predicting the score of a typical student who revises for 5.5 hours. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of GDC [M1] $r=0.341$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=0.407x+4.27$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Use of GDC on seven points [M1] $r=0.992$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Use of GDC [M1] $y=1.20x+1.90$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) The second line (seven students), since the point $(8,2.0)$ is an outlier caused by illness and distorts the first line [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A single unusual point can change both $r$ and the regression line dramatically. Always justify the decision to exclude data with a reason from the context, not just because it improves the fit.

subtopic: Using the mean point to find a missing value
statement: Five data pairs $(x,y)$ are given in the table, where $k$ is a constant. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline y & 4 & 6 & k & 9 & 12 \\ \hline \end{array}$ The regression line of $y$ on $x$ for these data is $y=1.9x+1.5$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Given that $\sum (x-\bar x)^2=10$, find the value of $\sum (x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)$. [2] (c) Find the residual for the data pair with $x=4$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=3$ [A1] Regression line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $\bar y=1.9(3)+1.5=7.2$ [M1] $\dfrac{4+6+k+9+12}{5}=7.2$, so $31+k=36$ and $k=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)}{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}$ [M1] $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=1.9\times10=19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Predicted $y=1.9(4)+1.5=9.1$; residual $=9-9.1=-0.1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the fact that the regression line passes through the mean point to turn a missing-value problem into a linear equation. A residual is observed minus predicted, so check the sign.

subtopic: Interpreting correlation and causation
statement: A study of 40 towns finds that the monthly ice-cream sales, $x$, and the number of sunburn cases treated at local clinics, $y$, have a product-moment correlation coefficient of $r=0.87$. (a) Describe the correlation between $x$ and $y$. [2] (b) A newspaper claims that eating ice cream causes sunburn. Comment on this claim. [2] (c) Every sales amount is converted from dollars to cents. Write down the new value of $r$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Strong [A1] positive (linear) correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) Correlation does not imply causation [R1] A likely explanation is a third variable, e.g. hot sunny weather, which increases both ice-cream sales and sunburn [R1] [2 marks] (c) $r=0.87$ (unchanged by a linear change of units) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Describe correlation with both a strength word and a direction word. In 'comment' questions, naming a plausible lurking variable earns the second mark.

subtopic: Residuals and prediction
statement: A trainee completes a daily practice test. The following table gives the number of daily practice sessions completed, $x$, and the test score, $y$, for eight trainees. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline y & 52 & 57 & 65 & 66 & 74 & 79 & 83 & 90 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient. [1] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Calculate the residual for the trainee with $x=3$. [2] (d) Estimate the score of a trainee who completes 10 practice sessions. Give your answer to the nearest integer. [1] (e) Interpret the value of the $y$-intercept of the regression line. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.995$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=5.31x+46.9$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Predicted score $=46.857+5.3095(3)=62.786$ [M1] Residual $=65-62.786=2.21$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=46.857+53.095=99.95\approx100$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) The predicted score for a trainee who completes no sessions is about 46.9 [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A residual is the observed value minus the value predicted by the line. Use unrounded regression coefficients stored in your calculator to avoid rounding errors in later parts.

subtopic: Regression from sums and sums of squares
statement: A sample of $n=8$ data pairs $(x,y)$ has the following summary values: $$\sum x=40,\quad \sum y=56,\quad \sum x^2=240,\quad \sum y^2=414.5,\quad \sum xy=304.$$ (a) Find $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ and $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)$. [2] (b) Given that $\sum(y-\bar y)^2=22.5$, find the product-moment correlation coefficient $r$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3]
tips: Rewrite sums of squares and products as deviations using $\sum x^2-\frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}$ and $\sum xy-\frac{\sum x\sum y}{n}$. Choose exact fractions rather than decimals to keep Paper 1 arithmetic clean.

subtopic: Linearizing an exponential model with logarithms
statement: The population $y$ (in thousands) of a bacterial colony is modeled by $y=ab^x$, where $x$ is the time in hours and $a,b>0$. A regression of $\ln y$ on $x$ gives the line $\ln y=1.2+0.4x$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$, giving your answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Use the model to estimate the population after 5 hours. [2] (c) Use the model to find the time at which the population first reaches 100 thousand. [2]
tips: When a regression is carried out on $\ln y$ versus $x$, undo the logarithm by exponentiating: the intercept gives $\ln a$ and the gradient gives $\ln b$. Keep full accuracy until the final rounding.

subtopic: Residual patterns and model suitability
statement: A scientist records the values of $x$ and $y$ given in the table. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 \\ \hline y & 2 & 5 & 10 & 17 & 26 & 37 & 50 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient. [1] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Calculate the residuals for $x=1$, $x=4$ and $x=7$. [3] (d) The residuals for all seven points follow the pattern positive, zero, negative, negative, negative, zero, positive. Explain why, in spite of the value of $r$, a linear model is not suitable for these data. [2] (e) The scientist instead uses the model $y=x^2+1$. Use this model to predict $y$ when $x=8$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.977$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=8x-11$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=1$: $2-(8-11)=5$ [A1] $x=4$: $17-(32-11)=-4$ [A1] $x=7$: $50-(56-11)=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The residuals show a systematic (curved, U-shaped) pattern rather than random scatter [R1] so the relationship is non-linear, even though $r$ is close to 1 [R1] [2 marks] (e) $y=8^2+1=65$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A value of $r$ close to 1 only shows a strong linear association; it does not prove that a straight line is the best model. A systematic pattern in the residuals indicates that a different model is needed.

subtopic: Interpreting a regression equation
statement: The regression line of the final exam score $y$ (in percent) on the number of hours $x$ of weekly study is $y=4.5x+32$, based on data with $2\le x\le 10$. The mean number of hours studied is $\bar x=8$. (a) Interpret the value $4.5$ in this context. [1] (b) Estimate the score of a student who studies 6 hours per week. [1] (c) Find the mean exam score $\bar y$. [1] (d) Explain why the model should not be used to predict the score of a student who studies 20 hours per week. [2]
markscheme: (a) Each extra hour of weekly study is associated with an average increase of $4.5$ percentage points in the score [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y=4.5(6)+32=59$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) The line passes through the mean point: $\bar y=4.5(8)+32=68$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $x=20$ is outside the range of the data (extrapolation) [R1] and the model would predict a score of 122, which is impossible (greater than 100) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: State what the gradient means in terms of the original variables, not just as a number. Checking whether a prediction is physically possible is a quick way to show a model has failed.

subtopic: Sum of squared residuals and least squares
statement: Three data points are $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,7)$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for these three points. [3] (b) Find the residual for each of the three points. [2] (c) Another student proposes the line $y=2x$. Find the sum of the squares of the residuals for this line and show that it is greater than the sum of the squares of the residuals for the regression line. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=2,\ \bar y=4$ [A1] $\sum(x-\bar x)^2=2$ and $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=(-1)(-2)+0+(1)(3)=5$ [M1] Gradient $=2.5$, so $y-4=2.5(x-2)$, i.e. $y=2.5x-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Predicted values $1.5,\ 4,\ 6.5$ [M1] Residuals: $0.5,\ -1,\ 0.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) For $y=2x$ the residuals are $2-2=0,\ 3-4=-1,\ 7-6=1$, so the sum of squares is $0+1+1=2$ [A1] For the regression line the sum of squares is $0.25+1+0.25=1.5<2$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The regression line is the line that minimizes the sum of the squared residuals, so any other line gives a larger total. Show every residual calculation clearly because a sign error is easy to make.

subtopic: Adding the mean point to a data set
statement: A sample of $n=10$ data pairs $(x,y)$ has $\bar x=4$, $\bar y=11$, $\sum(x-\bar x)^2=50$, $\sum(y-\bar y)^2=220$ and $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=100$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (b) Find the exact value of the product-moment correlation coefficient $r$. [2] An eleventh data pair $(4,11)$ is added to the sample. (c) Explain why neither the regression line nor $r$ changes. [2]
markscheme: (a) Gradient $=\dfrac{100}{50}=2$ [A1] $y-11=2(x-4)$, so $y=2x+3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $r=\dfrac{100}{\sqrt{50\times220}}=\dfrac{100}{\sqrt{11000}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{110}}\left(=\dfrac{\sqrt{110}}{11}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The new point is $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so the means are unchanged and its deviations are $0$ [R1] so each of the three sums $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$, $\sum(y-\bar y)^2$, $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)$ is unchanged, hence the gradient, the line and $r$ are unchanged [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Express $r$ and the gradient entirely in terms of the three deviation sums; adding a point at the mean contributes zero to each. Simplify $\sqrt{11000}$ by factoring out perfect squares.

subtopic: Regression for a demand model
statement: A shop records the price $x$ (in dollars) of a product and the number of items sold per day, $y$. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 & 10 \\ \hline y & 90 & 82 & 75 & 71 & 60 & 52 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the product-moment correlation coefficient and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Estimate the number of items sold per day when the price is $\$7.50$. Give your answer to the nearest integer. [2] (d) The regression line predicts that sales fall to zero at a certain price. Find this price, and comment on the reliability of this estimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=-0.994$ [A1] Very strong negative (linear) correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $y=-7.43x+127$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=127.381-7.4286(7.5)$ [M1] $=71.67\approx72$ items [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0=127.381-7.4286x$ gives $x=17.1$ dollars [A1] This is far outside the data range ($5\le x\le10$), so it is extrapolation and unreliable [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Remember that part (c) is interpolation, so it is reliable, whereas solving for zero sales requires extrapolation. Round to the integer only at the end because the number of items must be whole.

subtopic: Union, intersection and independence
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.7$. (a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2] (c) Find $P(A\mid B')$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1] $0.7=0.9-P(A\cap B)$, so $P(A\cap B)=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A)P(B)=0.4\times0.5=0.2$ [M1] This equals $P(A\cap B)$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(A\mid B')=\dfrac{P(A\cap B')}{P(B')}=\dfrac{0.4-0.2}{0.5}=0.4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: To test independence, compare $P(A\cap B)$ with $P(A)P(B)$ and state the conclusion explicitly. Use $P(A\cap B')=P(A)-P(A\cap B)$ for conditional probabilities involving a complement.

subtopic: Selection without replacement
statement: A bag contains 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random from the bag, one after the other, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that the two balls are the same color. [3] (b) Given that the two balls are the same color, find the probability that both are red. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(RR)=\dfrac58\times\dfrac47=\dfrac{20}{56}$ [A1] $P(BB)=\dfrac38\times\dfrac27=\dfrac{6}{56}$ [A1] $P(\text{same})=\dfrac{26}{56}=\dfrac{13}{28}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(RR\mid\text{same})=\dfrac{P(RR)}{P(\text{same})}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{20/56}{26/56}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{10}{13}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For draws without replacement, the second probability has both a reduced numerator and denominator. In conditional problems, write the formula first and then substitute the values you found earlier.

subtopic: Total probability and Bayes' theorem
statement: A factory has two machines, $A$ and $B$. Machine $A$ produces 60% of the items and machine $B$ produces the remaining 40%. Of the items produced by $A$, 3% are defective. Of the items produced by $B$, 5% are defective. An item is selected at random. (a) Find the probability that the item is defective. [3] (b) Given that the item is defective, find the probability that it was produced by machine $A$. [3]
tips: Draw a quick tree diagram: multiply along branches, add the branches that end in 'defective', and then divide for the reversed conditional probability. Give an exact fraction in Paper 1.

subtopic: Bayes' theorem with a medical test
statement: A disease affects 2% of a population. A test for the disease gives a positive result for 95% of people who have the disease and also gives a positive result for 10% of people who do not have the disease. A person is chosen at random from the population. (a) Find the probability that the person tests positive. [3] (b) Given that the person tests positive, find the probability that the person has the disease. [2] Suppose that a person takes the test twice, and that the results of the two tests are independent, given the person's disease status. (c) Given that both tests are positive, find the probability that the person has the disease. [3]
tips: When the base rate is low, even an accurate-looking test can give a small posterior probability. For two independent tests, square the test probabilities within each branch before applying Bayes.

subtopic: Two-set Venn diagram counts
statement: In a class of 40 students, 22 study French, 18 study Spanish and 7 study both languages. A student is chosen at random from the class. (a) Find the probability that the student studies neither language. [2] (b) Given that the student studies Spanish, find the probability that the student also studies French. [2] (c) Find the probability that the student studies exactly one of the two languages. [2]
markscheme: (a) Number studying at least one language $=22+18-7=33$ [M1] $P(\text{neither})=\dfrac{7}{40}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(F\mid S)=\dfrac{7}{18}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Only French $=15$, only Spanish $=11$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{26}{40}=\dfrac{13}{20}$ [A1] [2 marks]
