tips: Fill in the overlap first when building a Venn diagram, then subtract it from each set total. 'Given that' restricts the sample space to one set only.

subtopic: Independent events leading to a quadratic
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(B)=p$ and $P(A)=2p$, where $0<p<\frac12$. It is given that $P(A\cup B)=0.52$. (a) Show that $2p^2-3p+0.52=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the value of $p$. [4] (c) Find $P(A'\mid B)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=2p^2$ [M1] $P(A\cup B)=2p+p-2p^2=0.52$, so $2p^2-3p+0.52=0$ [AG] [M1] [2 marks] (b) Attempt to solve the quadratic, e.g. using the quadratic formula [M1] $p=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{9-4.16}}{4}=\dfrac{3\pm2.2}{4}$ [A1] $p=0.2$ or $p=1.3$ [A1] Since $p<\tfrac12$, reject $1.3$, so $p=0.2$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $A'$ and $B$ are independent, so $P(A'\mid B)=P(A')=1-0.4=0.6$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Independence gives $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$; substituting into the addition rule produces a quadratic in $p$. Always check each root against the stated restriction on the parameter.

subtopic: Sample space for two dice
statement: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled and the sum of the two numbers is recorded. (a) Find the probability that the sum is a prime number. [2] (b) Given that at least one of the dice shows a 6, find the probability that the sum is a prime number. [3]
markscheme: (a) Number of ways: sum 2 (1), 3 (2), 5 (4), 7 (6), 11 (2) gives $15$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{15}{36}=\dfrac{5}{12}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Outcomes with at least one 6: $11$ [A1] Of these the prime sums are $(6,1),(1,6),(6,5),(5,6)$, so $4$ [A1] $P=\dfrac{4}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: List the sample space systematically when it has only 36 outcomes. For a conditional probability, count favorable outcomes inside the reduced sample space, not the original one.

subtopic: Infinite geometric series in a game
statement: Anna and Ben take turns rolling a fair six-sided die, with Anna rolling first. The first person to roll a six wins the game. (a) Find the probability that Anna wins on her first roll. [1] (b) Find the probability that Anna wins on her second roll. [2] (c) Show that the probability that Anna wins the game is $\dfrac{6}{11}$. [3] (d) Write down the probability that Ben wins the game. [1] (e) Hence state whether the game is fair, giving a reason. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac16$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Anna, Ben and Anna's first roll all fail, then she rolls a six: $\left(\dfrac56\right)^2\times\dfrac16=\dfrac{25}{216}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(A\text{ wins})=\dfrac16+\dfrac16\left(\dfrac{25}{36}\right)+\dfrac16\left(\dfrac{25}{36}\right)^2+\cdots$ [M1] geometric series with first term $\dfrac16$ and common ratio $\dfrac{25}{36}$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{1/6}{1-25/36}=\dfrac{1/6}{11/36}=\dfrac{6}{11}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (d) $1-\dfrac{6}{11}=\dfrac{5}{11}$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) Not fair, since $\dfrac{6}{11}\ne\dfrac{5}{11}$ (the first player has an advantage) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Games with alternating turns lead to an infinite geometric series whose ratio is the probability that both players fail in a round. Check that $|r|<1$ before using $S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}$.

subtopic: Probability using combinations
statement: A committee of 5 people is chosen at random from a group of 6 men and 4 women. (a) Find the probability that the committee has exactly 2 women. [2] (b) Find the probability that the committee has at least 2 women. [2] (c) Given that the committee has at least 2 women, find the probability that it has exactly 2 women. [2]
tips: For 'at least' questions, the complement is often faster than adding many cases. Use combinations for unordered selections and keep the same total number of outcomes in every part.

subtopic: Probability with a transferred item
statement: Urn $A$ contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Urn $B$ contains 2 red balls and 4 blue balls. One ball is chosen at random from urn $A$ and placed into urn $B$. A ball is then chosen at random from urn $B$. (a) Find the probability that the ball chosen from urn $B$ is red. [3] (b) Given that the ball chosen from urn $B$ is red, find the probability that the ball moved from urn $A$ was red. [3]
markscheme: (a) If a red ball is moved, urn $B$ has 3 red among 7 balls; if a blue ball is moved, urn $B$ has 2 red among 7 balls [M1] $P(\text{red from }B)=\dfrac35\times\dfrac37+\dfrac25\times\dfrac27$ [A1] $=\dfrac{9}{35}+\dfrac{4}{35}=\dfrac{13}{35}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(\text{moved red}\mid\text{red})=\dfrac{9/35}{13/35}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac{9}{13}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Condition on what was transferred, because the composition of the second urn depends on it. Then reverse the conditioning with Bayes' theorem using the same two branch products.

subtopic: Three events, independence and exclusivity
statement: Events $A$, $B$ and $C$ are such that $P(A)=0.5$, $P(B)=0.4$ and $P(C)=0.3$. Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, events $A$ and $C$ are independent, and events $B$ and $C$ are mutually exclusive. (a) Find (i) $P(A\cap B)$; (ii) $P(A\cap C)$; (iii) $P(B\cup C)$. [3] (b) Find $P(A\cup B\cup C)$. [3] (c) Find the probability that none of the events $A$, $B$, $C$ occurs. [1]
tips: Use the three-event inclusion-exclusion formula and decide which pairwise and triple intersections are zero. Mutually exclusive events have an empty intersection, so any larger intersection containing them is also empty.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities
statement: A survey of 200 people records their gender and their main way of traveling to work. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline & Bus & Bicycle & Walk \\ \hline Male & 30 & 25 & 45 \\ \hline Female & 40 & 35 & 25 \\ \hline \end{array}$ A person is chosen at random from the 200 people. (a) Find the probability that the person cycles to work. [1] (b) Given that the person walks to work, find the probability that the person is female. [2] (c) Find the probability that the person is male and does not walk to work. [2]
markscheme: (a) Total cycling $=60$, so $P=\dfrac{60}{200}=0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Total walking $=70$ [M1] $P(F\mid W)=\dfrac{25}{70}=\dfrac{5}{14}=0.357$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Males not walking $=30+25=55$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{55}{200}=0.275$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Add the row and column totals first so that every probability can be read from the table. For a 'given that' question, divide by the total of the condition's row or column.

subtopic: Discrete random variable: expectation and variance
statement: The discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution given by $P(X=x)=kx^2$ for $x\in\{1,2,3\}$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
tips: The probabilities must sum to 1, which gives an equation for $k$. For the variance use $E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ and keep fractions exact.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities with a calculator
statement: A basketball player scores a free throw with probability $0.35$ on each attempt, independently of other attempts. She takes 12 free throws. Let $X$ be the number of free throws scored. (a) Find $P(X=4)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le3)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge5)$. [1] (d) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim B(12,0.35)$ [M1] $P(X=4)=0.237$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\le3)=0.347$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)=0.417$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Mean $=12\times0.35=4.2$ [A1] Standard deviation $=\sqrt{12\times0.35\times0.65}=1.65$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: State the distribution, including $n$ and $p$, before using the calculator. For 'at least' use the complement: $P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)$.

subtopic: Binomial distribution with exact answers
statement: The random variable $X$ is binomially distributed with $n=4$ and $p=\dfrac13$. (a) Find $P(X=2)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge1)$. [2] (c) Find $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(X=2)=\binom42\left(\dfrac13\right)^2\left(\dfrac23\right)^2$ [M1] $=6\times\dfrac19\times\dfrac49=\dfrac{24}{81}=\dfrac{8}{27}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0)=1-\left(\dfrac23\right)^4$ [M1] $=1-\dfrac{16}{81}=\dfrac{65}{81}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X)=np=\dfrac43$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=\dfrac43\times\dfrac23=\dfrac89$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write out the binomial probability in full, including the coefficient $\binom{n}{r}$. 'At least one' almost always means $1-P(X=0)$.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The heights of adult women in a town are normally distributed with mean $172$ cm and standard deviation $6.5$ cm. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen woman has a height between $160$ cm and $180$ cm. [2] (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen woman is taller than $185$ cm. [1] (c) The tallest $10\%$ of women are at least $h$ cm tall. Find $h$, correct to the nearest cm. [2] (d) In a random sample of 200 women, find the expected number who are taller than $185$ cm. [2]
tips: Identify the distribution and the required probability before using the calculator; for inverse normal, make sure you are using the area to the left. Expected frequency is $n\times$ probability.

subtopic: Finding the mean and standard deviation of a normal variable
statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $P(X<30)=0.2$ and $P(X>48)=0.1$. (a) Write down two equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$ that are satisfied. [3] (b) Find the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$. [3] (c) Hence find $P(X>40)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z$-value for $0.2$ is $-0.8416$ [A1] and for $0.9$ is $1.2816$ [A1] $\dfrac{30-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.8416$ and $\dfrac{48-\mu}{\sigma}=1.2816$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Subtract the equations: $18=2.1232\sigma$ [M1] $\sigma=8.48$ [A1] $\mu=37.1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $P(X>40)=0.368$ [M1][A1] Accept $0.368$ from unrounded values. [2 marks]
tips: Convert each probability to a standardized value with the inverse normal function and form simultaneous equations. Take care that $P(X>48)=0.1$ corresponds to a left-tail area of $0.9$.

subtopic: Linear combinations of independent random variables
statement: The random variable $X$ has $E(X)=5$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=4$. (a) Let $Y=3X-2$. Find $E(Y)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. [2] Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be two independent observations of $X$. (b) Find $E(2X_1-X_2)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(2X_1-X_2)$. [3] (c) Find $E(X^2)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $E(Y)=3(5)-2=13$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3^2\times4=36$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(2X_1-X_2)=2(5)-5=5$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(2X_1-X_2)=2^2\operatorname{Var}(X_1)+(-1)^2\operatorname{Var}(X_2)$ [M1] $=16+4=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+[E(X)]^2=4+25=29$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The variance of a linear combination of independent variables uses the squares of the coefficients and ignores constants, so subtraction still adds variances. Rearrange $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ for $E(X^2)$.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a quadratic pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(4-x), & 0\le x\le4,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$ where $k$ is a constant. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac{3}{32}$. [3] (b) Write down $E(X)$, giving a reason for your answer. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $P(X<1)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^4 kx(4-x)\,dx=1$ [M1] $k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^4=k\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)=\dfrac{32k}{3}$ [A1] $\dfrac{32k}{3}=1$, so $k=\dfrac{3}{32}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $E(X)=2$ [A1] The pdf is symmetric about $x=2$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=\dfrac{3}{32}\displaystyle\int_0^4 x^3(4-x)\,dx=\dfrac{3}{32}\left[x^4-\dfrac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^4=\dfrac{3}{32}\times\dfrac{256}{5}=\dfrac{24}{5}$ [M1][A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\dfrac{24}{5}-4=\dfrac45$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\displaystyle P(X<1)=\dfrac{3}{32}\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{32}\times\dfrac53=\dfrac{5}{32}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrate the pdf over its whole domain and set it equal to 1 to find $k$. For the variance use $E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$, with $E(X^2)=\int x^2f(x)\,dx$.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a trigonometric pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=k\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Show that $k=1$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [3] (c) Find the exact value of the median of $X$. [3] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}k\sin x\,dx=k[-\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}$ [M1] $=k(0+1)=k=1$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}x\sin x\,dx$ [M1] Integration by parts or GDC: $[\sin x-x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}$ [A1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Median $m$: $\displaystyle\int_0^m\sin x\,dx=\dfrac12$ [M1] $1-\cos m=\dfrac12$, so $\cos m=\dfrac12$ [A1] $m=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $E(X^2)=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\sin x\,dx=\pi-2$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\pi-2-1=\pi-3=0.142$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The median $m$ satisfies $\int_{-\infty}^m f(x)\,dx=\tfrac12$. Use your calculator to check integrals by parts, but write the setup so that method marks are secure.

subtopic: Binomial: finding the smallest n
statement: A shop finds that each customer independently buys a particular item with probability $0.15$. (a) Find the probability that, of 10 customers, at least 2 buy the item. [2] (b) Find the smallest number of customers $n$ such that the probability that at least one buys the item is greater than $0.95$. [4] (c) Find the expected number of customers who buy the item out of 10 customers. [1]
tips: For 'smallest $n$' problems write the inequality with the complement and take logarithms, reversing the inequality when dividing by a negative number. Confirm by evaluating the probability for $n$ and $n-1$.

subtopic: Normal then binomial
statement: The masses of apples from an orchard are normally distributed with mean $150$ g and standard deviation $12$ g. An apple is classified as premium if its mass is greater than $165$ g. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen apple is premium. [2] A box contains 12 apples chosen at random. (b) Find the probability that the box contains at least 3 premium apples. [3] (c) The heaviest $5\%$ of apples are rejected as oversized. Find the least mass of a rejected apple. [2] (d) Find the expected number of premium apples in the box. [1]
markscheme: (a) $M\sim N(150,12^2)$ [M1] $P(M>165)=0.106$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $Y$ be the number of premium apples: $Y\sim B(12,0.10565)$ [M1] $P(Y\ge3)=1-P(Y\le2)$ [M1] $=0.126$ [A1] Use the unrounded value of $p$ from part (a); accept $0.127$ if $p=0.106$ was used. [3 marks] (c) $P(M>w)=0.05$, so $P(M<w)=0.95$ [M1] $w=169.7$ g [A1] Accept $170$. [2 marks] (d) $12\times0.10565=1.27$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Store the unrounded probability from the normal calculation and reuse it as the binomial parameter. Link the two distributions explicitly by writing $Y\sim B(12,p)$.

subtopic: Inverse normal to set a mean
statement: A machine fills bottles with water. The volume of water in a bottle, $V$ ml, is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $4$ ml. The machine is set so that $2\%$ of bottles contain less than $500$ ml. (a) Find the value of $\mu$, correct to one decimal place. [3] (b) Given that $\mu=508.2$, find the probability that a randomly chosen bottle contains more than $510$ ml. [2] (c) Five bottles are chosen at random. Find the probability that at least one contains less than $500$ ml. [2]
tips: Standardize using the inverse normal function so that $\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ equals the $z$-value from the tail area, then solve for the unknown. In part (c), use the exact probability $0.02$ from the stem.

subtopic: Expected value and fair price of a game
statement: A fairground game costs $c$ dollars to play. The prize $X$ (in dollars) is $10$ with probability $0.1$, $3$ with probability $0.3$, and $0$ otherwise. (a) Find $E(X)$. [2] (b) Find the value of $c$ for which the game is fair. [1] (c) The game is played 500 times at a cost of $\$2.50$ per play. Find the expected total profit for the organizer. [2] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $E(X)=10(0.1)+3(0.3)+0(0.6)$ [M1] $=1.9$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) A fair game has expected gain $0$, so $c=\$1.90$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Expected profit per play $=2.50-1.90=0.60$ [M1] Expected total profit $=500\times0.60=\$300$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $E(X^2)=100(0.1)+9(0.3)=12.7$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=12.7-1.9^2=9.09$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A game is fair when the expected net gain is zero, so the entry fee equals the expected prize. By linearity of expectation the expected profit over many plays is the number of plays times the expected profit per play.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from grouped data
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by 40 students to complete a puzzle are summarized in the table. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline Time t & 0\le t<10 & 10\le t<20 & 20\le t<30 & 30\le t<40 & 40\le t<50 \\ \hline Frequency & 4 & 9 & 15 & 8 & 4 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Estimate the mean time taken. [2] (b) Estimate the standard deviation of the times. [2] (c) Write down the modal class. [1] (d) Find the percentage of students who took less than 20 minutes. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of midpoints $5,15,25,35,45$ [M1] $\bar t=\dfrac{990}{40}=24.75$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC (or formula) with midpoints [M1] $\sigma=11.1$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) $20\le t<30$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{4+9}{40}=32.5\%$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For grouped data always use the class midpoints and state that the results are estimates. Enter the midpoints and frequencies as two lists in your calculator and read off $\bar x$ and $\sigma_x$.

subtopic: Unbiased estimates from summed data
statement: A random sample of 10 values $x_1,\dots,x_{10}$ is taken from a population. The sample satisfies $\sum x=120$ and $\sum x^2=1500$. (a) Find the sample mean. [1] (b) Find the variance of the sample, $\sigma_n^2$ (dividing by $n$). [2] (c) Hence find the unbiased estimate of the population variance, $s_{n-1}^2$. [2] (d) Write down the exact value of the corresponding unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [1]
tips: Use $\sigma_n^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ and then convert with the factor $\frac{n}{n-1}$. Remember that the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation is the square root of the unbiased variance.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: A data set has lower quartile $Q_1=34$ and upper quartile $Q_3=52$. The smallest value in the data set is $3$ and the largest is $91$. (a) Find the interquartile range. [1] (b) Find the values that separate outliers from non-outliers, using the rule that a value is an outlier if it is more than $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. [2] (c) State which of the smallest and largest values are outliers. [1] (d) The largest value is changed to an integer $k$. Find the smallest value of $k$ for which the largest value is an outlier. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\text{IQR}=52-34=18$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $1.5\times18=27$ [M1] Lower boundary $34-27=7$ and upper boundary $52+27=79$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $3<7$ and $91>79$, so both are outliers [A1] [1 mark] (d) $k>79$, so the smallest integer is $k=80$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Calculate both boundaries of the rule, not just the one you expect to matter. For a strict inequality, the smallest integer satisfying $k>79$ is $80$, not $79$.

subtopic: Box plot interpretation from summary values
statement: The ages of the 120 members of a sports club are summarized by the following: minimum $12$, lower quartile $18$, median $23$, upper quartile $31$ and maximum $52$. The largest age that is not an outlier is $47$. A box-and-whisker plot of the ages is to be drawn. (a) Find the interquartile range. [1] (b) Show that the maximum age of $52$ is an outlier. [2] (c) Write down the values at the two ends of the whiskers on the box plot. [1] (d) Describe the skewness of the distribution, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $31-18=13$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}=31+19.5=50.5$ [M1] $52>50.5$, so $52$ is an outlier [A1] [2 marks] (c) $12$ and $47$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Median to $Q_3$ is $8$, which is greater than $Q_1$ to median ($5$) [R1] so the distribution is positively skewed (skewed to the right) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The upper whisker ends at the largest value that is not an outlier, and outliers are plotted separately. Compare the lengths of the two halves of the box to describe skewness.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: A data set $x$ has mean $14$, standard deviation $3$, median $13$ and interquartile range $5$. A new data set is defined by $y=2x-4$ for each value. (a) Write down the mean and standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Write down the median and interquartile range of $y$. [2] (c) Write down the variance of $y$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Mean $=2(14)-4=24$ [A1] Standard deviation $=2\times3=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Median $=2(13)-4=22$ [A1] Interquartile range $=2\times5=10$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $6^2=36$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Measures of location (mean, median) change with both the multiplier and the constant, but measures of spread (standard deviation, IQR) are affected only by the multiplier. Variance is the square of the standard deviation.

subtopic: Combining the mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: Group $A$ has 20 students with a mean test score of $60$ and a standard deviation of $5$. Group $B$ has 30 students with a mean test score of $70$ and a standard deviation of $4$. (The standard deviations are population standard deviations, $\sigma_n$.) (a) Find the mean score of all 50 students. [2] (b) Find the standard deviation of the scores of all 50 students. [4]
tips: You cannot average two standard deviations; instead recover $\sum x^2$ for each group, add them, and recompute the variance about the combined mean. Use unrounded values throughout.

subtopic: Stratified and convenience sampling
statement: A school has 900 students: 300 in Year 9, 240 in Year 10, 210 in Year 11 and 150 in Year 12. A survey is to be given to a stratified random sample of 90 students, with strata based on year group. (a) Find the number of students from each year group in the sample. [3] A teacher suggests instead surveying the first 90 students to arrive at school on Monday. (b) State one disadvantage of this sampling method. [1] (c) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) Sampling fraction $=\dfrac{90}{900}=\dfrac{1}{10}$ [M1] Year 9: $30$, Year 10: $24$ [A1] Year 11: $21$, Year 12: $15$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Any one of: the sample is a convenience sample and is likely biased (e.g. early arrivals may be unrepresentative); not random; not all students have an equal chance of selection [A1] [1 mark] (c) Any one of: each year group is represented in proportion to its size; reduces sampling variability; guarantees every year group appears in the sample [A1] [1 mark]
tips: In stratified sampling each stratum is represented in proportion to its size in the population. When criticizing a sampling method, refer to bias or lack of randomness.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: The following table gives the number of goals scored by a team in a number of matches. The mean number of goals per match is $3$. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline Goals x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline Frequency & 4 & k & 7 & 5 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the median number of goals. [2] (c) Find the variance of the number of goals per match. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum f=18+k$ and $\sum fx=4+2k+21+20+10=55+2k$ [A1] $\dfrac{55+2k}{18+k}=3$ [M1] $55+2k=54+3k$, so $k=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $n=19$, so the median is the 10th value [M1] Cumulative frequencies $4,5,12,\dots$, so the 10th value is $3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sum fx^2=4+4+63+80+50=201$ [A1] $\sigma^2=\dfrac{201}{19}-9=\dfrac{30}{19}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the mean as $\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$ and solve the resulting linear equation for the unknown frequency. For an odd total frequency, the median is the middle value, found from cumulative frequencies.

subtopic: Correcting a recorded data set
statement: A set of 25 numbers was recorded with a mean of $14.2$ and a standard deviation of $3.1$ (the population standard deviation, $\sigma_n$). It was later discovered that a value of $12$ had been wrongly recorded as $21$. (a) Find the correct mean. [3] (b) Find the correct standard deviation. [4]
tips: To correct a data set, recover $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the stated mean and variance, subtract the incorrect value and add the correct one. Do not simply adjust the mean or standard deviation directly.

subtopic: Unbiased estimates from a sample
statement: A random sample of the masses, in kg, of eight packages is $12.1,\ 11.8,\ 12.6,\ 12.3,\ 11.9,\ 12.4,\ 12.0,\ 12.5$. (a) Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean. [1] (b) Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance. [2] (c) Explain why the sample variance obtained by dividing $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ by $n$ is not used as an estimate of the population variance. [2] (d) Find the median mass of the eight packages. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=12.2$ kg [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC to obtain $s_{n-1}$ (sample standard deviation with $n-1$) [M1] $s_{n-1}^2=0.0857$ (or $\dfrac{0.6}{7}$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Dividing by $n$ gives a biased estimator [R1] which on average underestimates the population variance; dividing by $n-1$ corrects this [R1] [2 marks] (d) Ordered values $11.8,11.9,12.0,12.1,12.3,12.4,12.5,12.6$; median $=\dfrac{12.1+12.3}{2}=12.2$ kg [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Make sure you read $s_{n-1}$ from the calculator, not $\sigma_n$. Square it to obtain the unbiased estimate of the variance.

subtopic: Quartiles and outliers from a frequency table
statement: The following table gives the number of siblings for each of 40 students. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline Siblings & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline Frequency & 6 & 12 & 10 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the median number of siblings. [1] (b) Find the lower quartile, the upper quartile and the interquartile range. [3] (c) Show that a student with 7 siblings would be an outlier. [2] (d) Find the mean number of siblings. [1]
markscheme: (a) Cumulative frequencies $6,18,28,35,38,40$; the median is the mean of the 20th and 21st values, both equal to $2$, so the median is $2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Lower quartile $=1$ (10th and 11th values) [A1] Upper quartile $=3$ (30th and 31st values) [A1] $\text{IQR}=3-1=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Upper boundary $=3+1.5\times2=6$ [M1] $7>6$, so 7 siblings is an outlier [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{0+12+20+21+12+10}{40}=\dfrac{75}{40}=1.875$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For quartiles from a frequency table, build the cumulative frequency column and locate the required positions in the ordered data. Use the 1.5 IQR rule with Q3 for upper outliers.

subtopic: Systematic sampling
statement: The register of a school lists its 1260 students in order, numbered from 1 to 1260. A systematic sample of 90 students is to be taken. The first student chosen is number 9. (a) Find the interval between consecutive students selected. [1] (b) Find the number of the 90th student selected. [2] (c) The register alternates between boys and girls. Explain why this sample could be biased. [1] (d) State one advantage of systematic sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1260}{90}=14$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Selected numbers are $9+14(k-1)$ [M1] 90th: $9+14\times89=1255$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) With an even interval of $14$, all selected students have the same parity of number, so they would all be of the same gender [R1] [1 mark] (d) Any one of: easier or quicker to carry out; no need for random number generation; sample spread evenly across the population [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Systematic sampling picks every $k$th item after a start; the $m$th item selected is the first plus $(m-1)k$. Watch for periodic patterns in the list that line up with the interval.

subtopic: Separable equation with an inverse tangent
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\left(1+y^2\right)$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (b) The graph of the solution has vertical asymptotes. Find the exact value of the smallest positive $x$-coordinate at which an asymptote occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Separating variables: $\int\dfrac{1}{1+y^2}\,dy=\int 2x\,dx$ [M1] $\arctan y=x^2+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $\dfrac{\pi}{4}=C$ [M1] $y=\tan\left(x^2+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $y$ is undefined when $x^2+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $x^2=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration until you have used the initial condition; it fixes the phase of the tangent. In part (b), the first asymptote comes from the first time the argument of the tangent reaches $\pi/2$.

subtopic: First-order linear equation with an integrating factor
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2}{x}y=x^2$, for $x>0$. (a) Find the integrating factor for this differential equation, simplifying your answer. [2] (b) Hence find the solution of the differential equation given that $y=2$ when $x=1$. Give your answer in the form $y=f(x)$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}=e^{2\ln x}$ [M1] $=x^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2y\right)=x^2\cdot x^2=x^4$ [M1] $x^2y=\dfrac{x^5}{5}+C$ [A1] Substituting $x=1,\ y=2$: $2=\dfrac15+C$, so $C=\dfrac95$ [M1] $y=\dfrac{x^5+9}{5x^2}$ [A1] Accept $y=\dfrac{x^3}{5}+\dfrac{9}{5x^2}$. [4 marks]
tips: Because $x>0$ you may write $e^{2\ln x}=x^2$ with no modulus signs. Multiply the whole equation by the integrating factor so that the left side becomes a single product derivative.

subtopic: Euler's method and exact solution comparison
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-y$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with a step size of $h=0.25$ to estimate the value of $y$ when $x=1$. Show each step of your working. [4] (b) The exact solution of the differential equation is $y=2x-2+3e^{-x}$. Show that this function satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition. [3] (c) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (a). [2]
tips: Keep several extra decimal places in the intermediate Euler values and round only at the end. For a percentage error, divide by the exact value, not by the estimate.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation using y = vx
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}$, for $x>0,\ y>0$, where $y=2$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{v}$. [3] (b) Hence solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $y=vx$ so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [A1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+v^2x^2}{x\cdot vx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{v}$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{v}-v=\dfrac{1}{v}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int v\,dv=\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$ [M1] $\dfrac{v^2}{2}=\ln x+C$ [A1] When $x=1$, $v=2$: $2=C$ [M1] $v^2=2\ln x+4$ [A1] $y=x\sqrt{2\ln x+4}$ (positive root since $y>0$) [A1] [5 marks]
tips: After the substitution the new equation must be separable; if $v$ and $x$ do not separate, recheck the algebra. Substitute back $v=y/x$ at the end and choose the sign of the root from the initial condition.

subtopic: Slope field described in words, isoclines and a particular solution
statement: Consider a slope field for the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x-2y$. At each point $(x,y)$ the short line segment has gradient equal to $x-2y$. (a) Find the gradient of the line segment at (i) the point $(2,1)$; (ii) the point $(0,3)$. [2] (b) Describe the set of points at which the line segments are horizontal. [2] (c) Show that $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14$ is a solution of the differential equation. [3] (d) Find the solution of the differential equation whose graph passes through the origin. Give your answer in the form $y=f(x)$. [5] (e) Write down the equation of the straight line to which the solution curve in part (d) gets closer and closer as $x\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) (i) $2-2(1)=0$ [A1] (ii) $0-2(3)=-6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Horizontal segments occur where $x-2y=0$ [M1] that is, at all points on the straight line $y=\dfrac{x}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) If $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac12$ [A1] $x-2y=x-x+\dfrac12=\dfrac12$ [M1] so the differential equation is satisfied for all $x$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) Write as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=x$; integrating factor $e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}$ [A1] $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x}y\right)=xe^{2x}$ [M1] Integration by parts: $\int xe^{2x}dx=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{2x}-\int\dfrac12e^{2x}dx$ [M1] $e^{2x}y=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{2x}-\dfrac14e^{2x}+C$ [A1] Using $y=0$ when $x=0$: $C=\dfrac14$, so $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14+\dfrac14e^{-2x}$ [A1] [5 marks] (e) $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Every segment is found by substituting coordinates into the right-hand side; no solving is needed. To test a proposed solution, differentiate it and substitute both $y$ and $y'$ into the equation.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling as a separable equation
statement: The temperature $T$ degrees Celsius of a cup of coffee $t$ minutes after it is poured satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $k>0$ is a constant and the room temperature is $20^\circ$C. When the coffee is poured, its temperature is $90^\circ$C. (a) By solving the differential equation, show that $T=20+70e^{-kt}$. [4] (b) After $10$ minutes the temperature of the coffee is $60^\circ$C. Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the coffee to cool to $30^\circ$C, giving your answer in minutes to one decimal place. [2]
tips: Because $T-20>0$ throughout, you may write $\ln(T-20)$ without modulus signs. Use the unrounded value of $k$ (store it in your GDC) in part (c).

subtopic: Separable equation needing partial fractions
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y(4-y)$, where $0<y<4$ and $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $y=\dfrac{4}{1+3e^{-4x}}$. [6] (b) Write down the limiting value of $y$ as $x\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{1}{y(4-y)}\,dy=\int1\,dx$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{y(4-y)}=\dfrac14\left(\dfrac1y+\dfrac1{4-y}\right)$ [A1] $\dfrac14\ln y-\dfrac14\ln(4-y)=x+C$ [A1] Using $y=1$ at $x=0$: $C=\dfrac14\ln\dfrac13$, so $\ln\dfrac{y}{4-y}=4x+\ln\dfrac13$ [M1] $\dfrac{y}{4-y}=\dfrac{e^{4x}}{3}$, so $3y=4e^{4x}-ye^{4x}$ and $y=\dfrac{4e^{4x}}{3+e^{4x}}$ [M1] $y=\dfrac{4}{1+3e^{-4x}}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (b) $y\to4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Partial fractions is the key step for any equation of the form $y'=y(a-y)$. Because $0<y<4$ both logarithm arguments are positive, so no modulus signs are needed.

subtopic: Euler's method recursion and error analysis
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3-y$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Euler's method with step size $h$ is used to approximate the solution. Show that $y_{n+1}=(1-h)y_n+3h$. [2] (b) Use Euler's method with $h=0.5$ to estimate the value of $y$ when $x=2$. [3] (c) Solve the differential equation, and hence find the value of $y$ when $x=2$, giving your answer to four significant figures. [4] (d) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (b). [2] (e) State one change that would reduce the error in the estimate. [1]
tips: Writing the Euler recursion in simplified form saves effort when there are several steps. Here the DE is simple enough to check your numerical answer against the exact solution.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation leading to an implicit solution
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}{x-y}$, for $x>0$, where $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{1-v}$. [3] (b) Hence show that the solution of the differential equation satisfies $\arctan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)=\dfrac12\ln\left(x^2+y^2\right)$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [A1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{x+vx}{x-vx}=\dfrac{1+v}{1-v}$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v}{1-v}-v=\dfrac{1+v^2}{1-v}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{1-v}{1+v^2}\,dv=\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+v^2}-\dfrac{v}{1+v^2}\right)dv$ [A1] $\arctan v-\dfrac12\ln\left(1+v^2\right)=\ln x+C$ [A1] When $x=1$, $v=0$: $C=0$ [M1] $\arctan\dfrac{y}{x}=\ln x+\dfrac12\ln\left(1+\dfrac{y^2}{x^2}\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\ln x^2+\dfrac12\ln\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{x^2}=\dfrac12\ln\left(x^2+y^2\right)$ [A1][AG] [6 marks]
tips: Split the numerator before integrating so you can recognize an arctangent and a logarithm. When converting back, write $\ln x$ as $\tfrac12\ln x^2$ so the logarithms combine.

subtopic: Integrating factor with a trigonometric coefficient
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=\sin 2x$, for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that an integrating factor for this differential equation is $\sec x$. [3] (b) Hence show that $y=2\cos x-2\cos^2x$. [4] (c) Find the maximum value of $y$ for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int\tan x\,dx}$ [M1] $\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln(\cos x)=\ln(\sec x)$ [A1] so the integrating factor is $\sec x$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y\sec x\right)=\sin2x\sec x$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2\sin x\cos x}{\cos x}=2\sin x$ [A1] $y\sec x=-2\cos x+C$ [A1] When $x=0$, $y=0$: $0=-2+C$, so $C=2$, giving $y=2\cos x-2\cos^2x$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2\sin x+4\sin x\cos x$ [A1] Setting $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $2\sin x(2\cos x-1)=0$, so $\cos x=\dfrac12$ (since $\sin x=0$ gives the minimum $y=0$) [M1] $y=2\cdot\dfrac12-2\cdot\dfrac14=\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x$ so that the $\cos x$ cancels after multiplying by $\sec x$. For the maximum, you can also treat $y$ as a quadratic in $\cos x$.

subtopic: Separable equation modelling a draining tank
statement: Water drains from a tank. The depth of water $h$ centimeters at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.2\sqrt{h}$, where $h=25$ when $t=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $h=(5-0.1t)^2$. [4] (b) Find the time at which the tank is empty. [1] (c) Find the rate of change of the depth when $t=20$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int h^{-\frac12}\,dh=\int-0.2\,dt$ [M1] $2\sqrt h=-0.2t+c$ [A1] When $t=0$, $h=25$: $c=10$ [M1] $\sqrt h=5-0.1t$, so $h=(5-0.1t)^2$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $h=0$ when $5-0.1t=0$, so $t=50$ minutes [A1] [1 mark] (c) When $t=20$, $\sqrt h=3$, so $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.2\times3=-0.6$ cm per minute [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Write the square root as a power of $h$ before integrating. In part (c) you do not need to differentiate the solution; use the differential equation directly.

subtopic: Drug concentration modelled with an integrating factor
statement: After an injection, the concentration $C$ mg/L of a drug in the blood at time $t$ hours satisfies $\dfrac{dC}{dt}+0.4C=5e^{-0.1t}$, where $C=0$ when $t=0$. (a) Show that $e^{0.4t}$ is an integrating factor for this differential equation. [1] (b) Hence show that $C=\dfrac{50}{3}\left(e^{-0.1t}-e^{-0.4t}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the maximum concentration of the drug and the time at which it occurs. [3] (d) The drug is effective when the concentration exceeds $5$ mg/L. Find, to the nearest tenth of an hour, how long the drug is effective. [2]
markscheme: (a) $e^{\int0.4\,dt}=e^{0.4t}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(Ce^{0.4t}\right)=5e^{0.3t}$ [M1] $Ce^{0.4t}=\dfrac{5}{0.3}e^{0.3t}+K=\dfrac{50}{3}e^{0.3t}+K$ [A1] When $t=0$, $C=0$: $K=-\dfrac{50}{3}$ [M1] $C=\dfrac{50}{3}\left(e^{-0.1t}-e^{-0.4t}\right)$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (c) Sketch or differentiate: $\dfrac{dC}{dt}=0$ gives $e^{0.3t}=4$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln4}{0.3}=4.62$ hours [A1] $C_{\max}=7.87$ mg/L [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solving $\dfrac{50}{3}\left(e^{-0.1t}-e^{-0.4t}\right)=5$ with a GDC gives $t=1.413$ and $t=11.74$ [M1] Duration $=11.74-1.413=10.3$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite the equation in the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ first, then multiply by the integrating factor. In part (d) look at the graph of $C$ against $t$; there are two intersections with $C=5$.

subtopic: Series by successive differentiation of a root function
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{1+2x}$, for $x>-\dfrac12$. (a) Find $f'(x)$, $f''(x)$ and $f'''(x)$. [3] (b) Hence find the Maclaurin series of $f(x)$ up to and including the term in $x^3$. [2] (c) Use your series with $x=0.1$ to estimate $\sqrt{1.2}$, giving your answer to four decimal places. [2]
tips: Use the chain rule carefully: each differentiation of $(1+2x)^n$ brings down $n$ and an extra factor of $2$. Keep the factorials in the denominators when you assemble the series.

subtopic: Product of two standard series and term-by-term integration
statement: (a) Use the standard Maclaurin series for $e^x$ and $\sin x$ to find the Maclaurin series of $e^x\sin x$ up to and including the term in $x^3$. [4] (b) Hence find an approximation for $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}e^x\sin x\,dx$, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form. [3]
markscheme: (a) $e^x\sin x=\left(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\right)\left(x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\right)$ [M1] Coefficient of $x$ is $1$ [A1] Coefficient of $x^2$ is $1$ [A1] Coefficient of $x^3$ is $\dfrac12-\dfrac16=\dfrac13$ [A1] so $e^x\sin x\approx x+x^2+\dfrac{x^3}{3}$ [4 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\left(x+x^2+\frac{x^3}{3}\right)dx$ [M1] $=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{x^4}{12}\right]_0^{\frac12}$ [A1] $=\dfrac18+\dfrac1{24}+\dfrac1{192}=\dfrac{11}{64}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When multiplying series, gather terms by power of $x$ systematically, and stop at the required order. Integrate the truncated polynomial term by term; do not try to integrate $e^x\sin x$ directly.

subtopic: Evaluating a limit using series
statement: (a) Write down the Maclaurin series for $\ln(1+x)$ and for $\sin x$, each up to and including the term in $x^3$. [2] (b) Hence find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)-\sin x+\frac12x^2}{x^3}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\ln(1+x)=x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\cdots$ [A1] $\sin x=x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Numerator $=\left(x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right)-\left(x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}\right)+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+O(x^4)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x^3}{2}+O(x^4)$ [A1] Dividing by $x^3$: $\dfrac12+O(x)$ [M1] Limit $=\dfrac12$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For a limit of the form $0/0$, expand the numerator until the first nonzero term survives; the lower powers must cancel. Always track the order of the first omitted term, here $O(x^4)$.

subtopic: Series solution of a first-order differential equation
statement: The function $y(x)$ satisfies the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y^2$, with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=1+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, and find a similar expression for $\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}$. [3] (b) Hence find the Maclaurin series for $y$ up to and including the term in $x^3$. [4] (c) Use your series to estimate $y(0.2)$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) Differentiating $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y^2$ with respect to $x$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=1+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ [M1][A1][AG] $\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}=2\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2+2y\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) At $x=0$: $y=1$ and $y'=0+1=1$ [A1] $y''=1+2(1)(1)=3$ [A1] $y'''=2(1)^2+2(1)(3)=8$ [A1] $y\approx1+x+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+\dfrac{4x^3}{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y(0.2)\approx1+0.2+0.06+0.01067=1.27$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the product rule on $y\,y'$ when differentiating $y^2$ twice. Evaluate each derivative at $x=0$ in order, since each depends on the previous values.

subtopic: Series for e^(-x^2) and a definite integral
statement: (a) Use the Maclaurin series for $e^x$ to find the Maclaurin series for $e^{-x^2}$ up to and including the term in $x^6$. [2] (b) Hence find an approximation for $\displaystyle\int_0^1e^{-x^2}\,dx$ as a fraction in its simplest form. [3] (c) Use your GDC to evaluate the integral correct to four significant figures, and find the percentage error in your approximation from part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) Replacing $x$ by $-x^2$ in $e^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2!}+\dfrac{x^3}{3!}+\cdots$ [M1] $e^{-x^2}\approx1-x^2+\dfrac{x^4}{2}-\dfrac{x^6}{6}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Integrating term by term [M1] $\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{x^5}{10}-\dfrac{x^7}{42}\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=1-\dfrac13+\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{42}=\dfrac{26}{35}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Integral $=0.7468$ [A1] Percentage error $=\dfrac{|0.7468-0.7429|}{0.7468}\times100$ [M1] $=0.531\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substitute the whole expression $-x^2$ for $x$ in the standard series, including powers. The function $e^{-x^2}$ has no elementary antiderivative, which is why the series route is useful.

subtopic: Maclaurin series of tan x from a differential identity
statement: Let $y=\tan x$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+y^2$. [1] (b) By differentiating the result of part (a) twice more, find the Maclaurin series of $\tan x$ up to and including the term in $x^3$. [5] (c) Hence write down the Maclaurin series of $\sec^2x$ up to and including the term in $x^2$. [1] (d) Use your series for $\tan x$ and the series $\sin x=x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots$ to find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-\sin x}{x^3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x=1+y^2$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (b) $y''=2y\,y'$ [A1] $y'''=2(y')^2+2y\,y''$ [A1] At $x=0$: $y=0$, $y'=1$, $y''=0$ [A1] $y'''=2$ [A1] $\tan x\approx x+\dfrac{x^3}{3}$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $\sec^2x=\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x\approx1+x^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\tan x-\sin x=\left(x+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right)-\left(x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}\right)+O(x^5)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x^3}{2}+O(x^5)$ [A1] Limit $=\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Building the derivatives from $y'=1+y^2$ avoids messy trigonometric derivatives; each step only needs the previous values at $x=0$. Differentiating a Maclaurin series term by term gives the series of the derivative.

subtopic: Series for arctan from 1/(1+x^2) and an approximation of pi
statement: (a) Use the series $\dfrac{1}{1+u}=1-u+u^2-\cdots$ to find the Maclaurin series of $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$ up to and including the term in $x^4$. [2] (b) Hence find the Maclaurin series of $\arctan x$ up to and including the term in $x^5$. [2] (c) Use your series with $x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ to show that $\pi\approx\dfrac{82\sqrt3}{45}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Replacing $u$ by $x^2$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\approx1-x^2+x^4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\arctan x=\int_0^x\dfrac{1}{1+t^2}\,dt$ (since $\arctan0=0$) [M1] $\arctan x\approx x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{x^5}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\arctan\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $\dfrac\pi6\approx\dfrac1{\sqrt3}-\dfrac{1}{9\sqrt3}+\dfrac{1}{45\sqrt3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(1-\dfrac19+\dfrac1{45}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\dfrac{41}{45}$ [A1] $\pi\approx\dfrac{6}{\sqrt3}\cdot\dfrac{41}{45}=\dfrac{2\sqrt3\cdot41}{45}=\dfrac{82\sqrt3}{45}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks]
tips: The constant of integration is fixed because $\arctan 0=0$. For part (c), note that $\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)^3=\tfrac{1}{3\sqrt3}$ and $\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)^5=\tfrac{1}{9\sqrt3}$, so a common factor $\tfrac1{\sqrt3}$ appears.

subtopic: Composition of series for ln(cos x)
statement: (a) By writing $\cos x=1+u$ and using the standard series for $\cos x$ and $\ln(1+u)$, show that the Maclaurin series of $\ln(\cos x)$ begins $-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{12}$. [5] (b) Hence find an approximation for $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\ln(\cos x)\,dx$ as a fraction. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos x=1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^4}{24}-\cdots$, so $u=-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^4}{24}+\cdots$ [A1] $\ln(\cos x)=\ln(1+u)=u-\dfrac{u^2}{2}+\cdots$ [M1] $u^2=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+O(x^6)$ [A1] $\ln(\cos x)=-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^4}{24}-\dfrac{x^4}{8}+O(x^6)$ [A1] $=-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{12}+\cdots$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{12}\right)dx=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{6}-\dfrac{x^5}{60}\right]_0^{\frac12}$ [M1] $=-\dfrac1{48}-\dfrac1{1920}=-\dfrac{41}{1920}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When composing series, only the lowest-order terms of $u^2$ matter at this order; do not expand beyond the power requested. Check that your final fraction is negative, since $\ln(\cos x)<0$ on this interval.

subtopic: Finding parameters of a binomial series
statement: The Maclaurin series of $(1+ax)^n$, where $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $n\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$, begins $1-6x+54x^2+\cdots$. (a) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $n$. [5] (b) State the set of values of $x$ for which the series expansion is valid. [1] (c) Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the series. [2]
markscheme: (a) Coefficient of $x$: $na=-6$ [A1] Coefficient of $x^2$: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}a^2=54$, so $n(n-1)a^2=108$ [A1] Substituting $a=-\dfrac6n$: $\dfrac{36(n-1)}{n}=108$ [M1] $n-1=3n$, so $n=-\dfrac12$ [A1] $a=12$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) Valid for $|12x|<1$, that is $|x|<\dfrac1{12}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}a^3=\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)}{6}\times1728$ [M1] $=-540$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Equate coefficients one power at a time and eliminate one unknown. A quick check: with $n=-\tfrac12$ and $a=12$, the coefficient of $x^2$ is $\tfrac38\times144=54$.

subtopic: Maclaurin series of tan x via a differential identity and radius of convergence
statement: This question investigates the Maclaurin series of $f(x)=\tan x$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=1+\left[f(x)\right]^2$. [1] (b) Show that $f''(x)=2f(x)f'(x)$ and that $f'''(x)=2\left[f'(x)\right]^2+2f(x)f''(x)$. [3] (c) You are given that $f^{(4)}(x)=6f'(x)f''(x)+2f(x)f'''(x)$ and $f^{(5)}(x)=6\left[f''(x)\right]^2+8f'(x)f'''(x)+2f(x)f^{(4)}(x)$. Hence find the Maclaurin series of $\tan x$ up to and including the term in $x^5$. [4] The Maclaurin series of $\tan x$ is written $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n$. (d) Explain why $a_n=0$ for every even value of $n$. [2] (e) By equating the coefficients of $x^6$ on both sides of the identity $f'(x)=1+\left[f(x)\right]^2$, find the value of $a_7$. [4] (f) (i) Use the series up to and including the term in $x^7$ to estimate $\tan0.5$. (ii) Use your GDC to find $\tan0.5$, and hence find the percentage error in your estimate, giving your answer to two significant figures. [4] (g) (i) Calculate the ratios $\dfrac{a_5}{a_3}$ and $\dfrac{a_7}{a_5}$. (ii) It can be shown that $\dfrac{a_{n+2}}{a_n}\to\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}$ as $n\to\infty$. By comparing the series with a geometric series, explain why this suggests that the series converges for $|x|<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. [5] (h) Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\tan x-x-\frac13x^3}{x^5}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x=1+\left[f(x)\right]^2$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (b) Differentiating $f'=1+f^2$ using the chain rule: $f''=2f\,f'$ [M1][A1][AG] Differentiating with the product rule: $f'''=2f'f'+2f\,f''=2(f')^2+2f\,f''$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=1$ and $f''(0)=0$ [A1] $f'''(0)=2$ and $f^{(4)}(0)=0$ [A1] $f^{(5)}(0)=6(0)^2+8(1)(2)+0=16$ [A1] $\tan x\approx x+\dfrac{2x^3}{3!}+\dfrac{16x^5}{5!}=x+\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{2x^5}{15}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, so $f$ is an odd function [R1] Then $\sum a_n(-x)^n=-\sum a_nx^n$ for all $x$, so $a_n(-1)^n=-a_n$; for even $n$ this gives $a_n=0$ [R1] [2 marks] (e) The coefficient of $x^6$ in $f'(x)$ is $7a_7$ [M1] The coefficient of $x^6$ in $\left[f(x)\right]^2$ comes from products of pairs of odd-indexed terms with total power $6$: $2a_1a_5+a_3^2$ [M1] $=2(1)\left(\dfrac2{15}\right)+\dfrac19=\dfrac{17}{45}$ [A1] $7a_7=\dfrac{17}{45}$, so $a_7=\dfrac{17}{315}$ [A1] [4 marks] (f)(i) $\tan0.5\approx0.5+\dfrac{0.5^3}{3}+\dfrac{2(0.5)^5}{15}+\dfrac{17(0.5)^7}{315}$ [M1] $=0.54625$ [A1] (ii) GDC: $\tan0.5=0.546302$ [A1] Percentage error $=\dfrac{|0.54625-0.546302|}{0.546302}\times100=0.0087\%$ [A1] [4 marks] (g)(i) $\dfrac{a_5}{a_3}=\dfrac{2/15}{1/3}=\dfrac25=0.4$ [A1] $\dfrac{a_7}{a_5}=\dfrac{17/315}{2/15}=\dfrac{17}{42}=0.405$ (3 s.f.) [A1] (ii) The ratio of successive nonzero terms is $\dfrac{a_{n+2}x^{n+2}}{a_nx^n}=\dfrac{a_{n+2}}{a_n}x^2\to\dfrac{4x^2}{\pi^2}$, so for large $n$ the series behaves like a geometric series with common ratio $\dfrac{4x^2}{\pi^2}$ [R1] A geometric series converges when its common ratio has modulus less than $1$: $\dfrac{4x^2}{\pi^2}<1$ [M1] so $x^2<\dfrac{\pi^2}{4}$, that is $|x|<\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [5 marks] (h) $\tan x-x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}=\dfrac{2x^5}{15}+O(x^7)$ [M1] Limit $=\dfrac{2}{15}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In the early parts, keep the pattern: each new derivative of a product uses the product rule on the previous line. In part (e), list all pairs of indices whose sum is the required power; pairs such as $(1,5)$ and $(5,1)$ both count.

subtopic: Definite integral by substitution
statement: Use the substitution $u=x^2-1$ to find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^{\sqrt5}x\sqrt{x^2-1}\,dx$. [5]
markscheme: $du=2x\,dx$, so $x\,dx=\dfrac12du$ [M1] When $x=1$, $u=0$; when $x=\sqrt5$, $u=4$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^4\dfrac12u^{\frac12}\,du$ [A1] $=\left[\dfrac13u^{\frac32}\right]_0^4$ [A1] $=\dfrac13\times8=\dfrac83$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Change the limits when you change variable, so you never have to return to $x$. Check that all of the $x$ in the integrand is absorbed by $du=2x\,dx$.

subtopic: Integration by parts with a logarithm
statement: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^ex^2\ln x\,dx$. Give your answer in the form $\dfrac{ae^3+b}{c}$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [5]
markscheme: Integration by parts with $u=\ln x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=x^2$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int x^2\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x-\int\dfrac{x^2}{3}\,dx$ [A1] $=\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x-\dfrac{x^3}{9}\right]_1^e$ [A1] $=\left(\dfrac{e^3}{3}-\dfrac{e^3}{9}\right)-\left(0-\dfrac19\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2e^3+1}{9}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: For $\ln x$ times a power of $x$, choose $u=\ln x$ since it simplifies on differentiation. Remember $\ln1=0$ when evaluating the lower limit.

subtopic: Repeated integration by parts of e^x cos x
statement: Let $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\cos x\,dx$. (a) By using integration by parts twice, show that $2I=e^{\frac\pi2}-1$. [5] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\sin x\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) First application, $u=\cos x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^x$: $I=\left[e^x\cos x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}+\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\sin x\,dx$ [M1] $=-1+J$, where $J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\sin x\,dx$ [A1] Second application, $u=\sin x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^x$: $J=\left[e^x\sin x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}-\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\cos x\,dx$ [M1] $=e^{\frac\pi2}-I$ [A1] So $I=-1+e^{\frac\pi2}-I$, giving $2I=e^{\frac\pi2}-1$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] (b) $J=e^{\frac\pi2}-I$ [M1] $=e^{\frac\pi2}-\dfrac{e^{\frac\pi2}-1}{2}=\dfrac{e^{\frac\pi2}+1}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the original integral reappears after two rounds of parts, treat it as an unknown and solve an equation. Be consistent in your choice of $u$ and $dv$ in both applications, otherwise you will undo the first step.

subtopic: Area of a region bounded by a curve, a line and the x-axis
statement: Let $R$ be the region enclosed by the curve $y=\ln x$, the line $y=2-x$ and the $x$-axis. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $A$ where the curve $y=\ln x$ meets the line $y=2-x$. [2] (b) Find the area of $R$. [4] (c) Write down an integral with respect to $y$ that gives the area of $R$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solving $\ln x=2-x$ using a GDC [M1] $A=(1.56,\ 0.443)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $R$ lies under the curve from $x=1$ to $x=a$, where $a=1.557$ is the $x$-coordinate of $A$, and under the line from $x=a$ to $x=2$ [A1] Area $=\displaystyle\int_1^{1.557}\ln x\,dx+\int_{1.557}^{2}(2-x)\,dx$ [M1] $=0.1324+0.0981$ [A1] $=0.231$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $x$ ranges from $e^y$ (the curve) to $2-y$ (the line) for $0\le y\le0.443$ [A1] Area $=\displaystyle\int_0^{0.443}\left(2-y-e^y\right)dy$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch the curve and line first: the $x$-axis forms the lower boundary, and the upper boundary changes at the intersection point. Store the intersection value in your GDC so it is used without rounding error.

subtopic: Volume of revolution using a double-angle identity
statement: Let $y=\sin x+\cos x$, for $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$. The region between the graph of $y$ and the $x$-axis is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Show that $y^2=1+\sin2x$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact volume of the solid formed. [4]
markscheme: (a) $y^2=\sin^2x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x$ [M1] $=1+\sin2x$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\left(1+\sin2x\right)dx$ [M1] $=\pi\left[x-\dfrac12\cos2x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}$ [A1] $=\pi\left[\left(\dfrac\pi2+\dfrac12\right)-\left(0-\dfrac12\right)\right]$ [M1] $=\pi\left(\dfrac\pi2+1\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Square the function before integrating, and use $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $2\sin x\cos x=\sin2x$ to avoid integrating a square directly. Keep the factor of $\pi$ outside the integral.

subtopic: Partial fractions integrated over a definite interval
statement: (a) Find constants $A$ and $B$ such that $\dfrac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{B}{x+3}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)}\,dx=\ln\dfrac{32}{9}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3x+5\equiv A(x+3)+B(x+1)$ [M1] Substituting $x=-1$: $2=2A$, so $A=1$ [A1] Substituting $x=-3$: $-4=-2B$, so $B=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\dfrac1{x+1}+\dfrac2{x+3}\right)dx=\left[\ln(x+1)+2\ln(x+3)\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\ln2+2\ln4-2\ln3$ [M1] $=\ln2+\ln16-\ln9=\ln\dfrac{32}{9}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks]
tips: Substituting the roots of the denominator is the fastest way to find the constants. When combining logarithms, convert multiples into powers first: $2\ln4=\ln16$.

subtopic: Completing the square and an arctangent integral
statement: (a) Write $x^2+2x+5$ in the form $(x+p)^2+q$. [1] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2+4}\,dx$ is of the form $\int\dfrac{1}{u^2+a^2}\,du$ with $a=2$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\arctan\left(\dfrac{x+1}{2}\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\left[\arctan1-\arctan0\right]$ [M1] $=\dfrac\pi8$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A quadratic with no real roots in the denominator usually signals an arctangent. The formula booklet gives $\int\frac{1}{a^2+x^2}dx=\frac1a\arctan\frac xa+C$; do not forget the factor $\frac1a$.

subtopic: Odd power of cosine by substitution
statement: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^3x\,dx$. [5]
markscheme: $\cos^3x=\cos x\left(1-\sin^2x\right)$ [M1] Let $u=\sin x$, $du=\cos x\,dx$ [A1] Limits: $x=0\to u=0$ and $x=\dfrac\pi2\to u=1$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(1-u^2\right)du=\left[u-\dfrac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\dfrac23$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: For an odd power of sine or cosine, split off one factor and convert the rest with $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. The remaining single factor becomes $du$.

subtopic: Volumes of revolution about the y-axis and the x-axis
statement: The region $R$ is bounded by the curve $y=e^{\frac x2}$, the $y$-axis and the line $y=3$. (a) Show that the curve can be written as $x=2\ln y$. [1] (b) The region $R$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $y$-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed. [3] (c) The region $R$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\dfrac x2$, so $x=2\ln y$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int x^2\,dy$ [M1] $=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^3\left(2\ln y\right)^2dy$ [A1] $=12.9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $R$ lies between $y=e^{\frac x2}$ and $y=3$, for $0\le x\le2\ln3$ [A1] $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{2\ln3}\left(9-e^x\right)dx$ [M1] $=37.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For rotation about the $y$-axis you need $x$ in terms of $y$, and the limits are $y$-values. For rotation about the $x$-axis a region between two curves gives a washer: subtract the squares, not the square of the difference.

subtopic: Reduction formula for powers of sine and a limit
statement: This question investigates the integrals $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^nx\,dx$, where $n\in\mathbb{N}$. (a) Find the exact values of $I_0$ and $I_1$. [2] (b) For $n\ge2$, use integration by parts to show that $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$. [6] (c) Hence find the exact values of $I_4$ and $I_5$. [3] (d) Hence, using the substitution $u=\dfrac\pi2-x$, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^6x\,dx$. [3] (e) Show that $I_{n+1}\le I_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. [2] (f) Use the result of part (b) to show that $(n+1)I_{n+1}I_n=\dfrac\pi2$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. [4] (g) Hence show that $\dfrac{\pi}{2(n+1)}\le I_n^2\le\dfrac{\pi}{2n}$ for $n\ge1$, and deduce the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}nI_n^2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $I_0=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] $I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin x\,dx=\left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^{n-1}x\,\sin x\,dx$ [A1] Using parts with $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$ [M1] $I_n=\left[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}+(n-1)\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx$ [A1] The boundary term is $0$ for $n\ge2$ [A1] Using $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $I_n=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_n\right)$ [M1] $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (c) $I_2=\dfrac12I_0=\dfrac\pi4$ and $I_3=\dfrac23I_1=\dfrac23$ [M1] $I_4=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}$ [A1] $I_5=\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac8{15}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $I_6=\dfrac56I_4=\dfrac{5\pi}{32}$ [M1][A1] With $u=\dfrac\pi2-x$: $\cos x=\sin u$ and the limits swap and $dx=-du$, so $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^6x\,dx=\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^6u\,du=I_6$, hence the value is $\dfrac{5\pi}{32}$ [R1] [3 marks] (e) For $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$, $0\le\sin x\le1$, so $\sin^{n+1}x\le\sin^nx$ [R1] Integrating over $\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ preserves the inequality, so $I_{n+1}\le I_n$ [R1] [2 marks] (f) Applying (b) with $n$ replaced by $n+1$: $(n+1)I_{n+1}=nI_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$ [M1] Multiplying by $I_n$: $(n+1)I_{n+1}I_n=nI_nI_{n-1}$ [A1] so the quantity $(n+1)I_{n+1}I_n$ does not change as $n$ increases [R1] For $n=0$ it equals $I_1I_0=\dfrac\pi2$, hence it equals $\dfrac\pi2$ for all $n$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) For $n\ge1$, (e) gives $I_{n+1}\le I_n\le I_{n-1}$; multiplying by $I_n>0$: $I_nI_{n+1}\le I_n^2\le I_nI_{n-1}$ [M1] By (f): $I_nI_{n+1}=\dfrac{\pi}{2(n+1)}$ and $I_nI_{n-1}=\dfrac{\pi}{2n}$, which gives the stated inequality [A1] Multiplying by $n$: $\dfrac{n\pi}{2(n+1)}\le nI_n^2\le\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] As $n\to\infty$ the lower bound tends to $\dfrac\pi2$, so by the squeeze principle $nI_n^2\to\dfrac\pi2$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: In reduction-formula questions, always integrate by parts so that the original integral reappears on the right-hand side, then solve for it. In the later parts, look for a quantity that is unchanged from one index to the next; that usually signals a telescoping argument.

subtopic: Stationary points of a product with an exponential
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{-x}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Hence find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Find $f''(x)$ and use it to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3]
markscheme: (a) Product rule [M1] $f'(x)=2xe^{-x}-x^2e^{-x}=(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$: $x(2-x)e^{-x}=0$, and $e^{-x}\ne0$ [M1] Stationary points $(0,0)$ and $\left(2,4e^{-2}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f''(x)=(2-2x)e^{-x}-(2x-x^2)e^{-x}=\left(x^2-4x+2\right)e^{-x}$ [A1] $f''(0)=2>0$ and $f''(2)=-2e^{-2}<0$ [M1] $(0,0)$ is a local minimum and $\left(2,4e^{-2}\right)$ is a local maximum [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Factor $e^{-x}$ out of $f'$ so that setting it to zero is immediate; an exponential is never zero. When finding $f''$, differentiate the factored form $(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ again with the product rule.

subtopic: Implicit differentiation, tangent and horizontal tangents
statement: Consider the curve $C$ with equation $x^2+xy+y^2=7$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2x+y}{x+2y}$. [4] (b) The point $P(1,2)$ lies on $C$. Find the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$, giving your answer in the form $ax+by=c$ where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3] (c) Find the exact coordinates of the two points on $C$ at which the tangent is horizontal. [4]
markscheme: (a) Differentiating implicitly with respect to $x$ [M1] $\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy)=y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ [A1] $2x+y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ [A1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}(x+2y)=-(2x+y)$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2x+y}{x+2y}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) At $(1,2)$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{4}{5}$ [A1] $y-2=-\dfrac45(x-1)$ [M1] $4x+5y=14$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Horizontal tangent: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $2x+y=0$ and $y=-2x$ [M1][A1] Substituting into the curve: $x^2-2x^2+4x^2=7$, so $3x^2=7$ [M1] $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac73}$; the points are $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac73},-2\sqrt{\dfrac73}\right)$ and $\left(-\sqrt{\dfrac73},2\sqrt{\dfrac73}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Remember that $xy$ needs the product rule when differentiating implicitly. For a horizontal tangent set only the numerator to zero, and check that the denominator is not also zero at those points.

subtopic: Related rates for water filling a cone
statement: Water is poured at a constant rate of $20\ \text{cm}^3\,\text{s}^{-1}$ into a container in the shape of an inverted right circular cone with its vertex pointing downward. When the depth of water is $h$ cm, the radius of the circular surface of the water is $\dfrac h2$ cm. (a) Show that the volume $V$ of water in the cone is $V=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$. [2] (b) Find the exact rate of increase of $h$ at the instant when $h=10$. [3] (c) At this instant, find the rate of increase of the area of the circular surface of the water. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\dfrac13\pi r^2h$ with $r=\dfrac h2$ [M1] $V=\dfrac13\pi\cdot\dfrac{h^2}{4}\cdot h=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}$ [M1] $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{dV}{dh}\times\dfrac{dh}{dt}$, so $20=25\pi\dfrac{dh}{dt}$ at $h=10$ [M1] $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{4}{5\pi}\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=\pi r^2=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}$, so $\dfrac{dA}{dh}=\dfrac{\pi h}{2}$ [A1] $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=\dfrac{dA}{dh}\times\dfrac{dh}{dt}$ [M1] $=5\pi\times\dfrac{4}{5\pi}=4\ \text{cm}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Express the quantity you differentiate in terms of a single variable (here $h$) before applying the chain rule. Substitute the numerical value of $h$ only after differentiating.

subtopic: Optimization of a can with fixed volume
statement: A closed cylindrical can has radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm. Its volume is $500\ \text{cm}^3$. (a) Show that the total surface area $A$ of the can satisfies $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [2] (b) Find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$. [3] (c) Justify that this value of $r$ gives a minimum. [2] (d) Find the minimum surface area, correct to three significant figures. [1] (e) Show that for the can with minimum surface area, $h=2r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$, so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [M1] $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}$ [A1] Setting equal to zero: $r^3=\dfrac{250}{\pi}$ [M1] $r=4.30$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=4\pi+\dfrac{2000}{r^3}$ [A1] which is positive for $r>0$, so the stationary point is a minimum [R1] [2 marks] (d) $A_{\min}=349\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}=\dfrac{2\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}$ using $250=\pi r^3$ [M1] $=2r$ [A1][AG] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate $h$ using the volume constraint before differentiating. Use the unrounded value of $r$ when calculating the minimum area.

subtopic: Differentiating logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\sec x+\tan x\right)=\sec x$. [3] (b) Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\arcsin x+\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)=\arcsin x$, for $-1<x<1$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\arcsin x\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Chain rule [M1] $\dfrac{\sec x\tan x+\sec^2x}{\sec x+\tan x}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sec x\left(\tan x+\sec x\right)}{\sec x+\tan x}=\sec x$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Product rule on $x\arcsin x$ [M1] $\arcsin x+\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ [A1] and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{1-x^2}=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, so the sum is $\arcsin x$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\arcsin x\,dx=\left[x\arcsin x+\sqrt{1-x^2}\right]_0^{\frac12}$ [M1] $=\left(\dfrac\pi{12}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In a "show that" differentiation, aim for the target expression and factor to cancel. A result of the form "derivative of $F$ equals $f$" immediately gives you $\int f=F$, which is what part (c) uses.

subtopic: Second derivative, stationary point and point of inflexion
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$, for $x>0$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Show that $f''(x)=\dfrac{2\ln x-3}{x^3}$. [3] (d) Hence determine the nature of the stationary point. [1] (e) Find the exact coordinates of the point of inflexion, justifying that it is a point of inflexion. [3]
markscheme: (a) Quotient rule [M1] $f'(x)=\dfrac{\frac1x\cdot x-\ln x\cdot1}{x^2}=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$ gives $\ln x=1$ [M1] $\left(e,\dfrac1e\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f'(x)=(1-\ln x)x^{-2}$ [M1] $f''(x)=-\dfrac1x\cdot x^{-2}-2(1-\ln x)x^{-3}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{-1-2+2\ln x}{x^3}=\dfrac{2\ln x-3}{x^3}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (d) $f''(e)=\dfrac{2-3}{e^3}<0$, so the point is a local maximum [A1] [1 mark] (e) $f''(x)=0$ gives $\ln x=\dfrac32$, so $x=e^{\frac32}$ [M1] $f''$ changes sign from negative to positive as $x$ increases through $e^{\frac32}$ (because $x^3>0$ and $2\ln x-3$ changes sign) [R1] Point of inflexion $\left(e^{\frac32},\ \dfrac32e^{-\frac32}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A zero second derivative is not enough for a point of inflexion; you must show the sign of $f''$ changes. Using the product form with negative powers is often less error-prone than a second quotient rule.

subtopic: Tangent, normal and a triangle area for y = x ln x
statement: Let $f(x)=x\ln x$, for $x>0$. The point $P$ on the graph of $f$ has $x$-coordinate $e$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and hence the gradient of the tangent to the graph at $P$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent and the equation of the normal to the graph at $P$. [3] (c) The tangent and the normal meet the $x$-axis at $A$ and $B$ respectively. Find the exact area of triangle $PAB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\ln x+1$ [M1] At $x=e$: gradient $=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P=(e,e)$; tangent: $y-e=2(x-e)$, that is $y=2x-e$ [A1] Normal gradient $-\dfrac12$ [M1] Normal: $y-e=-\dfrac12(x-e)$, that is $y=-\dfrac x2+\dfrac{3e}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=\left(\dfrac e2,0\right)$ and $B=(3e,0)$ [A1] Area $=\dfrac12\times\left(3e-\dfrac e2\right)\times e$ [M1] $=\dfrac{5e^2}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the $y$-coordinate of $P$ from the function itself, not from the derivative. The height of the triangle is the $y$-coordinate of $P$ because the base lies on the $x$-axis.

subtopic: Differentiation from first principles
statement: (a) Use differentiation from first principles to show that the derivative of $f(x)=\sqrt x$ is $f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$, for $x>0$. [4] (b) The tangent to the graph of $y=\sqrt x$ at the point $Q$ is parallel to the line $y=\dfrac x4$. Find the coordinates of $Q$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the tangent at $Q$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{\sqrt{x+h}-\sqrt x}{h}$ [M1] Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x$ [M1] $=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{h}{h\left(\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x\right)}=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}=\dfrac14$ [M1] $\sqrt x=2$, so $Q=(4,2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y-2=\dfrac14(x-4)$, that is $y=\dfrac x4+1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: To rationalize a difference of square roots, multiply by the conjugate; the factor $h$ then cancels. Show the limit step explicitly, since first-principles questions award marks for it.

subtopic: Logistic growth model: rate of change and maximum growth rate
statement: The number of bacteria $P$, in thousands, in a culture $t$ hours after the start of an experiment is modeled by $P=\dfrac{200}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the initial number of bacteria in the culture. [1] (b) Write down the value that $P$ approaches as $t\to\infty$. [1] (c) Show that $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.5P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{200}\right)$. [4] (d) Use your GDC to find the maximum rate of increase of $P$, and the time at which this occurs. [3] (e) Find the number of bacteria, in thousands, at the time found in part (d). [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(0)=\dfrac{200}{10}=20$ thousand [A1] [1 mark] (b) $P\to200$ thousand [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P=200\left(1+9e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-1}$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{900e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.5t}\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] $1-\dfrac{P}{200}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}=\dfrac{9e^{-0.5t}}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$ [M1] $0.5P\left(1-\dfrac P{200}\right)=0.5\cdot\dfrac{200}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}\cdot\dfrac{9e^{-0.5t}}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}=\dfrac{900e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.5t}\right)^2}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (d) Graphing $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ and finding its maximum [M1] $t=4.39$ hours [A1] Maximum rate $=25.0$ thousand bacteria per hour [A1] [3 marks] (e) $P=100$ thousand [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the chain rule write the denominator as a negative power first. The maximum rate of increase occurs at the point of inflexion of $P$, which is where $P$ is half of its limiting value.

subtopic: Minimum distance from a point to a curve
statement: The point $A$ has coordinates $(4,0)$. The point $P(x,y)$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt x$, for $x\ge0$. Let $D$ be the distance $AP$. (a) Show that $D^2=x^2-7x+16$. [2] (b) Find the value of $x$ for which $D^2$ is a minimum. [3] (c) Justify that this value gives a minimum. [1] (d) Find the exact minimum distance from $A$ to the curve. [2]
markscheme: (a) $D^2=(x-4)^2+\left(\sqrt x\right)^2$ [M1] $=x^2-8x+16+x=x^2-7x+16$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dx}=2x-7$ [A1] Setting equal to zero [M1] $x=\dfrac72$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2\left(D^2\right)}{dx^2}=2>0$, so the stationary point is a minimum [R1] [1 mark] (d) $D^2=\dfrac{49}{4}-\dfrac{49}{2}+16$ [M1] $=\dfrac{15}{4}$, so $D=\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Minimizing $D^2$ gives the same $x$ as minimizing $D$ and avoids differentiating a square root. Remember to take the square root at the end to get the distance itself.

subtopic: Displacement from velocity and total distance with direction changes
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, for $t\ge0$, is given by $v=3t^2-12t+9$. When $t=0$ the particle is $2$ m from a fixed point $O$, with displacement $s=2$. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle at time $t$. [3] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first $4$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3t^2-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3)=0$ [M1] $t=1$ and $t=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s=\displaystyle\int\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt$ [M1] $s=t^3-6t^2+9t+c$ [A1] $s=0+c=2$, so $s=t^3-6t^2+9t+2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The particle changes direction at $t=1$ and $t=3$ [M1] $s(0)=2,\ s(1)=6,\ s(3)=2,\ s(4)=6$ [A1] Total distance $=4+4+4=12$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Total distance is not the same as displacement: split the time interval at each instant when the velocity is zero and add the absolute changes in $s$. Use $s(0)$ to fix the constant of integration.

subtopic: Velocity with an exponential factor: acceleration, integration by parts and limiting displacement
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$, is $v=6te^{-0.5t}$. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$ with displacement $s=0$. (a) Find an expression for the acceleration $a$ at time $t$, and hence find the time at which $a=0$. [3] (b) Find the maximum speed of the particle. [1] (c) Use integration by parts to show that the displacement is $s=24-12(t+2)e^{-0.5t}$. [4] (d) Find the distance traveled by the particle in the first $5$ seconds. [1] (e) Find the value that $s$ approaches as $t\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6e^{-0.5t}-3te^{-0.5t}$ [M1][A1] $a=3e^{-0.5t}(2-t)=0$ gives $t=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $v(2)=12e^{-1}=4.41\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int6te^{-0.5t}\,dt$; parts with $u=t$, $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=e^{-0.5t}$ [M1] $=6\left[-2te^{-0.5t}+2\displaystyle\int e^{-0.5t}\,dt\right]$ [A1] $=-12te^{-0.5t}-24e^{-0.5t}+C$ [A1] $s=0$ when $t=0$: $C=24$, so $s=24-12(t+2)e^{-0.5t}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (d) Since $v\ge0$ for $t\ge0$ the distance equals $s(5)=24-84e^{-2.5}=17.1$ m [A1] [1 mark] (e) $(t+2)e^{-0.5t}\to0$, so $s\to24$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the maximum speed, set the acceleration to zero and check that the velocity there is a maximum, not a minimum. When the velocity never changes sign, the distance traveled equals the displacement.

subtopic: Resistive acceleration using a = v dv/ds and a = dv/dt
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with $s$ meters its displacement from the origin $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The velocity of the particle is $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and its acceleration is $a=-\dfrac12v^2$. When $t=0$, $s=0$ and $v=8$. (a) By using $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$, show that $v=8e^{-\frac s2}$. [4] (b) Find the displacement of the particle when $v=2$. Give your answer in the form $k\ln2$. [2] (c) By using $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, show that $v=\dfrac{8}{4t+1}$. [3] (d) Find an expression for $s$ in terms of $t$, and hence verify your answer to part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-\dfrac12v^2$, so $\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-\dfrac12v$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int\dfrac1v\,dv=\int-\dfrac12\,ds$ [M1] $\ln v=-\dfrac s2+c$ [A1] Using $v=8$ when $s=0$: $v=8e^{-\frac s2}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $2=8e^{-\frac s2}$, so $e^{-\frac s2}=\dfrac14$ [M1] $s=2\ln4=4\ln2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-\dfrac12v^2$, so $\displaystyle\int v^{-2}\,dv=\int-\dfrac12\,dt$ [M1] $-\dfrac1v=-\dfrac t2+c$ and $v=8$ at $t=0$ gives $c=-\dfrac18$ [A1] $\dfrac1v=\dfrac t2+\dfrac18=\dfrac{4t+1}{8}$, so $v=\dfrac{8}{4t+1}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (d) $s=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{8}{4t+1}\,dt=2\ln(4t+1)+c$ [M1] $s=0$ when $t=0$ gives $c=0$, so $s=2\ln(4t+1)$ [A1] $v=2$ when $4t+1=4$, so $t=\dfrac34$ and $s=2\ln4=4\ln2$, which agrees with part (b) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choose the form of acceleration that matches the variables you are given: $v\,dv/ds$ when the variable is displacement, $dv/dt$ when it is time. Always use the initial values to find the constants of integration.

subtopic: Two particles moving on the same line: meeting time
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ move along the same straight line, with displacements $s_A$ and $s_B$ meters from a point $O$ at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le6$. Particle $A$ starts at $O$, and has velocity $v_A=6t-t^2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Particle $B$ starts at the point with $s=30$ and moves toward $O$ with constant speed $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (a) Find the maximum velocity of $A$. [2] (b) Show that $s_A=3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}$. [2] (c) Find the time at which the two particles meet, and their displacement from $O$ at that time. [3] (d) Find the velocity of $A$ when the particles meet. [1]
