markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dv_A}{dt}=6-2t=0$ gives $t=3$ [M1] $v_A(3)=9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s_A=\displaystyle\int\left(6t-t^2\right)dt=3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+c$ and $s_A(0)=0$ gives $c=0$ [M1][A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $s_B=30-2t$ [A1] Solving $3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}=30-2t$ with a GDC [M1] $t=3.55$ s, with displacement $22.9$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v_A=6(3.55)-(3.55)^2=8.70\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For a meeting problem write both displacements from the same origin and set them equal. $B$ moves toward $O$, so its displacement decreases: use a negative velocity.

subtopic: Velocity from acceleration and checking the particle never rests
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds, for $t\ge0$, is $a=6t-4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. When $t=0$ the velocity is $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the displacement is $s=0$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$. [2] (b) Show that the particle never changes direction. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the particle when $t=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int(6t-4)\,dt=3t^2-4t+c$ [M1] $v(0)=3$, so $v=3t^2-4t+3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Discriminant of $3t^2-4t+3$ is $16-36=-20<0$ [M1] so $v\ne0$ for all $t$ (and $v(0)>0$, so $v>0$): the particle never changes direction [R1] [2 marks] (c) $s=t^3-2t^2+3t$ [M1] $s(2)=8-8+6=6$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A particle can only change direction when its velocity changes sign, so look for real roots of $v=0$. The discriminant is a quick way to rule them out.

subtopic: Oscillating particle: velocity, acceleration and total distance
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its displacement from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$, is $s=3\sin t+4\cos t$ meters. (a) Find expressions for the velocity $v$ and the acceleration $a$ of the particle. [2] (b) Show that $a=-s$. [1] (c) Find the first time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first $2$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=3\cos t-4\sin t$ [A1] $a=-3\sin t-4\cos t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=-\left(3\sin t+4\cos t\right)=-s$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (c) $v=0$ gives $3\cos t=4\sin t$, so $\tan t=\dfrac34$ [M1][A1] $t=0.644$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) The velocity changes sign at $t=0.6435$ (the next zero is at $t=0.6435+\pi>2$) [M1] $s(0)=4$, $s(0.6435)=5$, $s(2)=1.063$ [A1] Distance $=(5-4)+(5-1.063)=4.94$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the GDC to radians for trigonometric motion. Distance requires splitting at every time the velocity is zero within the interval; compare the sign of $v$ at the endpoints.

subtopic: Piecewise velocity described in words: areas under a velocity-time graph
statement: A particle moves in a straight line during the first $16$ seconds of its motion. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is as follows. For $0\le t\le4$, the velocity increases at a constant rate from $0$ to $8$. For $4\le t\le10$, the velocity is constant and equal to $8$. For $10\le t\le16$, the velocity decreases at a constant rate from $8$ to $-4$. (a) Write down the acceleration of the particle in each of the three time intervals. [3] (b) Find the time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest after $t=10$. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting position at $t=16$. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the $16$ seconds. [2] (e) Find the average speed of the particle over the $16$ seconds. [1]
markscheme: (a) $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for $0<t<4$, $0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for $4<t<10$, and $-2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for $10<t<16$ [A1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) For $10\le t\le16$: $v=8-2(t-10)=28-2t$ [M1] $v=0$ at $t=14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Displacement is the signed area under the graph [M1] $\dfrac12(4)(8)+6(8)+\dfrac12(4)(8)-\dfrac12(2)(4)$ [A1] $=16+48+16-4=76$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Distance is the total unsigned area [M1] $16+48+16+4=84$ m [A1] [2 marks] (e) Average speed $=\dfrac{84}{16}=\dfrac{21}{4}=5.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Areas below the time axis count as negative for displacement but positive for distance. Average speed uses total distance, not displacement.

subtopic: Velocity with exponential and linear terms: direction change and return to start
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le6$, is $v=5e^{-0.4t}-t$. When $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$, with displacement $s=0$. (a) Find the time $T$ at which the particle is first instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle at time $T$. [2] (c) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ at time $t$, and hence find the displacement when $t=6$. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the $6$ seconds. [3] (e) Find the value of $t$, for $t>0$, at which the particle returns to $O$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solving $5e^{-0.4t}-t=0$ with a GDC [M1] $T=2.13$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-2e^{-0.4t}-1$ [M1] $a(T)=-1.85\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int\left(5e^{-0.4t}-t\right)dt=-12.5e^{-0.4t}-\dfrac{t^2}{2}+c$ and $s(0)=0$ gives $c=12.5$ [M1] $s=12.5\left(1-e^{-0.4t}\right)-\dfrac{t^2}{2}$ [A1] $s(6)=-6.63$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v$ is positive for $t<T$ and negative after, since $v$ is decreasing, so $s(T)=4.90$ m [A1] Distance $=s(T)+\left(s(T)-s(6)\right)$ [M1] $=4.90+(4.90+6.63)=16.4$ m [A1] [3 marks] (e) Solving $s=0$ for $t>0$ using a GDC [M1] $t=4.58$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use your GDC to find the root of $v$ and store it, since $T$ is needed for both the acceleration and the distance. The particle turns around at $T$, so the distance is not simply $|s(6)|$.

subtopic: Z-interval for a mean with known standard deviation
statement: The time, in seconds, that a caller waits before speaking to an agent is normally distributed with standard deviation $7.2$ seconds. A random sample of $40$ callers has a mean waiting time of $52.3$ seconds. (a) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean waiting time. [3] (b) Write down the margin of error of this interval, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) A manager claims that the population mean waiting time is $50$ seconds. State, with a reason, whether the confidence interval supports this claim. [2]
markscheme: (a) Use of a $z$-interval with $\sigma=7.2$, $n=40$, $\bar x=52.3$ [M1] Lower end $=50.1$ [A1] Upper end $=54.5$ [A1] so the interval is $(50.1,\,54.5)$. [3 marks] (b) Margin of error $=1.96\times\dfrac{7.2}{\sqrt{40}}=2.23$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $50$ is not in the interval $(50.1,\,54.5)$ [R1] so the interval does not support the manager's claim (the true mean is likely greater than $50$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Because $\sigma$ is known you use a $z$-interval (the normal distribution), not a $t$-interval. For the margin of error, it is half the width of the interval.

subtopic: T-interval from raw data
statement: A random sample of $12$ lengths, in cm, of a species of leaf is recorded: $23.4,\ 25.1,\ 22.8,\ 26.0,\ 24.3,\ 23.9,\ 25.5,\ 22.6,\ 24.8,\ 23.1,\ 25.9,\ 24.4$. (a) Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and population standard deviation. [2] (b) Find a $99\%$ confidence interval for the population mean length. [3] (c) State one assumption you made in part (b). [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=24.3$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=1.18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of a $t$-interval with $n-1=11$ degrees of freedom [M1] Lower end $=23.3$ [A1] Upper end $=25.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The lengths are (approximately) normally distributed [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Population standard deviation is unknown here, so use the $t$-interval with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. Use $s_{n-1}$ (the unbiased estimate), not the value $\sigma_n$ that your calculator also displays.

subtopic: Margin of error and required sample size
statement: The masses of ostrich eggs are normally distributed with standard deviation $15$ g. A random sample of $n$ eggs is used to construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean mass. (a) Show that the margin of error of the interval is $\dfrac{29.4}{\sqrt n}$ grams. [2] (b) Find the smallest sample size for which the margin of error is at most $2$ g. [3] (c) Find the smallest sample size needed for a margin of error of at most $2$ g if a $99\%$ confidence interval is used instead. [2]
markscheme: (a) Margin of error $=z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ with $z=1.96$ for $95\%$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1.96\times15}{\sqrt n}=\dfrac{29.4}{\sqrt n}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{29.4}{\sqrt n}\le2$ [M1] $\sqrt n\ge14.7$, so $n\ge216.09$ [A1] $n=217$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=2.576$ so $\dfrac{2.576\times15}{\sqrt n}\le2$ [M1] $n\ge373.2$, so $n=374$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When asked for a minimum sample size, always round up to the next integer, even if the decimal part is small. Check that your value actually satisfies the inequality.

subtopic: Recovering sample standard deviation from an interval
statement: A random sample of $25$ values is taken from a normal population. A $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean, calculated using the $t$-distribution, is $(14.2,\ 17.8)$. (a) Write down the sample mean. [1] (b) Find the value of the unbiased estimate $s_{n-1}$ of the population standard deviation. [3] (c) A second interval is calculated from the same sample mean and the same value of $s_{n-1}$, but using the normal critical value $1.96$ instead of the $t$ critical value. State, with a reason, whether the second interval is wider or narrower than the first. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=\dfrac{14.2+17.8}{2}=16.0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Margin of error $=\dfrac{17.8-14.2}{2}=1.8$ [M1] $t_{24,\,0.975}=2.064$ so $2.064\times\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{25}}=1.8$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=4.36$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Narrower [A1] because $1.96<2.064$ (the $z$ critical value is smaller than the $t$ critical value) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The centre of a confidence interval is the sample mean and its half-width is the margin of error; use both to work backwards. The $t$ critical value depends on $n-1=24$ degrees of freedom.

subtopic: Paired data: confidence interval for mean difference
statement: Eight athletes complete as many push-ups as they can in one minute before and after a six-week programme. The results are given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Athlete}&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline \text{Before}&10&14&10&11&9&13&8&12\\\hline \text{After}&12&15&9&14&11&16&10&13\\\hline\end{array}$$ Let $d$ be the number of push-ups after minus the number before. (a) Find the mean and the standard deviation $s_{n-1}$ of $d$. [2] (b) Assuming that the differences are normally distributed, find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean difference. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the interval suggests that the programme increases the mean number of push-ups. [2]
markscheme: (a) Differences are $2,\,1,\,-1,\,3,\,2,\,3,\,2,\,1$ [M1] $\bar d=1.625$ and $s_{n-1}=1.30$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of a $t$-interval with $7$ degrees of freedom [M1] Lower end $=0.536$ [A1] Upper end $=2.71$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Zero is not in the interval $(0.536,\,2.71)$ [R1] and the whole interval is positive, so there is evidence that the mean number of push-ups increases [A1] [2 marks]
tips: With paired data, work with the differences and treat them as a single sample. A confidence interval for a mean difference that excludes zero is evidence of a real change.

subtopic: Interpreting a confidence interval (no calculator)
statement: A random sample of $36$ observations is taken from a normal population with standard deviation $12$. The sample mean is $80$. (a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. [1] (b) Given that the critical value for a $95\%$ confidence interval is $1.96$, find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean. [2] (c) The sample size is increased to $144$ and the sample mean is still $80$. State, with a reason, how the width of the $95\%$ confidence interval changes. [2] (d) Ravi says: 'There is a $95\%$ probability that the population mean lies in the interval found in part (b).' Explain why this statement is not correct. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $80\pm1.96\times2$ [M1] $(76.08,\ 83.92)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The width is halved [A1] because the standard error becomes $\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{144}}=1$, half of the previous value [R1] [2 marks] (d) The population mean is a fixed (unknown) number, so it either is or is not in this particular interval [R1] The $95\%$ refers to the method: in repeated sampling, about $95\%$ of such intervals would contain the mean [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Quadrupling the sample size halves the width because the margin of error is proportional to $1/\sqrt n$. In interpretation questions, say that the confidence level describes the long-run behavior of the method, not the probability for one fixed interval.

subtopic: Comparing 90% and 99% intervals
statement: A random sample of $30$ pieces of fruit from a large orchard has mean mass $18.5$ g and standard deviation $s_{n-1}=4.2$ g. Assume the masses are normally distributed. (a) Find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the population mean mass. [2] (b) Find a $99\%$ confidence interval for the population mean mass. [2] (c) Find the width of each interval, and explain why they differ. [2]
markscheme: (a) $t$-interval with $29$ degrees of freedom [M1] $(17.2,\ 19.8)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(16.4,\ 20.6)$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) Widths: $2.61$ g for $90\%$ and $4.23$ g for $99\%$ [A1] A higher confidence level needs a larger critical value, so the interval must be wider [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Same data, higher confidence level means a wider interval: you buy more certainty with less precision. Use your calculator's interval function rather than computing critical values by hand.

subtopic: Interval for a mean from a frequency table
statement: A shop records the number of items $x$ in each of $50$ randomly chosen customer transactions. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \text{Frequency}&4&9&15&12&7&3\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean number of items per transaction. [3] (c) The shop owner states that the mean number of items is at least $4$. Comment on this statement. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=3.36$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=1.32$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t$-interval with $49$ degrees of freedom [M1] $(2.98,\ 3.74)$ [A1] [A1] [3 marks] (c) $4$ is greater than the upper end $3.74$, so the data do not support the owner's statement [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Enter the data into the calculator as a list with a frequency list. Make sure you read off $s_{n-1}$ (the sample standard deviation) and not $\sigma_n$.

subtopic: Finding the confidence level from an interval
statement: The lifetimes of a type of battery have standard deviation $10$ hours. A random sample of $50$ batteries is used to construct a confidence interval $(117.5,\ 122.5)$ for the population mean lifetime. (a) Write down the sample mean. [1] (b) Find the confidence level of this interval, as a percentage correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) The confidence level is kept the same. Find the sample size needed to halve the width of the interval. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=120$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Margin of error $=2.5$, so $z\times\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{50}}=2.5$ [M1] $z=1.768$ [A1] Confidence level $=P(-1.768<Z<1.768)=2\Phi(1.768)-1$ [M1] $=92.3\%$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Halving the width requires $\sqrt n$ to double, so $n=200$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Work backwards: margin of error, then the critical $z$-value, then the central probability. The area between $-z$ and $z$ is the confidence level.

subtopic: T-interval and scaling to a total
statement: A random sample of $18$ bags of flour has mean mass $502.4$ g and standard deviation $s_{n-1}=6.1$ g. The masses are assumed to be normally distributed. (a) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean mass of a bag, giving the endpoints correct to one decimal place. [3] (b) A pallet holds $200$ such bags. Use your interval from part (a) to find a $95\%$ confidence interval, in kilograms to the nearest kilogram, for the mean total mass of the flour on a pallet. [2] (c) Explain why it is necessary to assume the masses are normally distributed. [1]
markscheme: (a) $t$-interval with $17$ degrees of freedom [M1] Lower end $=499.4$ [A1] Upper end $=505.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Multiply both ends by $200$ [M1] $(99.9\text{ kg},\ 101.1\text{ kg})$ giving $(100\text{ kg},\ 101\text{ kg})$ to the nearest kilogram [A1] Accept answers obtained from unrounded endpoints. [2 marks] (c) The sample size is small, so the $t$-interval is only valid if the population is normal [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Multiplying a mean by a constant multiplies both ends of its confidence interval by the same constant. Be careful with units when converting from grams to kilograms.

subtopic: Estimates from summary statistics then t-interval
statement: A random sample of $15$ observations of a normally distributed variable $X$ gives $\sum x=312.0$ and $\sum x^2=6549.8$. (a) Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and population variance. [3] (b) Find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the population mean. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=\dfrac{312.0}{15}=20.8$ [A1] $s^2=\dfrac{6549.8-15\times20.8^2}{14}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{60.2}{14}=4.30$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $s=\sqrt{4.3}=2.07$ and use of a $t$-interval with $14$ degrees of freedom [M1] Lower end $=19.9$ [A1] Upper end $=21.7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The unbiased variance estimate divides by $n-1$, not by $n$. Keep the unrounded value of $s$ when you substitute into the interval.

subtopic: Confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and power
statement: This question investigates the connection between confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for the mean of a normal population with known standard deviation. The variable $X$ is normally distributed with unknown mean $\mu$ and known standard deviation $\sigma=6$. A random sample of $n$ observations has sample mean $\bar x$. (a) For $n=36$ and $\bar x=48.5$, find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$. [2] (b) For a general $n$, show that the margin of error of a $95\%$ confidence interval is $\dfrac{11.76}{\sqrt n}$, and hence find the smallest $n$ for which the margin of error is at most $1$. [3] (c) Using the data in part (a), test $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=50$ against $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu\neq50$ at the $5\%$ significance level. Find the $z$-statistic and the $p$-value, state your conclusion, and state whether $50$ lies in the interval found in part (a). [5] (d) Show that, for any value $\mu_0$, the test of $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=\mu_0$ against $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu\neq\mu_0$ at the $5\%$ level rejects $\mathrm{H}_0$ if and only if $\mu_0$ lies outside the interval $\bar x\pm1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$. [3] (e) Ten independent random samples are taken and a $95\%$ confidence interval is calculated from each. Find the probability that (i) all ten intervals contain $\mu$; (ii) at least one interval does not contain $\mu$. Find also the expected number of intervals that do not contain $\mu$. [4] (f) For $n=36$, the test in part (c) is used with critical region determined at the $5\%$ level. Suppose the true mean is actually $\mu=47$. Find the critical values for $\bar X$, and hence find the probability that the test correctly rejects $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=50$ (the power of the test). [4] (g) Hence, or otherwise, find the smallest sample size $n$ for which the power of the test of $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=50$ at the $5\%$ level is at least $0.91$ when the true mean is $47$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Standard error $=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{36}}=1$ [M1] $(46.5,\ 50.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Margin of error $=1.96\times\dfrac{6}{\sqrt n}=\dfrac{11.76}{\sqrt n}$ [A1][AG] $\dfrac{11.76}{\sqrt n}\le1$ so $n\ge11.76^2=138.3$ [M1] $n=139$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=\dfrac{48.5-50}{6/\sqrt{36}}=-1.5$ [M1] [A1] $p$-value $=2P(Z<-1.5)=0.134$ [A1] $0.134>0.05$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is insufficient evidence that $\mu\ne50$ [A1] $50$ lies in $(46.5,\,50.5)$, consistent with not rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ [A1] [5 marks] (d) Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ iff $\left|\dfrac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\right|>1.96$ [M1] iff $|\bar x-\mu_0|>1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ [A1] iff $\mu_0<\bar x-1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ or $\mu_0>\bar x+1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$, i.e. $\mu_0$ outside the interval [R1] [3 marks] (e) (i) $0.95^{10}=0.599$ [A1] (ii) $1-0.95^{10}=0.401$ [A1] Number not containing $\mu$ is $\mathrm{B}(10,0.05)$ [M1] Expected number $=10\times0.05=0.5$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}\left(50,\,1^2\right)$; critical values $50\pm1.96=48.04$ and $51.96$ [A1] When $\mu=47$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}(47,\,1^2)$ [M1] Power $=P(\bar X<48.04)+P(\bar X>51.96)$ [M1] $=0.851$ (the upper tail is negligible) [A1] [4 marks] (g) Critical values $50\pm1.96\dfrac{6}{\sqrt n}$ [M1] Power $=P\left(\bar X<50-\dfrac{11.76}{\sqrt n}\right)+P\left(\bar X>50+\dfrac{11.76}{\sqrt n}\right)$ where $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}\left(47,\dfrac{36}{n}\right)$ [M1] Evaluate for increasing $n$ (table or solver): $n=43$ gives $0.906$ [A1] $n=44$ gives $0.913$, so smallest $n=44$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Part (d) is the key idea: a two-sided $5\%$ test and a $95\%$ confidence interval use exactly the same critical value, so they always agree. In part (g), compute the power for several values of $n$ with your GDC, remembering that both the critical values and the standard error change with $n$.

subtopic: One-sample t-test, one-tailed
statement: A machine is set to fill bottles with $50.0$ cl of juice. An inspector suspects that the machine underfills. The volumes, in cl, of a random sample of $10$ bottles are: $48.2,\ 51.5,\ 49.8,\ 47.9,\ 50.6,\ 46.8,\ 49.1,\ 48.5,\ 50.2,\ 47.4$. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (c) Perform a $t$-test and find the $p$-value. [2] (d) Using a $5\%$ significance level, state the conclusion of the test in context. [2] (e) State one assumption needed for the test to be valid. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=49.0$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=1.51$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=50$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu<50$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) One-sample $t$-test with $9$ degrees of freedom, $t=-2.10$ [M1] $p=0.0325$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0325<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level that the machine underfills (mean volume is less than $50$ cl) [A1] [2 marks] (e) The volumes are (approximately) normally distributed [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The alternative hypothesis is one-tailed here because the inspector suspects underfilling, not just a difference. Always finish with a conclusion in the context of the question.

subtopic: Two-tailed z-test for a mean
statement: The lifetime of a type of light bulb is normally distributed with standard deviation $12$ hours. The manufacturer claims that the mean lifetime is $100$ hours. A random sample of $64$ bulbs has a mean lifetime of $103.2$ hours. A test is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level to see whether the mean lifetime differs from the claim. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value of the test. [3] (c) State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=100$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu\ne100$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $z=\dfrac{103.2-100}{12/\sqrt{64}}=2.13$ [M1] [A1] $p=2P(Z>2.13)=0.0329$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.0329<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that the mean lifetime differs from $100$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a two-tailed test, double the tail probability before comparing with the significance level. A known population standard deviation means a $z$-test.

subtopic: Two-sample pooled t-test
statement: Two teaching methods, A and B, are compared. Method A is used with a random sample of $12$ students and method B with an independent random sample of $15$ students. Test scores (assumed normally distributed with equal population variances) are summarised below, where $s$ is the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline &n&\text{mean}&s\\\hline \text{Method A}&12&34.2&3.1\\\hline \text{Method B}&15&31.8&2.7\\\hline\end{array}$$ A teacher claims that method A gives a higher mean score than method B. (a) State the hypotheses for a test of the claim. [2] (b) Find the pooled estimate of the common population variance. [2] (c) Find the $p$-value for a pooled two-sample $t$-test. [2] (d) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu_A=\mu_B$ [A1] $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu_A>\mu_B$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s_p^2=\dfrac{11\times3.1^2+14\times2.7^2}{25}$ [M1] $=8.31$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Pooled two-sample $t$-test with $25$ degrees of freedom [M1] $t=2.15$, $p=0.0207$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0207<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that method A gives a higher mean score [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The alternative hypothesis follows the teacher's claim, so the test is one-tailed. Choose the pooled option on your GDC because equal variances are assumed.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit: testing a die
statement: A die is rolled $130$ times with the results shown. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Score}&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \text{Frequency}&18&25&14&22&31&20\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test at the $5\%$ significance level is used to test whether the die is fair. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Find the expected frequency for each score, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) Find the value of the $\chi^2$ statistic. [2] (d) Write down the number of degrees of freedom and the $p$-value. [2] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the die is fair (scores are uniformly distributed) [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{130}{6}=21.7$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1] $\chi^2=8.00$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\nu=5$ [A1] $p=0.156$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $0.156>0.05$ (equivalently $8.00<11.07$), so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is insufficient evidence that the die is unfair [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For a goodness of fit test with no estimated parameters, degrees of freedom are the number of categories minus one. Not rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ does not prove the die is fair.

subtopic: Chi-squared test for independence with a contingency table
statement: Students at two schools, P and Q, were asked how they usually travel to school. The results are given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline &\text{Walk}&\text{Bus}&\text{Car}\\\hline \text{School P}&30&45&25\\\hline \text{School Q}&50&40&30\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Show that the expected number of School P students who travel by bus is $38.6$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the $\chi^2$ statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the method of travel is independent of the school [A1] [1 mark] (b) Row total $=100$, column total $=85$, grand total $=220$ [M1] $E=\dfrac{100\times85}{220}=38.6$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1] $\chi^2=3.96$ [A1] $p=0.138$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.138>0.05$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is insufficient evidence that travel method depends on school [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Expected frequency is row total times column total divided by grand total. Degrees of freedom for an $r\times c$ table are $(r-1)(c-1)$.

subtopic: Goodness of fit to a Poisson model with combining cells
statement: The number of cars passing a checkpoint in each of $100$ one-minute intervals is recorded. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Cars}&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\text{ or more}\\\hline \text{Frequency}&10&28&26&19&10&5&2\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test is used at the $5\%$ significance level to test whether the number of cars per minute follows a Poisson distribution with mean $2$. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Find the expected frequency for $2$ cars, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) The expected frequencies for $5$ cars and for $6$ or more cars are $3.61$ and $1.66$. Explain why these two categories must be combined, and write down the observed and expected frequencies of the combined category. [3] (d) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (e) Find the $\chi^2$ statistic and the $p$-value. [2] (f) State the conclusion of the test. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the number of cars per minute follows $\mathrm{Po}(2)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $100\times P(X=2)=100\times\dfrac{e^{-2}2^2}{2!}=27.1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Expected frequencies below $5$ make the $\chi^2$ approximation unreliable [R1] Combined category is '$5$ or more' with observed frequency $5+2=7$ [A1] and expected frequency $3.61+1.66=5.27$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) There are $6$ categories after combining, so $\nu=6-1=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $\chi^2=1.72$ [A1] $p=0.886$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) $0.886>0.05$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; the Poisson model with mean $2$ is a reasonable fit [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Check every expected frequency before you run the test and combine neighboring categories if any is below $5$; the degrees of freedom are based on the number of categories after combining.

subtopic: One-tailed binomial test and critical region
statement: Historically, $30\%$ of patients with a certain condition recover within a week. A new treatment is given to $25$ randomly chosen patients, and $13$ recover within a week. Let $p$ be the probability that a patient given the new treatment recovers within a week. A test at the $5\%$ significance level is carried out to see whether the treatment improves the recovery rate. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value of the test. [3] (c) State the conclusion of the test in context. [2] (d) Find the critical region for the test, and the actual significance level of the test. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.3$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p>0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(25,0.3)$ [M1] $p$-value $=P(X\ge13)=1-P(X\le12)$ [M1] $=0.0175$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.0175<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is sufficient evidence that the treatment improves the recovery rate [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X\ge12)=0.0442\le0.05$ but $P(X\ge11)=0.0978>0.05$ [M1] Critical region is $X\ge12$ [A1] Actual significance level $=0.0442$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For an upper-tailed binomial test the $p$-value is $P(X\ge x_{\text{obs}})$, so use $1-P(X\le x_{\text{obs}}-1)$. The critical region contains the largest set of extreme values whose probability does not exceed the significance level.

subtopic: Type I and Type II errors in a binomial test
statement: A website owner claims that $40\%$ of visitors click on an advertisement. A skeptic believes the proportion $p$ is lower. The skeptic selects $20$ visitors at random and decides to reject the owner's claim if at most $3$ of them click on the advertisement. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the probability of a Type I error. [2] (c) Show that the critical region $\{0,1,2,3\}$ is the largest that gives a probability of a Type I error of at most $5\%$. [2] (d) Describe, in context, what a Type I error would mean. [1] (e) Suppose the true value of $p$ is $0.2$. Find the probability of a Type II error. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.4$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p<0.4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.4)$ [M1] $P(X\le3)=0.0160$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X\le4)=0.0510$ [A1] which is greater than $0.05$, so $X\le3$ is the largest critical region [R1] [2 marks] (d) Concluding that fewer than $40\%$ of visitors click when in fact $40\%$ do [A1] [1 mark] (e) Type II error means accepting $\mathrm{H}_0$ when it is false, i.e. $X\ge4$ [M1] With $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.2)$ [M1] $P(X\ge4)=1-P(X\le3)=0.589$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A Type I error is rejecting a true $\mathrm{H}_0$, and its probability is the probability of landing in the critical region when $p=p_0$. A Type II error uses the true (alternative) value of $p$ and the acceptance region.

subtopic: Poisson test for a mean with a changed interval
statement: A factory's cutting process leaves on average $2.5$ defects per sheet of metal, and defects occur randomly and independently. After a change to the process, a total of $4$ defects is found on $4$ randomly chosen sheets. A test at the $5\%$ significance level is carried out to see whether the mean number of defects per sheet has decreased. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value. [2] (c) State the conclusion of the test in context. [2] (d) Find the critical region for the total number of defects on $4$ sheets, and the probability of a Type I error. [2] (e) The new process actually produces a mean of $1.5$ defects per sheet. Find the probability of a Type II error. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:\lambda=2.5$ per sheet, $\mathrm{H}_1:\lambda<2.5$ per sheet [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, the total defects on $4$ sheets $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(10)$ [M1] $p$-value $=P(X\le4)=0.0293$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.0293<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is sufficient evidence that the mean number of defects per sheet has decreased [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X\le5)=0.0671>0.05$ so the critical region is $X\le4$ [A1] Probability of a Type I error $=0.0293$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Now $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(6)$ [M1] Type II error $=P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)=0.715$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Scale the Poisson mean to match the sample: four sheets means a mean of $4\lambda$. The probability of a Type II error is calculated with the true value of the parameter, outside the critical region.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit by hand
statement: A genetics model predicts that the offspring of a certain cross of plants have four types of seed in the ratio $9:3:3:1$. In an experiment, $160$ offspring are observed with $84$, $36$, $28$ and $12$ plants of the four types respectively. A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) Find the expected frequencies under the model. [2] (b) Show that the value of the $\chi^2$ statistic is $\dfrac{32}{15}$. [3] (c) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. Given that the critical value at the $5\%$ level is $7.815$, state the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{9}{16}\times160=90$ [M1] Expected frequencies $90,\ 30,\ 30,\ 10$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\chi^2=\dfrac{(84-90)^2}{90}+\dfrac{(36-30)^2}{30}+\dfrac{(28-30)^2}{30}+\dfrac{(12-10)^2}{10}$ [M1] $=\dfrac25+\dfrac65+\dfrac2{15}+\dfrac25$ [A1] $=\dfrac{32}{15}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) $\nu=4-1=3$ [A1] $\dfrac{32}{15}=2.13<7.815$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; the data are consistent with the $9:3:3:1$ ratio [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the ratio to split the total into expected counts: divide $160$ by $9+3+3+1=16$ first. Simplify each fraction before adding so the arithmetic stays manageable without a calculator.

subtopic: Paired t-test and confidence interval for improvement
statement: Eight trainees take a skills test before and after a training course. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Trainee}&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline \text{Before}&78&74&85&70&71&80&70&76\\\hline \text{After}&82&75&90&68&77&85&72&80\\\hline\end{array}$$ Assume the differences (after minus before) are normally distributed. (a) State suitable hypotheses for a test of whether the course improves the mean score. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value for a suitable $t$-test. [3] (c) State the conclusion of the test at the $1\%$ significance level. [2] (d) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean improvement. [2] (e) Explain why a two-sample $t$-test would not be appropriate for this data. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu_d=0$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu_d>0$ where $d=$ after $-$ before [A1] [1 mark] (b) Differences $4,1,5,-2,6,5,2,4$ with $\bar d=3.125$, $s_{n-1}=2.64$ [M1] Paired one-tailed $t$-test with $7$ degrees of freedom [M1] $p=0.00617$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.00617<0.01$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is sufficient evidence that the course improves mean score [A1] [2 marks] (d) $t$-interval with $7$ degrees of freedom [M1] $(0.916,\ 5.33)$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) The two sets of scores come from the same trainees, so they are not independent samples [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Paired data requires a test on the differences, not a comparison of two separate samples. Define the direction of the difference clearly so your alternative hypothesis matches it.

subtopic: Chi-squared independence test by hand
statement: A survey of $200$ people records their favorite brand (Brand X or Brand Y) and their age group. The results are shown. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|}\hline &\text{Brand X}&\text{Brand Y}\\\hline \text{Under 30}&20&30\\\hline \text{30 to 49}&40&30\\\hline \text{50 and over}&40&40\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Show that the expected frequency for the 'Under 30, Brand X' cell is $25$. [1] (c) Given that the expected frequencies for the other cells are $25$, $35$, $35$, $40$, $40$ (in the order of the table, row by row), show that the $\chi^2$ statistic is $\dfrac{24}{7}$. [3] (d) The critical value at the $5\%$ level is $5.991$. Write down the number of degrees of freedom and state the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: favorite brand is independent of age group [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{50\times100}{200}=25$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (c) $\chi^2=\dfrac{(20-25)^2}{25}+\dfrac{(30-25)^2}{25}+\dfrac{(40-35)^2}{35}+\dfrac{(30-35)^2}{35}+0+0$ [M1] $=1+1+\dfrac57+\dfrac57$ [A1] $=\dfrac{24}{7}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (d) $\nu=(3-1)(2-1)=2$ [A1] $\dfrac{24}{7}=3.43<5.991$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; no evidence that brand preference depends on age group [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Terms where the observed and expected frequencies are equal contribute zero, so scan the table for them first. Compare the statistic with the critical value, not with the significance level.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities, mean, variance and mode
statement: The random variable $X$ is binomially distributed with $n=15$ and $p=0.35$. (a) Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X=5)$. [1] (c) Find $P(X\ge8)$. [2] (d) Write down the mode of $X$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{E}(X)=15\times0.35=5.25$ [A1] $\mathrm{Var}(X)=15\times0.35\times0.65=3.41$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X=5)=0.212$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P(X\ge8)=1-P(X\le7)$ [M1] $=0.113$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Mode $=5$ [A1] (since $P(X=5)=0.212$ is the largest probability, compared with $P(X=4)=0.179$ and $P(X=6)=0.191$) [1 mark]
tips: For 'at least' probabilities use the complement, $1-P(X\le k-1)$, taking care with the boundary value. The mode is the value with the largest probability; check its neighbors on your GDC.

subtopic: Poisson probabilities over different time intervals
statement: Calls arrive at a help desk randomly and independently at a mean rate of $3.4$ calls per hour. (a) Find the probability that at least $2$ calls arrive in a given hour. [2] (b) Find the probability that exactly $5$ calls arrive in a given two-hour period. [2] (c) Find the probability that no calls arrive in a given $30$-minute period. [2] (d) Find the expected number of calls in an $8$-hour day. [1]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(3.4)$, $P(X\ge2)=1-P(X\le1)$ [M1] $=0.853$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Mean for two hours is $6.8$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(6.8)$ [M1] $P(Y=5)=0.135$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Mean for $30$ minutes is $1.7$ [M1] $P(W=0)=e^{-1.7}=0.183$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $3.4\times8=27.2$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Always rescale the Poisson mean to match the length of the interval in the question before calculating a probability. The mean is proportional to the time interval.

subtopic: Normal distribution: finding mean and standard deviation from percentiles
statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $P(X<42)=0.1$ and $P(X>71)=0.2$. (a) Find the values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [5] (b) Find $P(X>65)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{42-\mu}{\sigma}=-1.2816$ [A1] $\dfrac{71-\mu}{\sigma}=0.8416$ [A1] Attempt to solve the simultaneous equations (e.g. subtract) [M1] $\sigma=\dfrac{29}{2.1232}=13.7$ [A1] $\mu=59.5$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $X\sim\mathrm{N}(59.5,\,13.7^2)$ [M1] $P(X>65)=0.344$ [A1] (using unrounded values from part (a); accept $0.343$ to $0.344$) [2 marks]
tips: Convert each percentile to a $z$-value with the inverse normal function; the lower percentile gives a negative $z$. Use unrounded values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$ in later parts.

subtopic: Sum of independent Poisson random variables and conditional probability
statement: The number of customers arriving at counter A in a $10$-minute period is $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(2.5)$ and the number arriving at counter B in the same period is $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(3.1)$. The variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent. Let $S=X+Y$. (a) State the distribution of $S$ and find $P(S\ge8)$. [3] (b) Find $P(X=2\mid S=5)$. [4] (c) Find the probability that, over three independent $10$-minute periods, the total number of customers arriving at the two counters is at most $15$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $S\sim\mathrm{Po}(5.6)$ [A1] $P(S\ge8)=1-P(S\le7)$ [M1] $=0.203$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(X=2\mid S=5)=\dfrac{P(X=2)\,P(Y=3)}{P(S=5)}$ [M1] [M1] $=\dfrac{0.2565\times0.2237}{0.1697}$ [A1] $=0.338$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Total over three periods $\sim\mathrm{Po}(16.8)$ [M1] $P(\le15)=0.390$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the means added. For the conditional probability, write the event $\{X=2\}\cap\{S=5\}$ as $\{X=2\}\cap\{Y=3\}$ and use independence.

subtopic: Linear combinations of independent normal random variables
statement: A box of tea has mass (in grams) $B\sim\mathrm{N}(120,\,5^2)$. Each of six identical tins that are put in the box has mass $X\sim\mathrm{N}(250,\,4^2)$. All masses are independent. Let $T$ be the total mass of the box and its six tins. (a) Find $\mathrm{E}(T)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(T)$. [3] (b) Find $P(T>1630)$. [2] (c) Find the probability that the mean mass of the six tins is greater than $253$ g. [3]
tips: The variance of a sum of six independent copies is $6\sigma^2$, not $36\sigma^2$; the latter would be for $6X$. For a mean of $n$ values, the variance is $\sigma^2/n$.

subtopic: Central limit theorem for a sample mean
statement: The length of a phone call to a service center has a skewed distribution with mean $7.2$ minutes and standard deviation $3.5$ minutes. A random sample of $50$ calls is taken, and $\bar X$ denotes the mean length of these calls. (a) Explain why $\bar X$ can be modeled by a normal distribution. [1] (b) Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $\bar X$. [2] (c) Find $P(\bar X>8)$. [2] (d) Explain why this approach cannot be used to find the probability that a single call lasts more than $8$ minutes. [1]
markscheme: (a) By the central limit theorem, the sample mean of a large sample ($n=50$) is approximately normally distributed [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathrm{E}(\bar X)=7.2$ [A1] standard deviation $=\dfrac{3.5}{\sqrt{50}}=0.495$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}(7.2,\,0.495^2)$ [M1] $P(\bar X>8)=0.0530$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) A single call has a skewed distribution, so it is not normal [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The central limit theorem applies to the sample mean, not to individual observations. The standard deviation of the sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

subtopic: Unbiased estimates from one sample and combining two samples
statement: A random sample of $8$ values of a variable is: $12.4,\ 13.1,\ 11.8,\ 12.9,\ 13.5,\ 12.2,\ 12.7,\ 13.0$. (a) Find the sample mean and an unbiased estimate of the population variance, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) A second independent random sample of $12$ values from the same population has mean $13.0$ and unbiased estimate of variance $0.35$. The two samples are combined into a single sample of size $20$. Find (i) the mean of the combined sample; (ii) an unbiased estimate of the population variance based on the combined sample, correct to 3 significant figures. [6]
tips: To combine samples, work with sums of squares: $\sum x^2=(n-1)s^2+n\bar x^2$ for each sample. You cannot simply average the two variances.

subtopic: Discrete random variable: expectation and variance (no calculator)
statement: The discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution $P(X=x)=k(5-x)$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{10}$. [2] (b) Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $\mathrm{E}(3X-2)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(3X-2)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $k(4+3+2+1)=1$ [M1] $10k=1$, so $k=\dfrac1{10}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\mathrm{E}(X)=\dfrac{1\times4+2\times3+3\times2+4\times1}{10}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{20}{10}=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathrm{E}(X^2)=\dfrac{1\times4+4\times3+9\times2+16\times1}{10}=5$ [M1] [A1] $\mathrm{Var}(X)=5-2^2=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathrm{E}(3X-2)=3\times2-2=4$ [A1] $\mathrm{Var}(3X-2)=3^2\times1=9$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The probabilities must sum to $1$; use this to find $k$ first. A constant added to $X$ shifts the mean but not the variance, while a multiplier is squared in the variance.

subtopic: Poisson distribution with exact answers
statement: The random variable $X$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $4$. (a) Show that $P(X\le1)=5e^{-4}$. [2] (b) Find $P(X=2\mid X\ge1)$, giving your answer in terms of $e$. [3] (c) Find $\mathrm{E}(2X+1)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(2X+1)$. [2]
tips: For a Poisson distribution the mean and variance are equal, which gives $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4$. In a conditional probability where the condition contains the event, the numerator is just the probability of the event.

subtopic: Binomial: smallest sample size and standard deviation
statement: Each component produced by a machine is defective with probability $0.15$, independently of other components. (a) A batch contains $12$ components. Find the probability that at least $2$ components in the batch are defective. [2] (b) Find the smallest number of components that must be tested so that the probability of finding at least one defective component is greater than $0.9$. [3] (c) A sample of $40$ components is tested. Find the standard deviation of the number of defective components. [1]
tips: For 'at least one' questions use $1-P(\text{none})=1-q^n$ and solve the inequality with logarithms (dividing by $\ln0.85$, which is negative, reverses the inequality), and check by substitution. Round the answer up.

subtopic: Normal probability feeding a binomial model
statement: The mass of coffee in a jar is normally distributed with mean $50$ g and standard deviation $3$ g. A jar is classed as underweight if its mass is less than $48$ g. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen jar is underweight. [2] (b) Eight jars are chosen at random. Using the unrounded value from part (a), find the probability that exactly two of them are underweight. [2] (c) Find the probability that at least two of the eight jars are underweight. [2] (d) State one assumption needed for the calculations in parts (b) and (c). [1]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim\mathrm{N}(50,\,3^2)$, $P(X<48)$ [M1] $=0.252$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $Y\sim\mathrm{B}(8,\,0.2525)$ [M1] $P(Y=2)=0.311$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(Y\ge2)=1-P(Y\le1)$ [M1] $=0.639$ [A1] (accept $0.638$ if the rounded value $0.252$ was used) [2 marks] (d) The masses of the jars are independent (or each jar has the same probability of being underweight) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Store the unrounded probability from part (a) in your calculator and reuse it. A normal calculation for one jar becomes the success probability of a binomial model for several jars.

subtopic: Finding a Poisson mean from a probability
statement: The number of faults $X$ in a roll of cable is modeled by a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$. It is known that $P(X=0)=0.15$. (a) Show that $\lambda=\ln\dfrac{20}{3}$ and write down its value correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [2] (c) Two independent rolls are inspected. Find the probability that the total number of faults is exactly $4$. [2] (d) Find the smallest integer $k$ such that $P(X\le k)\ge0.99$. [2]
tips: Use the exact value of $\lambda=-\ln0.15$ in later parts. For sums of independent Poisson variables, add the means.

subtopic: Pearson correlation and linear regression with prediction
statement: Eight students record the number of hours $x$ they studied for a test and their score $y$ out of $50$. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&2&3&5&6&8&9&11&12\\\hline y&14&17&21&26&28&33&35&41\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient $r$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Use your equation to predict the score of a student who studies for $7$ hours. [1] (d) Interpret the gradient of the regression line in context. [1] (e) Explain why the equation should not be used to predict the score of a student who studies for $30$ hours. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.989$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y=2.53x+9.15$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=26.9$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Each extra hour of study is associated with an increase of about $2.53$ marks [A1] [1 mark] (e) $30$ hours is outside the range of the data (extrapolation), and the predicted score would exceed the maximum of $50$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A strong correlation lets you use the regression line for prediction, but only within the range of the observed data. Interpret the gradient with units: marks per hour.

subtopic: Spearman's rank correlation from raw scores
statement: Two judges score eight dancers. The scores given are given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Dancer}&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline \text{Judge A}&88&95&77&91&68&84&71&80\\\hline \text{Judge B}&8.9&8.1&7.2&9.4&5.5&6.5&6.1&7.6\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Rank the dancers for each judge, giving rank $1$ to the highest score. [2] (b) Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$. [3] (c) Comment on the level of agreement between the two judges. [1]
markscheme: (a) Judge A ranks: $3,1,6,2,8,4,7,5$ [A1] Judge B ranks: $2,3,5,1,8,6,7,4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Differences $d$: $1,-2,1,1,0,-2,0,1$ and $\sum d^2=12$ [M1] [A1] $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\times12}{8(8^2-1)}=\dfrac{6}{7}=0.857$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $r_s$ is close to $1$, so there is strong positive agreement between the judges [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Rank both sets in the same direction before comparing. Spearman's coefficient is the Pearson coefficient calculated on the ranks, and you can also obtain it with your GDC from the rank lists.

subtopic: Regression and correlation from summary statistics (no calculator)
statement: For ten pairs of data $(x,y)$, the following summary statistics are known: $$\sum x=50,\quad\sum y=120,\quad\sum xy=700,\quad\sum x^2=290,\quad\sum y^2=1800.$$ (a) Find $S_{xx}=\sum x^2-\dfrac{(\sum x)^2}{n}$, $S_{yy}=\sum y^2-\dfrac{(\sum y)^2}{n}$ and $S_{xy}=\sum xy-\dfrac{\sum x\sum y}{n}$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (c) Find the value of the Pearson correlation coefficient $r=\dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}$. [2]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ always passes through the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$, which gives the intercept quickly. Look for perfect squares under the square root: $40\times360=14400=120^2$.

subtopic: Exponential model using a log transformation
statement: The number of subscribers $y$ (in thousands) to a streaming service is recorded $t$ years after it was launched. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline t&0&1&2&3&4&5\\\hline y&120&148&175&222&265&330\\\hline\end{array}$$ The relationship is modeled by $y=ab^t$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. In parts (b) to (e), use unrounded values from part (a). (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $\ln y$ on $t$. [2] (b) Hence find the values of $a$ and $b$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Use the regression line from part (a) to predict the number of subscribers when $t=8$. [1] (d) Interpret the value of $b$ in context. [1] (e) Find the time taken for the number of subscribers to double according to the model. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=0.201t+4.79$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\ln y=\ln a+t\ln b$ so $a=e^{4.7854}=120$ [A1] $b=e^{0.2012}=1.22$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=e^{4.7854+8\times0.2012}=599$ thousand [A1] (accept $598$ to $599$) [1 mark] (d) The number of subscribers is multiplied by $1.22$ each year (an increase of about $22.3\%$ per year) [A1] [1 mark] (e) $\dfrac{\ln2}{0.2012}=3.44$ years [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Taking logs turns $y=ab^t$ into a straight line: $\ln y=\ln a+(\ln b)\,t$, so the gradient is $\ln b$ and the intercept is $\ln a$. Keep unrounded coefficients when you predict, as small rounding errors are magnified by the exponential.

subtopic: Power model using log-log regression
statement: The data in the table give the dosage $x$ (mg) of a medicine and the response time reduction $y$ (minutes). $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&5&8&10\\\hline y&3.1&5.2&7.0&10.3&15.8&19.0\\\hline\end{array}$$ A model of the form $y=ax^b$ is suggested. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $\ln y$ on $\ln x$. [2] (b) Hence write down the values of $a$ and $b$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Use the model to estimate $y$ when $x=6$. [1] (d) The correlation coefficient between $\ln x$ and $\ln y$ is $0.999$, correct to 3 significant figures. Comment on the suitability of the model. [1] (e) State what the value of $b$ tells you about how $y$ changes as $x$ increases. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=0.787\ln x+1.11$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $b=0.787$ [A1] $a=e^{1.1058}=3.02$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=3.02\times6^{0.787}=12.4$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $r$ is very close to $1$, so a power model is a good fit for the data [A1] [1 mark] (e) Since $b<1$, $y$ increases as $x$ increases but at a decreasing rate [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For $y=ax^b$ take logs of both variables: $\ln y=\ln a+b\ln x$, and $b$ is the gradient. A strong linear correlation on the log-log scale supports the power model.

subtopic: Chi-squared test for independence with a 3 by 3 table
statement: A transport company surveys $220$ people about their usual way of traveling to work (rail, bus or car) and their age group. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline &\text{Rail}&\text{Bus}&\text{Car}\\\hline \text{Under 30}&22&31&17\\\hline \text{30 to 49}&35&28&27\\\hline \text{50 and over}&13&21&26\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (c) Find the expected frequency for people under $30$ who travel by rail. [1] (d) Find the $\chi^2$ statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (f) State the conclusion at the $10\%$ significance level. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: mode of travel and age group are independent [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(3-1)(3-1)=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{70\times70}{220}=22.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1] $\chi^2=9.12$ [A1] $p=0.0581$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.0581>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level of a relationship between travel mode and age group [A1] [2 marks] (f) $0.0581<0.10$, so reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $10\%$ level; there is evidence of an association [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Check that all expected frequencies exceed $5$ before relying on the test. The conclusion can change with the significance level, so always compare the $p$-value with the level stated.

subtopic: Regression of x on y versus y on x
statement: A coach records the weekly training time $x$ (hours) and the performance score $y$ of seven athletes. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&4&7&9&12&15&18&20\\\hline y&30&36&35&45&48&55&52\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Use the regression line to estimate the score of an athlete who trains for $10$ hours per week. [1] (c) The coach wants to estimate the training time of an athlete with a score of $40$. Find the equation of the appropriate regression line and use it to give an estimate. [2] (d) A student rearranges the equation in part (a) to estimate the training time for a score of $40$ and gets a different answer. Find this answer and explain why it is not the appropriate method. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.967$ [A1] $y=1.56x+24.1$ [A1] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=39.7$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Regression line of $x$ on $y$: $x=0.601y-13.7$ [A1] $x=10.3$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x=\dfrac{40-24.1}{1.56}=10.2$ hours [A1] The regression line of $y$ on $x$ minimizes vertical distances (errors in $y$), so it is only valid for predicting $y$ from $x$; to predict $x$ from $y$ the line of $x$ on $y$ (minimizing horizontal distances) must be used [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ predicts $y$ from $x$; to predict $x$ from $y$ you need the regression line of $x$ on $y$ because the two lines are different unless $r=\pm1$. Use unrounded coefficients for the final estimate.

subtopic: Quadratic regression model
statement: The height $h$ (metres) of a drone above the ground is measured $t$ seconds after it is launched. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline t&0&1&2&3&4&5\\\hline h&2.0&6.1&8.2&8.4&6.3&2.2\\\hline\end{array}$$ Use unrounded values from part (a) in parts (b) and (c). (a) Find a quadratic model of the form $h=at^2+bt+c$ for this data. [2] (b) According to the model, find the maximum height of the drone and the time at which it occurs. [2] (c) Find the time, according to the model, at which the drone lands. [2] (d) The coefficient of determination for the model is $R^2=0.9996$. Comment on the fit of the model. [1]
markscheme: (a) $h=-1.03t^2+5.21t+1.96$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (b) Vertex at $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=2.52$ s [A1] Maximum height $=8.54$ m [A1] (accept $8.54$ or $8.55$) [2 marks] (c) Solve $h=0$ [M1] $t=5.40$ s [A1] [2 marks] (d) $R^2$ is very close to $1$, so the quadratic model fits the data very well [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For a quadratic model, the maximum or minimum occurs at $t=-b/(2a)$, and the landing time is the positive root of $h=0$. Reject the negative root because it makes no sense in context.

subtopic: Regression line properties and linear changes of variables (no calculator)
statement: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ for a set of data is $y=1.5x+4$. The mean of the $x$-values is $10$. (a) Find the mean of the $y$-values. [2] (b) Use the line to estimate $y$ when $x=14$. [1] (c) Each $x$-value is now doubled to give a new variable $u=2x$, and $3$ is added to each $y$-value to give a new variable $v=y+3$. Find the equation of the regression line of $v$ on $u$. [3]
markscheme: (a) The regression line passes through the mean point [M1] $\bar y=1.5\times10+4=19$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=1.5\times14+4=25$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x=\dfrac{u}{2}$ and $y=v-3$ [M1] $v-3=1.5\times\dfrac{u}{2}+4$ [M1] $v=0.75u+7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substituting the transformed variables into the original line is the most reliable approach. Halving the gradient follows from doubling $x$, while adding $3$ to $y$ raises the intercept by $3$.

subtopic: Pearson versus Spearman for a monotonic non-linear relationship
statement: A biologist records the age $x$ (days) and the population $y$ of a bacterial colony. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline y&2&5&11&19&45&80&150&400\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient $r$. [1] (b) Find the Spearman rank correlation coefficient $r_s$. [2] (c) Explain why $r_s$ is greater than $r$ for this data. [2] (d) State which coefficient better describes the relationship, and why. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.807$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Both $x$ and $y$ are in increasing order, so the ranks are identical [M1] $r_s=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y$ increases with $x$ throughout, so the relationship is perfectly monotonic [R1] but it is not linear (it grows faster and faster), so $r<1$ [R1] [2 marks] (d) Spearman's coefficient, because it measures how well the relationship is monotonic, which is what the data show [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Pearson's $r$ measures linear association, whereas Spearman's $r_s$ measures monotonic association using ranks. If the ranks match perfectly then $r_s=1$ regardless of the curve's shape.

subtopic: Logarithmic regression model and extrapolation
statement: A researcher records the skill score $y$ of a learner after $x$ weeks of practice. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&4&7&10&15&20\\\hline y&12.1&17.8&24.5&31.0&35.2&40.8&44.6\\\hline\end{array}$$ The data are modeled by $y=a+b\ln x$. In part (c), use unrounded values from part (a). (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Use the model to estimate the skill score after $12$ weeks. [1] (c) Find the number of weeks of practice that the model predicts is needed to reach a score of $50$. [2] (d) The correlation coefficient between $\ln x$ and $y$ is $0.996$. Comment on the strength of the model. [1] (e) Comment on the reliability of your answer to part (c). [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=10.7$ [A1] $b=10.9$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=10.7+10.9\ln12=37.8$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $50=10.667+10.915\ln x$ [M1] $x=e^{(50-10.667)/10.915}=36.7$ weeks [A1] (accept $36.7$ to $36.8$) [2 marks] (d) $r$ is very close to $1$, so there is a strong linear relationship between $\ln x$ and $y$, and the model fits the data well [A1] [1 mark] (e) $36.7$ weeks is well outside the range of the data ($1$ to $20$ weeks), so it is an extrapolation [R1] and it may be unreliable because the model might not continue to hold (a learner's skill may level off) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The model $y=a+b\ln x$ is linear in $\ln x$, so regress $y$ on $\ln x$ and solve with an exponential to find $x$. Always comment on whether your estimate comes from within the data range.

subtopic: Residuals and the least-squares property
statement: The following table gives five pairs of data. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5\\\hline y&5&7&12&13&18\\\hline\end{array}$$ The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=3.2x+1.4$. (a) Calculate the predicted value $\hat y$ and the residual $y-\hat y$ for each data point. [3] (b) Find the sum of the squares of the residuals for this line. [2] (c) Another line, $y=3x+2$, is considered. Find the sum of the squares of the residuals for this line, and explain how your answer relates to the least-squares regression line. [2]
markscheme: (a) Predicted values: $4.6,\ 7.8,\ 11.0,\ 14.2,\ 17.4$ [A1] Residuals: $0.4,\ -0.8,\ 1.0,\ -1.2,\ 0.6$ [A1] [A1] (follow through for the residuals) [3 marks] (b) $0.4^2+0.8^2+1.0^2+1.2^2+0.6^2$ [M1] $=3.6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Predicted values $5,8,11,14,17$, residuals $0,-1,1,-1,1$, so the sum of squares is $4$ [A1] This is greater than $3.6$, consistent with the regression line minimizing the sum of squared residuals [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A residual is observed minus predicted. The least-squares regression line is the line that makes the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible.

subtopic: Exponential growth model from a regression of ln y on t
statement: The number of followers $F$ (in thousands) of a social media account $t$ months after it was created is modeled using regression of $\ln F$ on $t$, using data for $0\le t\le12$. The regression line is $\ln F=3.20+0.0750\,t$. (a) Show that the model can be written as $F=ab^t$, and find $a$ and $b$ correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Interpret the value of $b$ in context, as a percentage. [1] (c) Find the time taken for the number of followers to double. [2] (d) Use the regression line to estimate the number of followers when $t=30$, and comment on the reliability of the estimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $F=e^{3.2+0.075t}=e^{3.2}\left(e^{0.075}\right)^t$ [M1] $a=e^{3.2}=24.5$ [A1] $b=e^{0.075}=1.08$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The number of followers increases by about $7.8\%$ each month [A1] [1 mark] (c) $e^{0.075t}=2$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln2}{0.075}=9.24$ months [A1] [2 marks] (d) $F=e^{3.2+0.075\times30}=233$ thousand [A1] This is an extrapolation well outside the data range $0\le t\le12$, so it is unreliable [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For an exponential model, $b=e^{\text{gradient}}$ and $a=e^{\text{intercept}}$. For the prediction in part (d), use the regression line directly: the rounded $a$ and $b$ lose accuracy when raised to a large power.

subtopic: Tree diagrams and Bayes' theorem
statement: A factory has two machines. Machine $A$ produces $60\%$ of the items and machine $B$ produces the other $40\%$. Of the items produced by $A$, $3\%$ are defective, and of the items produced by $B$, $5\%$ are defective. An item is chosen at random from the factory's output. (a) Find the probability that the item is defective. [2] (b) Given that the item is defective, find the probability that it was produced by machine $B$. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form. [2] (c) Two items are chosen independently and at random. Find the probability that both are defective. [2]
tips: Draw a quick tree diagram: each branch product is one route to a defective item, and the conditional probability is the route you want divided by the total. In part (c) the items are independent, so multiply the probabilities from part (a).

subtopic: Independent events and set notation
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=0.6$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.8$. (a) Find $P(B)$. [3] (b) Find $P(A'\cap B)$. [2] (c) Find $P(B\mid A\cup B)$, giving your answer as a fraction. [2]
markscheme: (a) Independence: $P(A\cap B)=0.6\,P(B)$ [M1] $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$, so $0.8=0.6+P(B)-0.6P(B)$ [M1] $0.4P(B)=0.2$, so $P(B)=0.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(A'\cap B)=P(B)-P(A\cap B)=0.5-0.3$ [M1] $=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(B\mid A\cup B)=\dfrac{P(B)}{P(A\cup B)}$ [M1] (since $B\subseteq A\cup B$) $=\dfrac{0.5}{0.8}=\dfrac{5}{8}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$; substitute this into the addition formula to get an equation in one unknown. In part (c) the intersection of $B$ with $A\cup B$ is just $B$.

subtopic: Binomial distribution in a sports context
statement: A basketball player scores on each free throw with probability $0.72$, independently of other throws. In a practice session she takes $15$ free throws. Let $X$ be the number of throws she scores. (a) Find the probability that she scores exactly $11$ throws. [2] (b) Find the probability that she scores at least $12$ throws. [2] (c) Find the probability that she scores more throws than the mean number of throws scored. [2] (d) She now takes $n$ throws. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability that she misses at least once exceeds $0.99$. [3]
tips: In part (c) the mean is not an integer, so translate carefully: scoring more than $10.8$ means scoring at least $11$. In part (d) use the complement, 'at least one miss' is $1-P(\text{no misses})$.

subtopic: Normal distribution and inverse normal
statement: The mass, $M$ grams, of eggs laid by a flock of hens is normally distributed with mean $58$ and standard deviation $3.2$. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen egg has mass greater than $60$ grams. [2] (b) The heaviest $10\%$ of eggs are classified as jumbo. Find the minimum mass of a jumbo egg. [2] (c) A carton contains $12$ eggs chosen at random. Find the probability that exactly $2$ of the eggs in the carton are jumbo. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(M>60)$ using the normal distribution on GDC [M1] $=0.266$ ($0.26598\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(M>m)=0.1$, i.e. $P(M<m)=0.9$ [M1] $m=62.1$ ($62.10\ldots$) grams [A1] [2 marks] (c) Number of jumbo eggs $\sim B(12,0.1)$ [M1] $P(=2)=0.230$ ($0.23012\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For 'the heaviest 10%' use the 90th percentile in the inverse normal function. Part (c) needs a switch of distribution: once each egg is simply jumbo or not, the carton count is binomial with $p=0.1$.

subtopic: Poisson distribution and scaling the mean
statement: Calls arrive at a help desk at random, at an average rate of $3.4$ calls every $10$ minutes. Assume the number of calls follows a Poisson distribution. (a) Find the probability that exactly $5$ calls arrive in a given $10$-minute period. [2] (b) Find the probability that at least $2$ calls arrive in a given $5$-minute period. [2] (c) Find the probability that more than $20$ calls arrive in a given hour. [2]
tips: Always rescale the Poisson mean to match the time period in the question before using the GDC. 'More than 20' means $21$ or more, so use $1-P(W\le 20)$.

subtopic: Discrete random variable and linear transformation
statement: The discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution $P(X=x)=k(x+1)$ for $x\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{10}$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) The random variable $Y$ is defined by $Y=5X-4$. Find $E(Y)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $k(1+2+3+4)=1$ [M1] $10k=1$, so $k=\dfrac{1}{10}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $E(X)=\dfrac{0\times1+1\times2+2\times3+3\times4}{10}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{20}{10}=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=\dfrac{0+1\times2+4\times3+9\times4}{10}=\dfrac{50}{10}=5$ [M1][A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=5-2^2=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $E(Y)=5(2)-4=6$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=25\times1=25$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ and remember that the constant shift in $aX+b$ does not affect the variance, while $a$ is squared.

subtopic: Normal distribution with unknown mean and standard deviation
statement: The time, $T$ minutes, taken by a courier to deliver a parcel is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $P(T<40)=0.2$ and $P(T>55)=0.1$. (a) Write down the $z$-values corresponding to $T=40$ and $T=55$. [2] (b) Find the values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [3] (c) Find $P(T>50)$. [1] (d) Find $P(T>50\mid T>40)$. [2]
tips: Standardize both conditions to get a pair of simultaneous equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$; keep full GDC accuracy until the final answer. In part (d), $P(T>40)=0.8$ because $P(T<40)=0.2$.

subtopic: Sampling without replacement
statement: A bag contains $5$ red, $4$ blue and $3$ green counters. Two counters are drawn at random from the bag without replacement. (a) Find the probability that the two counters are the same color. Give your answer as a fraction. [3] (b) Find the probability that at least one of the counters is blue. [2] (c) Given that at least one of the counters is blue, find the probability that both are blue. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(RR)=\dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{4}{11}=\dfrac{20}{132}$, $P(BB)=\dfrac{4}{12}\times\dfrac{3}{11}=\dfrac{12}{132}$, $P(GG)=\dfrac{3}{12}\times\dfrac{2}{11}=\dfrac{6}{132}$ [M1][A1] (equivalently $\dfrac{\binom52+\binom42+\binom32}{\binom{12}{2}}$) $P=\dfrac{38}{132}=\dfrac{19}{66}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(\text{no blue})=\dfrac{8}{12}\times\dfrac{7}{11}=\dfrac{56}{132}=\dfrac{14}{33}$ [M1] $P(\text{at least one blue})=1-\dfrac{14}{33}=\dfrac{19}{33}$ ($0.576$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(BB)=\dfrac{12}{132}=\dfrac{1}{11}$ [A1] $P(BB\mid\text{at least one blue})=\dfrac{1/11}{19/33}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{19}$ ($0.158$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Without replacement the second probability changes: reduce both the numerator and denominator after the first draw. For conditional probability, note that 'both blue' is a subset of 'at least one blue'.

subtopic: Binomial parameters from mean and variance
statement: The random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution with mean $12$ and variance $7.2$. (a) Find the number of trials $n$ and the probability of success $p$. [3] (b) Find $P(X=12)$. [1] (c) Find $P(10\le X\le14)$. [2]
tips: Dividing the variance by the mean immediately gives $1-p$. For a range like $10\le X\le14$, subtract cumulative probabilities carefully: the lower cumulative value is $P(X\le9)$, not $P(X\le10)$.

subtopic: Poisson sums and combined distributions
statement: The number of typing errors on a page of a report written by Anya follows a Poisson distribution with mean $0.8$. The number of typing errors on a page written by Ben follows an independent Poisson distribution with mean $1.3$. A page is formed by combining a section typed by Anya with a section typed by Ben, so that the total number of errors, $T$, on the page is the sum of the two numbers of errors. (a) Write down the distribution of $T$ and find $P(T=2)$. [2] (b) Given that $T=2$, find the probability that Anya made exactly one error. [3] (c) A report has $12$ independent pages, each with the distribution of $T$. Find the probability that at most one page contains no errors. [3]
tips: The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the means added. In part (b), 'one error each' is the only way to have $A=1$ and total $2$, so the numerator is a product of two single-error probabilities.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation of grouped data
statement: The times, in minutes, spent in a store by $50$ customers are summarized in the table. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Time } t & 0\le t<10 & 10\le t<20 & 20\le t<30 & 30\le t<40 & 40\le t<50\\\hline \text{Frequency} & 4 & 11 & 18 & 10 & 7\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Find an estimate for the mean time spent in the store. [2] (b) Find an estimate for the population standard deviation of the times. [2] (c) Write down the modal class and the class that contains the median. [2]
markscheme: (a) midpoints $5,15,25,35,45$ [M1] $\bar t=\dfrac{4(5)+11(15)+18(25)+10(35)+7(45)}{50}=\dfrac{1300}{50}=26$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (b) using GDC with midpoints and frequencies [M1] $\sigma=11.4$ ($11.357\ldots$) minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) modal class: $20\le t<30$ [A1] cumulative frequencies $4,15,33$ so the $25$th and $26$th values lie in $20\le t<30$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use class midpoints as the data values, then enter the list and frequencies in the GDC. Make sure you quote the population standard deviation ($\sigma_x$), not the sample one, when the question says so.

subtopic: Quartiles and the effect of changing a data value
statement: A data set contains the following $11$ values: $$3,\ 5,\ 6,\ 8,\ 9,\ 11,\ 12,\ 13,\ 15,\ 16,\ 34$$ In this question, the lower quartile $Q_1$ is the median of the lower half of the ordered data and the upper quartile $Q_3$ is the median of the upper half, in each case excluding the overall median. (a) Find the median, $Q_1$ and $Q_3$. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) The value $34$ is removed from the data set. Find the mean of the remaining $10$ values. [2] (d) Instead of removing it, the value $34$ is replaced by $20$. State, with a reason, which of the mean, the median and the interquartile range change. [2]
markscheme: (a) median $=11$ [A1] lower half $3,5,6,8,9$ so $Q_1=6$ [A1] upper half $12,13,15,16,34$ so $Q_3=15$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=15-6=9$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) sum of all values is $132$, so the remaining sum is $132-34=98$ [M1] mean $=\dfrac{98}{10}=9.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) the mean changes (the total decreases) [A1] the median ($11$) and the quartiles ($6$ and $15$) are unchanged because the order of the middle values is unchanged, so the median and the IQR do not change [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The mean uses every value, while the median and quartiles depend only on positions in the ordered list. Check whether a replaced value alters the quartile positions before claiming the IQR changes.

subtopic: Pearson correlation and regression line
statement: A cafe records the daily maximum temperature, $x\ ^\circ\text{C}$, and the number of cold drinks sold, $y$, on eight days. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 14 & 17 & 19 & 22 & 24 & 27 & 29 & 31\\\hline y & 185 & 205 & 250 & 270 & 320 & 335 & 385 & 400\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Find the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient $r$ and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient of the regression line in this context. [1] (d) Use the regression line to estimate the number of cold drinks sold on a day with maximum temperature $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$. [1] (e) Explain why the regression line should not be used to estimate sales on a day with maximum temperature $5\ ^\circ\text{C}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.991$ ($0.99076\ldots$) [A1] strong positive (linear) correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=13.1x-7.03$ ($y=13.149\ldots x-7.0329\ldots$) [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) for each $1\ ^\circ\text{C}$ increase in maximum temperature, about $13$ more cold drinks are sold [A1] [1 mark] (d) $y=13.149(25)-7.033=322$ (accept $320$ to $322$) [A1] [1 mark] (e) $5$ is outside the range of the data ($14$ to $31$), so this is extrapolation and may be unreliable [R1] [1 mark]
tips: When interpreting a gradient, always state both variables with units and say 'on average'. Predictions are only reliable within the range of the data (interpolation).

subtopic: Spearman's rank correlation
statement: Two judges score eight contestants in a talent show. Judge $A$ scores out of $10$ and judge $B$ scores out of $100$. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Contestant} & 1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline \text{Judge } A & 7.5&6.0&8.5&9.0&5.5&7.0&6.5&8.0\\\hline \text{Judge } B & 72&65&70&88&60&75&62&80\\\hline\end{array}$$ (a) Write down the rank of each contestant for each judge, giving rank $1$ to the lowest score. [2] (b) Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$. [2] (c) Interpret your value of $r_s$ in context. [1] (d) State one reason why Spearman's coefficient is more appropriate than Pearson's coefficient for comparing the judges' scores. [1]
markscheme: (a) ranks for $A$: $5,2,7,8,1,4,3,6$ [A1] ranks for $B$: $5,3,4,8,1,6,2,7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $r_s$ is the Pearson coefficient of the ranks [M1] $r_s=0.810$ ($0.80952\ldots=\dfrac{17}{21}$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) fairly strong positive association: the two judges tend to rank the contestants in a similar order [A1] [1 mark] (d) the judges use different scales (scores out of $10$ and out of $100$), so only the order of the scores is comparable [R1] (accept: the relationship need not be linear) [1 mark]
tips: Convert both lists to ranks first; the GDC then gives $r_s$ as the Pearson coefficient of the ranks. Spearman's coefficient measures how consistently the order agrees, not whether the relationship is linear.

subtopic: Linear transformations of data
statement: The daily maximum temperatures in a city over a month have a mean of $15\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and a standard deviation of $4\ ^\circ\text{C}$. (a) The temperatures are converted to degrees Fahrenheit using $F=1.8C+32$. Find the mean and standard deviation of the temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit. [2] (b) A set of test scores $x$ has mean $50$ and standard deviation $5$. Each score is transformed using $y=ax+b$, where $a>0$. The transformed scores have mean $70$ and standard deviation $15$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [3] (c) The median of the original scores $x$ is $48$. Write down the median of the transformed scores. [1]
markscheme: (a) mean $=1.8(15)+32=59\ ^\circ\text{F}$ [A1] standard deviation $=1.8\times4=7.2\ ^\circ\text{F}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the standard deviation is multiplied by $a$: $5a=15$ [M1] $a=3$ [A1] $50(3)+b=70$, so $b=-80$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $3(48)-80=64$ [A1] [1 mark]
