markscheme: (a) Once in state $3$ the probability of staying there is $1$ (the third column is $(0,0,1)^T$), so the machine can never leave [R1] [1 mark] (b) Third entry of $\mathbf{T}^4\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1] $0.590$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Probability scrapped after $13$ weeks is $0.945$ and after $14$ weeks is $0.956$ [M1][A1] $n=14$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{T}^{40}\mathbf{s}_0\approx\begin{pmatrix}0.0000532\\0.0000798\\1.00\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] The machine is eventually scrapped with probability tending to $1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: An absorbing state has a column with a $1$ on the leading diagonal. Use the table feature of your GDC to test successive values of $n$ and show the two values either side of your answer.

subtopic: Powers of a matrix by diagonalisation
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}7&-3\\10&-4\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Hence find an expression for $\mathbf{A}^n$ in terms of $n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(7-\lambda)(-4-\lambda)+30=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2-3\lambda+2=0$ [A1] $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=1$: $6x-3y=0$ [M1] giving $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=2$: $5x-3y=0$, giving $\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&5\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{D}^n=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2^n\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1] $\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-5&3\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Attempt to multiply the three matrices [M1] $\mathbf{A}^n=\begin{pmatrix}6\times2^n-5&3-3\times2^n\\10\times2^n-10&6-5\times2^n\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: After finding $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$, test your formula with $n=1$, which must give $\mathbf{A}$. Remember that $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ for a $2\times2$ matrix swaps the leading diagonal, negates the other entries and divides by the determinant.

subtopic: Rate of convergence to a steady state
statement: The weather in a town is either sunny or rainy each day. The transition matrix is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.4\\0.3&0.6\end{pmatrix}$, where the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ (sunny, rainy) to state $i$ on the next day. Today is sunny. (a) Find the steady state probability vector. [3] (b) Find the smallest number of days after which the probability that it is sunny is within $0.001$ of its steady state value. [3] (c) The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $\lambda$. Find $\lambda$, and explain why the probabilities converge to the steady state. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ gives $0.3a=0.4b$ [M1] With $a+b=1$: $a=\frac47\approx0.571$ [A1] $b=\frac37\approx0.429$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Probability sunny after $n$ days from $\mathbf{T}^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] After $5$ days: $0.57247$, difference from $0.571429$ is $0.00104>0.001$ [A1] After $6$ days: difference is $0.00031<0.001$, so $6$ days [A1] [3 marks] (c) Trace $=1.3$, so $\lambda=0.3$ [A1] Since $|\lambda|<1$, the term $\lambda^n$ tends to $0$, so the probabilities approach the steady state [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Compare the difference from the steady state value for consecutive days, and show both so that the smallest $n$ is clear. The second eigenvalue controls how fast the chain converges.

subtopic: Characteristic equation and the inverse
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Show that $\mathbf{A}^2=7\mathbf{A}-10\mathbf{I}$. [2] (c) Hence show that $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{10}\left(7\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}\right)$, and write down $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ as a matrix. [2] (d) Express $\mathbf{A}^3$ in the form $p\mathbf{A}+q\mathbf{I}$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0$ [A1] $\lambda=2$ or $\lambda=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{A}^2=\begin{pmatrix}18&14\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $7\mathbf{A}-10\mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}18&14\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{A}^2-7\mathbf{A}=-10\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{A}(7\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})=10\mathbf{I}$ [M1] $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{A}^3=7\mathbf{A}^2-10\mathbf{A}=7(7\mathbf{A}-10\mathbf{I})-10\mathbf{A}$ [M1] $=39\mathbf{A}-70\mathbf{I}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A $2\times2$ matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, which gives a quick route to inverses and higher powers. Check by multiplying $\mathbf{A}$ by your inverse.

subtopic: General two-state Markov chain from long-term data
statement: A two-state Markov chain has transition matrix $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a&b\\a&1-b\end{pmatrix}$, where $0<a<1$ and $0<b<1$, and the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. (a) Show that $1$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{T}$. [2] (b) Find the other eigenvalue of $\mathbf{T}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [2] It is given that the other eigenvalue is $0.5$ and that the long-term probability of being in state $1$ is $0.4$. (c) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{I})=(-a)(-b)-ba$ [M1] $=0$, so $1$ is an eigenvalue [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) Sum of eigenvalues equals the trace $=2-a-b$ [M1] Other eigenvalue $=1-a-b$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-a-b=0.5$, so $a+b=0.5$ [M1] The steady state $(0.4,0.6)^T$ satisfies $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$, so $0.4(1-a)+0.6b=0.4$ [M1] Hence $-0.4a+0.6b=0$, so $a=1.5b$ [A1] $a=0.3$ and $b=0.2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The long-term vector is an eigenvector for eigenvalue $1$, and the trace gives the sum of the eigenvalues. Write both conditions as equations in $a$ and $b$ and solve them simultaneously.

subtopic: General two-state Markov chain and powers of the transition matrix
statement: This question investigates the long-term behaviour of a two-state Markov chain. A system moves between states $1$ and $2$ in steps. Its transition matrix is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a&b\\a&1-b\end{pmatrix}$, where $0<a<1$ and $0<b<1$. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. The state vector after $n$ steps is $\mathbf{s}_n=\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$. Let $\mu=1-a-b$. (a) Show that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $\mu$. [3] (b) Show that $\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ are eigenvectors of $\mathbf{T}$ corresponding to $1$ and $\mu$ respectively. [2] (c) Let $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}b&1\\a&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Find $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$, and hence show that $$\mathbf{T}^n=\frac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b+a\mu^n&b-b\mu^n\\a-a\mu^n&a+b\mu^n\end{pmatrix}.$$ [5] (d) Given that $|\mu|<1$, find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbf{T}^n$, and deduce that for any initial state vector $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix}p\\1-p\end{pmatrix}$, the long-term state vector is $\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$. [3] (e) Let $a=0.3$ and $b=0.2$, and suppose the system starts in state $2$. Let $p_n$ be the probability that the system is in state $1$ after $n$ steps. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $p_n$ is within $0.001$ of its long-term value. [3] (f) For general $a$ and $b$, let $p_n$ be the probability of being in state $1$ after $n$ steps. (i) Show that $p_{n+1}=\mu p_n+b$. (ii) Let $L=\dfrac{b}{a+b}$. Show that $L=\mu L+b$, and hence show that $p_n-L=\mu^n(p_0-L)$. [4] (g) Let $a=0.7$ and $b=0.6$, and suppose the system starts in state $1$. Find $\mu$ and an expression for $p_n-L$. Hence explain why $p_n$ alternates between values below and above $L$. [3] (h) Now let $a=b=1$. Write down $\mathbf{T}$, find $\mathbf{T}^n$ for even and odd $n$, and explain why the long-term behaviour in part (d) does not occur. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{T}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(1-a-\lambda)(1-b-\lambda)-ab$ [M1] $=\lambda^2-(2-a-b)\lambda+(1-a-b)$ [A1] $=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-(1-a-b))$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and $\mu=1-a-b$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}(1-a)b+ba\\ab+(1-b)a\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a-b\\a-1+b\end{pmatrix}=\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{P}=-(a+b)$, so $\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\a&-b\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n=\begin{pmatrix}b&\mu^n\\a&-\mu^n\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Multiplication by $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1] Correct entries leading to the given result [A1][AG] [5 marks] (d) Since $|\mu|<1$, $\mu^n\to0$ [R1] $\mathbf{T}^n\to\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b&b\\a&a\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Then $\mathbf{s}_n\to\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b(p+1-p)\\a(p+1-p)\end{pmatrix}=\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$, independent of $p$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Here $\mu=0.5$ and the long-term value is $0.4$; starting in state $2$, $p_n$ is the entry in row $1$, column $2$ of $\mathbf{T}^n$, which is $0.4(1-0.5^n)$ [M1] $0.4\times0.5^n<0.001$ [A1] $n=8$ gives $0.00156$ and $n=9$ gives $0.00078$, so $n=9$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) (i) $p_{n+1}=(1-a)p_n+b(1-p_n)$ [M1] $=(1-a-b)p_n+b=\mu p_n+b$ [A1][AG] (ii) $\mu L+b=\dfrac{(1-a-b)b+b(a+b)}{a+b}=\dfrac{b}{a+b}=L$ [A1] Subtracting: $p_{n+1}-L=\mu(p_n-L)$, so $p_n-L=\mu^n(p_0-L)$ [R1] [4 marks] (g) $\mu=1-1.3=-0.3$ [A1] $L=\frac{6}{13}$ and $p_0=1$, so $p_n-L=\frac{7}{13}(-0.3)^n$ [A1] Since $\mu<0$, the sign of $(-0.3)^n$ alternates, so $p_n$ alternates above and below $L$ [R1] [3 marks] (h) $\mathbf{T}$ has rows $(0,\ 1)$ and $(1,\ 0)$, with $\mathbf{T}^n=\mathbf{I}$ for even $n$ and $\mathbf{T}^n=\mathbf{T}$ for odd $n$ [A1] Here $\mu=-1$, so $|\mu|=1$ and $\mu^n$ does not tend to $0$; the chain keeps alternating and has no limit [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For part (c), keep the common factor $\frac{1}{a+b}$ outside the matrices while you multiply. In parts (e) and (g), connect each numerical answer back to the general formula you proved earlier.

subtopic: Solving a 3x3 system by elimination
statement: Solve the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}x+y+z&=6\\2x-y+z&=3\\x+2y-z&=2\end{aligned}$$ [6]
markscheme: Attempt to eliminate one variable [M1] Adding the first and third equations: $2x+3y=8$ [A1] Subtracting the first equation from the second: $x-2y=-3$ [A1] Attempt to solve the two equations in $x$ and $y$ [M1] $x=1$, $y=2$ [A1] $z=3$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations so that you get two equations in two unknowns. Substitute your solution into all three original equations to check.

subtopic: Ticket prices from daily takings
statement: A zoo sells adult, student and child tickets at fixed prices of $\$a$, $\$s$ and $\$c$ respectively. On Monday, $3$ adult, $2$ student and $4$ child tickets were bought by a group for a total of $\$75$. On Tuesday, $5$ adult, $3$ student and $2$ child tickets cost $\$96.50$. On Wednesday, $2$ adult, $4$ student and $3$ child tickets cost $\$74.50$. (a) Write down a system of three linear equations in $a$, $s$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the system. [2] (c) Find the cost of tickets for a group of $2$ adults, $3$ students and $1$ child. [2]
tips: Define your variables clearly and write one equation per day. Use the simultaneous equation solver on your GDC and check one equation by substitution.

subtopic: Parameters, infinitely many solutions and no solution
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}x+y+z&=2\\2x+3y+4z&=5\\x+2y+kz&=m\end{aligned}$$ where $k,m\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. [3] (c) For these values of $k$ and $m$, find the general solution of the system, using the parameter $t$ where $z=t$. [2] (d) State what happens when $k$ takes the value found in part (a) and $m$ takes any other value. [1]
markscheme: (a) Attempt to find the determinant or to row reduce [M1] $\det=1(3k-8)-1(2k-4)+1(4-3)=k-3$ [A1] $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Subtract $2\times$ equation $1$ from equation $2$: $y+2z=1$; subtract equation $1$ from equation $3$: $y+2z=m-2$ [M1] Both are expressions for $y+2z$, so we need $m-2=1$ [A1] $m=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=t$, $y=1-2t$ [M1] $x=1+t$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The system has no solution (it is inconsistent) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A zero determinant means the system has either no solution or infinitely many, and the right-hand sides decide which. Row reduce and compare the two equations that become parallel.

subtopic: Fitting a quadratic model through three points
statement: The height $h$ metres of a drone above the ground, $t$ seconds after it is launched, is modelled by $h=at^2+bt+c$. The drone is at a height of $2$ m when $t=0$, $12$ m when $t=2$, and $18$ m when $t=4$. (a) Write down a system of three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the system to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the maximum height reached by the drone, and the time at which this occurs. [3] (d) Find the time at which the drone lands, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $c=2$ [A1] $4a+2b+c=12$ and $16a+4b+c=18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC or elimination [M1] $a=-0.5$, $b=6$, $c=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=6$ [M1] Maximum height $=-0.5(36)+36+2=20$ m [A1] at $t=6$ seconds [A1] [3 marks] (d) $-0.5t^2+6t+2=0$ [M1] $t=12.3$ seconds (reject the negative root) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each data point gives one equation in the unknown coefficients. Once you have the model, use your GDC to find the maximum and the zeros, and reject any root that is not physically sensible.

subtopic: Systems with a parameter: unique, none or infinite solutions
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}x+y+z&=1\\x+ky+kz&=0\\x+ky+k^2z&=0\end{aligned}$$ where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is $k(k-1)^2$. [2] (b) Find the general solution of the system when $k=0$, using $z=\lambda$. [3] (c) Show that the system has no solution when $k=1$. [2] (d) For $k\neq0$ and $k\neq1$, find the unique solution in terms of $k$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&k&k\\1&k&k^2\end{pmatrix}=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&k-1&k-1\\0&k-1&k^2-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=(k-1)(k^2-1)-(k-1)^2=(k-1)(k^2-k)=k(k-1)^2$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) With $k=0$: equations are $x+y+z=1$, $x=0$, $x=0$ [M1] $x=0$ [A1] $y=1-\lambda$, $z=\lambda$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) With $k=1$ the first two equations are $x+y+z=1$ and $x+y+z=0$ [M1] These contradict each other, so there is no solution [R1] [2 marks] (d) Subtracting equation $2$ from equation $3$: $k(k-1)z=0$, so $z=0$ [M1][A1] Then $x+y=1$ and $x+ky=0$, giving $(k-1)y=-1$ [M1] $y=-\dfrac{1}{k-1}$, $x=\dfrac{k}{k-1}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: When a determinant vanishes for specific parameter values, substitute each value back and solve or look for a contradiction separately. In the general case, look for a pair of equations whose difference simplifies.

subtopic: Mixing fertilisers
statement: A farmer mixes three fertilisers $F_1$, $F_2$ and $F_3$. The percentages by mass of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) in each fertiliser are shown below. $$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{N} & \text{P} & \text{K}\\ \hline F_1 & 10\% & 5\% & 20\%\\ F_2 & 20\% & 10\% & 5\%\\ F_3 & 5\% & 20\% & 10\% \end{array}$$ The farmer uses $a$ kg of $F_1$, $b$ kg of $F_2$ and $c$ kg of $F_3$ to supply exactly $33$ kg of nitrogen, $34$ kg of phosphorus and $38$ kg of potassium. (a) Write down three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Solve the equations. [2] The fertilisers cost $\$0.45$, $\$0.60$ and $\$0.50$ per kilogram respectively. (c) Find the total cost of the fertiliser used. [2]
tips: Convert each percentage to a decimal and write one equation for each nutrient, not for each fertiliser. Check your solution against all three nutrient totals.

subtopic: Traffic flow with a free parameter
statement: Four one-way roads form a ring through junctions $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$. The numbers of vehicles per hour on the roads are $x$ ($A$ to $B$), $y$ ($B$ to $C$), $z$ ($C$ to $D$) and $w$ ($D$ to $A$). Vehicles also enter and leave the ring at each junction, as given in the table. $$\begin{array}{c|cccc} & A & B & C & D\\ \hline \text{Enter from outside} & 300 & 150 & 50 & 250\\ \text{Leave to outside} & 100 & 250 & 200 & 200 \end{array}$$ At each junction, the number of vehicles arriving equals the number leaving. (a) Write down four equations that $x$, $y$, $z$ and $w$ must satisfy. [4] (b) Solve the equations, giving $x$, $y$ and $z$ in terms of $w$. [3] (c) Each road can carry at most $400$ vehicles per hour, and no flow can be negative. Find the possible values of $w$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Junction $A$: $300+w=x+100$ [A1] Junction $B$: $x+150=y+250$ [A1] Junction $C$: $y+50=z+200$ [A1] Junction $D$: $z+250=w+200$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $x-w=200$, $x-y=100$, $y-z=150$, $z-w=-50$ (the fourth is not independent of the others) [M1] $x=w+200$ [A1] $y=w+100$ and $z=w-50$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z\ge0$ gives $w\ge50$ [M1] $x\le400$ gives $w\le200$ (and $y\le400$ gives $w\le300$, $w\le400$) [A1] $50\le w\le200$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At each junction write 'flow in $=$ flow out' including the outside traffic. A consistent system with fewer independent equations than unknowns has a free parameter, and the constraints on flows restrict its range.

subtopic: Fitting a cubic model through four points
statement: The monthly running cost, $C$ thousand dollars, of a machine in month $x$ is modelled by $C=px^3+qx^2+rx+s$. The costs recorded are $6$ when $x=0$, $5$ when $x=1$, $2$ when $x=2$ and $3$ when $x=3$. (a) Write down a system of four linear equations for $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$. [2] (b) Solve the system. [2] (c) For $0\le x\le4$, treating $x$ as continuous, find the minimum cost predicted by the model and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [4]
markscheme: (a) $s=6$ [A1] $p+q+r+s=5$, $8p+4q+2r+s=2$ and $27p+9q+3r+s=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $p=1$, $q=-4$, $r=2$, $s=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $C'(x)=3x^2-8x+2=0$ [M1] $x=2.39$ (the other stationary point at $x=0.279$ is a local maximum) [A1] $C(2.387)=1.58$ [A1] Comparison with the end values $C(0)=6$ and $C(4)=14$ shows this is the minimum on the interval [R1] [4 marks]
tips: A cubic has four unknown coefficients, so you need four data points and four equations. When asked for an extreme value on an interval, compare the stationary value with the values at the endpoints.

subtopic: Matrix inverse and solving several systems
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\1&4&2\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$. [1] (b) Find $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, giving your answer with exact fractions. [2] (c) Use your answer to part (b) to solve (i) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}13\\11\\21\end{pmatrix}$ and (ii) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}16\\17\\27\end{pmatrix}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{A}=3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac13\begin{pmatrix}16&1&-10\\1&1&-1\\-10&-1&7\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B}$ [M1] (i) $\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (ii) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: Once you have the inverse, each new right-hand side needs only a single matrix multiplication, with the inverse on the left. Check one answer by substituting into the original matrix equation.

subtopic: Balancing a chemical equation
statement: Butane burns in oxygen according to the reaction $$a\,\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}+b\,\text{O}_2\to c\,\text{CO}_2+d\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are positive integers. The number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides. (a) Write down three equations connecting $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, one for each of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. [3] (b) Show that the equations have infinitely many solutions, and express $b$, $c$ and $d$ in terms of $a$. [3] (c) Find the smallest positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ that balance the equation. [2]
markscheme: (a) Carbon: $4a=c$ [A1] Hydrogen: $10a=2d$ [A1] Oxygen: $2b=2c+d$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Three equations in four unknowns, so there is a free parameter [R1] $c=4a$ and $d=5a$ [A1] $2b=8a+5a$, so $b=\frac{13}{2}a$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $b=\frac{13a}{2}$ must be an integer, so $a$ must be even [M1] Smallest values: $a=2$, $b=13$, $c=8$, $d=10$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Count atoms of each element separately, then express every unknown in terms of one parameter. Remember to impose the integer condition at the end, which may require scaling the solution.

subtopic: Composite of a rotation and a reflection
statement: Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the matrix of an anticlockwise rotation through $90^\circ$ about the origin, and let $\mathbf{S}$ be the matrix of a reflection in the line $y=x$. (a) Write down $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{S}$. [2] (b) Find the single matrix that represents the rotation followed by the reflection. [2] (c) Describe fully the single transformation represented by your answer to part (b). [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Rotation first, then reflection: the matrix is $\mathbf{SR}$ [M1] $\mathbf{SR}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) A reflection in the $x$-axis [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For 'A followed by B' the matrix product is written $\mathbf{BA}$, with the first transformation on the right. You can check your answer by following the image of the point $(1,0)$ through both steps.

subtopic: Determinant as area scale factor
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}$ represents a linear transformation of the plane. Triangle $OBC$ has vertices $O(0,0)$, $B(2,1)$ and $C(1,3)$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. [1] (b) Find the area of triangle $OBC$. [2] (c) Hence find the area of the image of triangle $OBC$ under the transformation. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the image of $B$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=3\times4-1\times(-2)=14$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Area $=\tfrac12|2\times3-1\times1|$ [M1] $=\tfrac52$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area of image $=|\det\mathbf{M}|\times$ original area [M1] $=14\times\tfrac52=35$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6+1\\-4+4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\0\end{pmatrix}$, so the image is $(7,0)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The absolute value of the determinant is the area scale factor, so you never need to find the image vertices to answer part (c). Use the vertices only when the question asks for their coordinates.

subtopic: Composite stretch, reflection and enlargement
statement: A transformation of the plane is made in three stages: $S$: a horizontal stretch (parallel to the $x$-axis) with scale factor $3$; $R$: a reflection in the $x$-axis; $E$: an enlargement with centre the origin and scale factor $2$. (a) Write down the matrix of each of $S$, $R$ and $E$. [3] (b) Find the single matrix $\mathbf{T}$ that represents $S$, followed by $R$, followed by $E$. [2] (c) The parabola with equation $y=x^2$ is transformed by $\mathbf{T}$. Find the equation of the image curve. [3] (d) A region of area $5$ square units is transformed by $\mathbf{T}$. Find the area of its image. [2]
markscheme: (a) $S=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $E=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}=ERS$ [M1] $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) A point $(x,y)$ maps to $(X,Y)=(6x,-2y)$, so $x=\dfrac X6$ and $y=-\dfrac Y2$ [M1] Substituting into $y=x^2$: $-\dfrac Y2=\dfrac{X^2}{36}$ [M1] The image curve is $y=-\dfrac{x^2}{18}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{T}=-12$, so the area scale factor is $12$ [M1] Image area $=12\times5=60$ square units [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The matrix for 'first S, then R, then E' is the product written right to left, $\mathbf{ERS}$. For the image of a curve, express the old coordinates in terms of the new ones and substitute into the original equation.

subtopic: Reflection in a line through the origin using a formula
statement: The matrix of a reflection in the line $y=x\tan\theta$ is $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\theta&\sin2\theta\\ \sin2\theta&-\cos2\theta\end{pmatrix}$. Let $\theta=35^\circ$. (a) Write down the matrix $\mathbf{M}$, giving each entry correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the image of the point $P(4,-3)$ under this reflection, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the distance from the origin to the image of $P$, and explain why this answer is expected. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2\theta=70^\circ$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}0.342&0.940\\0.940&-0.342\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.342(4)+0.940(-3)\\0.940(4)+0.342(3)\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Image is $(-1.45,\ 4.78)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\sqrt{(-1.45)^2+4.78^2}=5.00$ [A1] The origin lies on the mirror line, so a reflection preserves its distance from the origin; $|OP|=\sqrt{16+9}=5$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Set your calculator to degrees before evaluating $\cos70^\circ$ and $\sin70^\circ$. Keeping unrounded matrix entries in your GDC for part (b) avoids accumulating rounding errors.

subtopic: Exact rotation matrix through 60 degrees
statement: Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the matrix of an anticlockwise rotation through $60^\circ$ about the origin. (a) Write down $\mathbf{R}$, giving exact values for each entry. [2] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the image of $A(4,2)$ under this rotation. [2] (c) Find $\mathbf{R}^3$, and hence describe the single transformation represented by $\mathbf{R}^3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos60^\circ&-\sin60^\circ\\ \sin60^\circ&\cos60^\circ\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12&-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}&\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{R}\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2-\sqrt3\\2\sqrt3+1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Image is $(2-\sqrt3,\ 2\sqrt3+1)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Three rotations of $60^\circ$ give a rotation of $180^\circ$, so $\mathbf{R}^3=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] This is a rotation through $180^\circ$ about the origin (equivalently an enlargement with scale factor $-1$ and centre the origin) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Learn the exact values of $\sin$ and $\cos$ at $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; they appear constantly in rotation matrices. Repeating a rotation just adds the angles, which is faster than multiplying matrices out.

subtopic: Inverse matrix to recover an original point
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane. The point $P$ is mapped by $\mathbf{T}$ to the point $P'(7,12)$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{T}$. [1] (b) Find $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence find the coordinates of $P$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{T}=2\times2-1\times3=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{T}^{-1}=\dfrac11\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-3&2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-3&2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{T}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}7\\12\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}14-12\\-21+24\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $P=(2,3)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To undo a transformation, multiply the image by the inverse matrix on the left. Always verify by applying $\mathbf{T}$ to your answer and checking that you recover the image point.

subtopic: Finding a matrix from two image points
statement: A linear transformation is represented by the matrix $\mathbf{M}$. It maps the point $(1,2)$ to $(4,5)$ and the point $(3,-1)$ to $(5,-6)$. (a) Find $\mathbf{M}$. [4] (b) Find the area of the image of a region of area $4.5$ square units. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\5&-6\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\5&-6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}$ [M1] with $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=-\dfrac17\begin{pmatrix}-1&-3\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{M}=6+1=7$ [A1] Area scale factor $=7$ [M1] Image area $=7\times4.5=31.5$ square units [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When a matrix is unknown, write one matrix equation that holds both pairs of points at once, then multiply by an inverse on the right. Check the result by applying $\mathbf{M}$ to both original points.

subtopic: Enlargement composed with a rotation, exact values
statement: The transformation $T$ is an enlargement with centre the origin and scale factor $3$, followed by an anticlockwise rotation through $45^\circ$ about the origin. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf{T}$ that represents $T$, giving exact entries. [3] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the image of $P(4,-2)$ under $T$. [2] (c) Find the exact coordinates of the point whose image under $T$ is $(6,0)$. [3] (d) Write down the area scale factor of $T$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}&-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\\ \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}&\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Multiplying by the enlargement factor $3$ [M1] $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}&-\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}\\ \tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}&\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}(4+2)\\ \tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}(4-2)\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Image is $(9\sqrt2,\ 3\sqrt2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\0\end{pmatrix}$: the second row gives $\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}(x+y)=0$, so $x+y=0$, and the first row gives $\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}(x-y)=6$ [M1] $x-y=2\sqrt2$ [A1] $(x,y)=(\sqrt2,\,-\sqrt2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $3^2=9$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: An enlargement and a rotation about the same centre commute, so their order does not change the matrix. For the area scale factor of a pure enlargement, square the linear scale factor.

subtopic: Invariant points and invariant line
statement: Let $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$ represent a transformation of the plane. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. [1] (b) Find all the points that are mapped to themselves by the transformation. [3] (c) Show that every point on the line $y=x$ is mapped to a point on the line $y=x$, and state the factor by which its distance from the origin is multiplied. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=6-2=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Invariant points satisfy $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$, so $(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{I})\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{0}$ [M1] $2x+y=0$ (both rows give this equation) [A1] The invariant points are all points on the line $y=-2x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}t\\t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4t\\4t\end{pmatrix}$, which lies on $y=x$ [A1] The distance from the origin is multiplied by $4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Invariant points come from $(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$; because the determinant of $\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{I}$ is zero here, a whole line of solutions appears rather than a single point.

subtopic: Order of composite reflection and rotation
statement: Let $A$ be a reflection in the $y$-axis and let $B$ be a clockwise rotation through $90^\circ$ about the origin. (a) Write down the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. [2] (b) Find the matrix of the transformation '$A$ followed by $B$', and describe the single transformation it represents. [3] (c) Find the matrix of the transformation '$B$ followed by $A$', and describe the single transformation it represents. [3] (d) State whether $\mathbf{AB}=\mathbf{BA}$, and give a reason. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) '$A$ then $B$' is $\mathbf{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Reflection in the line $y=x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) '$B$ then $A$' is $\mathbf{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Reflection in the line $y=-x$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{AB}\neq\mathbf{BA}$ because the two products are different matrices (the order of transformations matters) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so always decide which transformation is applied first before multiplying. Testing the image of a simple point such as $(1,0)$ quickly confirms the geometric description.

subtopic: Modelling a rotated and enlarged image
statement: A graphics program transforms every point of an image by rotating it clockwise through $25^\circ$ about the origin and then enlarging it by scale factor $1.5$ with centre the origin. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf{T}$ of this transformation, giving each entry to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the image of the point $(3.2,\,1.8)$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) After the transformation, a point appears at $(10,-4)$. Find the coordinates of the original point, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) An object has area $8.4\ \text{cm}^2$ before the transformation. Find its area afterwards. [2]
markscheme: (a) Clockwise rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos25^\circ&\sin25^\circ\\-\sin25^\circ&\cos25^\circ\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Multiplying by $1.5$ [M1] $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}1.36&0.634\\-0.634&1.36\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}3.2\\1.8\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=(5.49,\ 0.418)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{T}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}10\\-4\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=(7.17,\ 0.401)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{T}=1.5^2=2.25$ [M1] Area $=2.25\times8.4=18.9\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A clockwise rotation has the transposed sine signs compared with the usual anticlockwise matrix, so draw a quick sketch to check the signs. Store the unrounded matrix in your GDC and use its inverse for part (c).

subtopic: Determinant equation with orientation reversal
statement: Let $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}k&2\\3&k+1\end{pmatrix}$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find an expression for $\det\mathbf{M}$ in terms of $k$. [1] (b) Triangle $T$ has area $6$. Its image under the transformation represented by $\mathbf{M}$ has area $24$ and the orientation of the vertices is reversed. Find the possible values of $k$. [5] (c) For the positive value of $k$ found in part (b), find the image of the point $(2,-3)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=k(k+1)-6=k^2+k-6$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Area scale factor $=\dfrac{24}{6}=4$, so $|\det\mathbf{M}|=4$ [M1] Reversed orientation means $\det\mathbf{M}$ is negative, so $\det\mathbf{M}=-4$ [R1] $k^2+k-6=-4$ [M1] $k^2+k-2=0$, so $(k+2)(k-1)=0$ [A1] $k=1$ or $k=-2$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $k=1$: $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2-6\\6-6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\0\end{pmatrix}$, so the image is $(-4,0)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A negative determinant means the transformation reverses orientation, while its absolute value is the area scale factor. Use both facts to form a single equation for the determinant.

subtopic: Right pyramid: volume, surface area and edge angle
statement: A right pyramid has a square base of side length $10$ cm. Its vertex is $12$ cm vertically above the centre of the base. (a) Find the volume of the pyramid. [2] (b) Find the total surface area of the pyramid, including the base. [4] (c) Find the angle between a sloping edge of the pyramid and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\tfrac13\times10^2\times12$ [M1] $=400\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Distance from the centre of the base to the midpoint of a base edge is $5$, so the slant height of a triangular face is $\sqrt{12^2+5^2}$ [M1] $=13\ \text{cm}$ [A1] Area of four faces $=4\times\tfrac12\times10\times13=260$ [M1] Total surface area $=260+100=360\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Half the base diagonal $=\tfrac12\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=5\sqrt2\ (=7.07)$ [A1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{12}{5\sqrt2}$ [M1] $\theta=59.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Right-angled triangles inside the solid do all the work: one with the height and half the base edge for the face, another with the height and half the base diagonal for the edge. Label every length you find on your own sketch.

subtopic: Cone: volume, curved area and unrolled sector
statement: A solid cone has base radius $6$ cm and slant height $10$ cm. (a) Find the vertical height of the cone. [2] (b) Find the volume of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the curved surface area of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The curved surface is cut along a slant edge and laid flat to form a sector of a circle of radius $10$ cm. Find the angle of the sector in degrees. [2]
markscheme: (a) $h=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}$ [M1] $=8\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\tfrac13\pi(6)^2(8)$ [M1] $=96\pi=302\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A=\pi rl=\pi(6)(10)$ [M1] $=60\pi=188\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The arc length of the sector equals the base circumference $2\pi(6)$, so $\dfrac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi(10)=12\pi$ [M1] $\theta=216^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The slant height, radius and vertical height of a cone form a right-angled triangle with the slant height as hypotenuse. When a cone is unrolled, the arc length of the sector equals the circumference of the base.

subtopic: Cylinder with hemispherical top: volume and area
statement: A storage silo is made from a cylinder of radius $2.5$ m and height $h$ m with a hemisphere of radius $2.5$ m attached to the top. (a) Find the volume of the hemisphere, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) The silo must have a total volume of $180\ \text{m}^3$. Find the value of $h$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Using $h=7.50$, find the area of the curved surfaces of the silo (the curved side of the cylinder and the hemisphere, excluding the base), correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Keep unrounded values in your GDC between parts so that your final answer is accurate to three significant figures. Check which faces are included: here the base of the cylinder and the join between the solids are not painted.

subtopic: Cuboid diagonals and angles with lines
statement: $ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $ABCD$ the horizontal base and $AE$, $BF$, $CG$, $DH$ vertical edges. $AB=8$ cm, $AD=6$ cm and $AE=5$ cm. (a) Find the length $AC$. [2] (b) Find the length $AG$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (d) Find the angle between $AG$ and $AB$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}$ [M1] $=10\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $AG=\sqrt{10^2+5^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{125}=11.2\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The angle $GAC$ satisfies $\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{10}$ [M1] $\theta=26.6^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $AB$ is perpendicular to $BG$ (since $AB\perp$ face $BCGF$), so $\cos\phi=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{125}}$ [M1] $\phi=44.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its projection onto the plane. For an angle between two lines through a vertex, look for a right-angled triangle containing both lines.

subtopic: Angles between faces of a rectangular pyramid
statement: A right pyramid has a rectangular base of length $12$ cm and width $8$ cm. The vertex is $9$ cm vertically above the centre of the base. (a) Find the angle between a triangular face containing a $12$ cm base edge and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the angle between a triangular face containing an $8$ cm base edge and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (c) Find the volume of the pyramid. [2]
markscheme: (a) The perpendicular distance from the centre of the base to a $12$ cm edge is half the width, $4$ cm [A1] $\tan\alpha=\dfrac94$ [M1] $\alpha=66.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The perpendicular distance from the centre to an $8$ cm edge is $6$ cm, so $\tan\beta=\dfrac96$ [M1] $\beta=56.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $V=\tfrac13\times12\times8\times9$ [M1] $=288\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The angle between a face and the base is measured along a line perpendicular to the shared edge, so use the distance from the centre to the edge, not to the corner. The longer base edge is closer to the centre, which gives the steeper face.

subtopic: Plane section of a sphere
statement: A sphere has centre $O$ and radius $13$ cm. A plane cuts the sphere in a circle. The perpendicular distance from $O$ to the plane is $5$ cm. (a) Find the radius of the circle of intersection. [2] (b) Find the area of this circle, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. [1] (c) Find the volume of the sphere, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) The radius of the circle, $r$, satisfies $r^2+5^2=13^2$ [M1] $r=12\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=\pi(12)^2=144\pi\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $V=\tfrac43\pi(13)^3$ [M1] $=\dfrac{8788\pi}{3}\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A right-angled triangle always links the sphere's radius, the distance from the centre to the plane and the radius of the circular section. Leave answers in terms of $\pi$ when the question asks.

subtopic: Frustum of a cone using similar cones
statement: A solid cone has base radius $10$ cm and vertical height $24$ cm. It is cut by a plane parallel to its base at a height of $15$ cm above the base, forming a smaller cone at the top and a frustum below. (a) Find the height and the base radius of the smaller cone. [2] (b) Find the volume of the smaller cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the volume of the frustum, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height of small cone $=24-15=9$ cm [A1] The cones are similar with ratio $\tfrac{9}{24}=\tfrac38$, so radius $=10\times\tfrac38=3.75$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\tfrac13\pi(3.75)^2(9)$ [M1] $=42.1875\pi=133\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Volume of whole cone $=\tfrac13\pi(10)^2(24)=800\pi$ [A1] Frustum $=800\pi-42.1875\pi$ [M1] $=757.8125\pi=2380\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Similar solids have linear ratio $k$, so lengths scale by $k$ and volumes by $k^3$. Subtracting the small cone from the whole cone is the quickest route to the frustum.

subtopic: Angles of elevation from two points to a tower
statement: A vertical tower $TB$ of height $30$ m stands on level ground, with $T$ the top and $B$ the base. Points $A$ and $C$ are on the ground. The angle of elevation of $T$ from $A$ is $28^\circ$ and from $C$ is $35^\circ$. Angle $ABC=110^\circ$. (a) Find the distance $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the distance $BC$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the distance $AC$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: First reduce the 3D situation to right-angled triangles in a vertical plane to find the ground distances, then use the cosine rule in the horizontal triangle $ABC$. Use unrounded values from part (a) and (b) to protect your third significant figure.

subtopic: Ambiguous case of the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=9$ cm, $AC=12$ cm and angle $BAC=40^\circ$. (a) Find the two possible values of angle $ABC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the two possible values of $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the area of the larger of the two possible triangles, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin B}{12}=\dfrac{\sin40^\circ}{9}$ [M1] $B=59.0^\circ$ [A1] or $B=180^\circ-59.0^\circ=121.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $B=59.0^\circ$: $C=81.0^\circ$ and $AB=\dfrac{9\sin81.0^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}=13.8\ \text{cm}$ [M1] [A1] For $B=121.0^\circ$: $C=19.0^\circ$ and $AB=\dfrac{9\sin19.0^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}=4.56\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Larger triangle has $AB=13.83$: area $=\tfrac12(12)(13.83)\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=53.3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When you are given two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can give two angles; always check whether $180^\circ-\theta$ also fits. The two triangles are different, so compute each third side and area separately.

subtopic: Cosine rule, angles and area from three sides
statement: A triangle has sides of length $7$ cm, $9$ cm and $12$ cm. (a) Find the size of the largest angle, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the area of the triangle, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the size of the smallest angle, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) The largest angle $\theta$ is opposite the side of length $12$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{7^2+9^2-12^2}{2(7)(9)}$ [M1] [A1] $\theta=96.4^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(7)(9)\sin96.38^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $=31.3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The smallest angle $\phi$ is opposite the side $7$: $\cos\phi=\dfrac{9^2+12^2-7^2}{2(9)(12)}$ [M1] $\phi=35.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The largest angle is always opposite the longest side, and a negative cosine tells you it is obtuse. Use the area formula $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ with the unrounded angle from your calculator.

subtopic: Bearings and the cosine rule
statement: A ship leaves port $P$ and sails $12$ km on a bearing of $065^\circ$ to a buoy $B$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to a point $Q$. (a) Show that angle $PBQ=95^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $PQ$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $P$ from $Q$, correct to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) The bearing of $P$ from $B$ is $065^\circ+180^\circ=245^\circ$ [M1] Angle $PBQ=245^\circ-150^\circ=95^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $PQ^2=12^2+9^2-2(12)(9)\cos95^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $PQ=15.6\ \text{km}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin\angle BQP}{12}=\dfrac{\sin95^\circ}{15.61}$ so $\angle BQP=49.9^\circ$ [M1] The bearing of $B$ from $Q$ is $150^\circ+180^\circ=330^\circ$ [A1] The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $330^\circ-49.9^\circ=280^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a north line at each point and mark the interior angle using alternate angles: bearings differing by $180^\circ$ describe the return direction. Keep the unrounded value of $PQ$ for the sine rule in part (c).

subtopic: Height of a tower using two angles of elevation
statement: Points $A$ and $B$ lie on level ground in a straight line with the base of a vertical tower, with $B$ between $A$ and the tower. $AB=50$ m. The angles of elevation of the top $T$ of the tower from $A$ and from $B$ are $25^\circ$ and $40^\circ$ respectively. (a) Find the size of angle $ATB$. [2] (b) Find the distance $AT$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the height of the tower, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Angle $ABT=180^\circ-40^\circ=140^\circ$ [M1] Angle $ATB=180^\circ-25^\circ-140^\circ=15^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{AT}{\sin140^\circ}=\dfrac{50}{\sin15^\circ}$ [M1] [A1] $AT=124\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Height $=AT\sin25^\circ$ [M1] $=52.5\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the two observation points are in line with the tower, the exterior angle at $B$ gives an oblique triangle: use the sine rule there, then a right-angled triangle for the height. Check your answer with $h=50/(\cot25^\circ-\cot40^\circ)$.

subtopic: Arc length, sector and segment
statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $8$ cm. Chord $AB$ subtends an angle of $1.2$ radians at $O$. (a) Find the length of the minor arc $AB$ and the area of the minor sector $OAB$. [2] (b) Find the area of the segment bounded by the chord $AB$ and the minor arc $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the perimeter of this segment, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Arc length $=8\times1.2=9.6$ cm [A1] Sector area $=\tfrac12(8)^2(1.2)=38.4\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Triangle $OAB$ has area $\tfrac12(8)^2\sin1.2$ [M1] $=29.8$ [A1] Segment area $=38.4-29.8=8.57\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Chord $AB=2(8)\sin0.6$ or $\sqrt{8^2+8^2-2(8)(8)\cos1.2}$ [M1] $=9.03$ [A1] Perimeter $=9.6+9.03=18.6\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Switch your calculator to radian mode for $\sin1.2$. A segment is a sector minus a triangle, and its perimeter is the arc plus the chord.

subtopic: Two triangles from a given area
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=10$ cm, $AC=14$ cm and the area of the triangle is $56\ \text{cm}^2$. Angle $BAC$ is $\theta$. (a) Find the two possible values of $\theta$, in degrees, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the two possible lengths of $BC$, correct to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\tfrac12(10)(14)\sin\theta=56$ [M1] $\sin\theta=0.8$ [A1] so $\theta=53.1^\circ$ or $\theta=127^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $BC^2=10^2+14^2-2(10)(14)\cos\theta$ [M1] For $\theta=53.13^\circ$, $\cos\theta=0.6$: $BC^2=128$, $BC=11.3\ \text{cm}$ [A1] For $\theta=126.87^\circ$, $\cos\theta=-0.6$: $BC^2=464$ [M1] $BC=21.5\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: An area equation $\tfrac12ab\sin\theta=A$ gives two angles between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, one acute and one obtuse. Remember that $\cos$ changes sign for the obtuse angle.

subtopic: Land plot split by a diagonal
statement: A four-sided plot of land $ABCD$ has $AB=45$ m, $BC=60$ m, $CD=50$ m and $DA=70$ m. Angle $ABC=80^\circ$. The vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are in order around the boundary and the plot is convex. (a) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the size of angle $ADC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (c) Find the total area of the plot, correct to three significant figures. [4]
tips: Split any quadrilateral along a diagonal into two triangles, then alternate cosine rule and area formula. Do not round the diagonal until the final answer.

subtopic: Tidal depth model and time above a threshold
statement: The depth of water, $D$ metres, in a harbor $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $D(t)=4.7-2.8\cos(bt)$, for $t\ge0$, where $b>0$ and the argument of cosine is in radians. The time between consecutive high tides is $12.4$ hours. (a) Find the minimum and maximum depths predicted by the model. [2] (b) Show that $b=0.507$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) A ship can enter the harbor only when the depth is at least $6$ m. Find the times, in the first $12.4$ hours, between which the ship can enter, giving each time to the nearest minute. [3] (d) Find the total time in each $12.4$ hour cycle during which the depth is at least $6$ m, in hours correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Minimum $=4.7-2.8=1.9$ m [A1] Maximum $=4.7+2.8=7.5$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}=12.4$ [M1] $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12.4}=0.507$ (0.50670...) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $4.7-2.8\cos(bt)=6$ using $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12.4}$ [M1] $t=4.05$ hours [A1] and $t=8.35$ hours [A1] i.e. between about 04:03 and 08:21 (accept 4 h 3 min to 4 h 4 min and 8 h 21 min; accept 4.05 h and 8.35 h) [3 marks] (d) Duration $=8.347-4.053$ (using unrounded values, or $12.4-2(4.053)$) [M1] $=4.29$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $b$ in your GDC and sketch the graph to see which intersections you need. For the duration, subtract the two unrounded times instead of the rounded ones.

subtopic: Ferris wheel height and time above 35 m
statement: A Ferris wheel has diameter $40$ m. Its centre is $22$ m above the ground, and it completes one full revolution every $8$ minutes. A passenger boards at the lowest point of the wheel when $t=0$, where $t$ is the time in minutes. The height $h$ meters of the passenger above the ground is modeled by $h(t)=22-20\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$, where the argument of cosine is in radians. (a) Find the height of the passenger when $t=3$. [2] (b) Find the times in the first revolution when the passenger is exactly $35$ m above the ground, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the percentage of each revolution for which the passenger is above $35$ m, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $h(3)=22-20\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$ [M1] $=36.1$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $22-20\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)=35$ [M1] $t=2.90$ minutes [A1] and $t=5.10$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (c) Time above $35$ m $=5.0991-2.9009=2.198$ minutes [M1] Fraction $=\dfrac{2.198}{8}$ [M1] $=27.5\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Make sure your GDC is in radian mode because the argument of the cosine contains $\pi$. The second intersection can be found by symmetry about $t=4$.

subtopic: Finding parameters of a sinusoidal function from extrema
statement: The function $f(x)=a\sin\big(b(x-c)\big)+d$, where $a>0$, $b>0$ and $0<c<6$, has a maximum point at $(2,9)$. The next minimum point after this maximum is at $(5,1)$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $d$. [2] (b) Find the value of $b$. [2] (c) Find the value of $c$. [2] (d) Find the exact value of $f(10)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{9-1}{2}=4$ [A1] $d=\dfrac{9+1}{2}=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Half a period is $5-2=3$, so the period is $6$ [M1] $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{6}=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) At the maximum, $\dfrac\pi3(2-c)=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $2-c=\dfrac32$, so $c=\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $f(10)=4\sin\left(\dfrac\pi3\times9.5\right)+5=4\sin\left(\dfrac{19\pi}{6}\right)+5$ [M1] $\sin\dfrac{19\pi}{6}=-\dfrac12$, so $f(10)=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A maximum-to-minimum distance is half a period. Set the sine's argument equal to $\pi/2$ at the maximum to find the horizontal shift, and use the stated restriction on $c$ to pick the right value.

subtopic: Solving a quadratic-in-sine equation
statement: Consider the equation $2\cos^2x+\sin x=2$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$. (a) Show that the equation can be written as $\sin x\,(1-2\sin x)=0$. [3] (b) Hence solve the equation. [3]
markscheme: (a) Using $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $2(1-\sin^2x)+\sin x=2$ [M1] $-2\sin^2x+\sin x=0$ [A1] $\sin x\,(1-2\sin x)=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sin x=0$ gives $x=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$ [A1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Never divide through by $\sin x$: you would lose the solutions where $\sin x=0$. Check that the interval includes both endpoints, $0$ and $2\pi$.

subtopic: Range, period and solutions of a cosine function
statement: Let $f(x)=3\cos(2x)+1$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$. (a) Solve $f(x)=2.5$. [4] (b) Write down the range of $f$. [2] (c) Write down the period of $f$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $3\cos2x+1=2.5$ gives $\cos2x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $2x=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$ (all solutions in $0\le2x\le4\pi$) [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ [A1] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $-3+1\le f(x)\le3+1$ [M1] $-2\le f(x)\le4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When the angle is $2x$, the interval for $2x$ doubles to $[0,4\pi]$, so look for twice as many solutions. Award yourself the A marks only when every solution in the interval is listed.

subtopic: Daylight hours model and rate of change
statement: The number of hours of daylight in a northern city is modeled by $D(t)=2.4\sin\big(0.0172(t-80)\big)+12.1$, where $t$ is the day of the year ($t=1$ is 1 January) and the argument of sine is in radians. (a) Find the maximum number of hours of daylight predicted by the model, and the day on which it occurs, correct to the nearest day. [3] (b) Find the number of days in the year for which there are more than $13$ hours of daylight, correct to the nearest day. [3] (c) Find $D'(100)$, correct to three significant figures, and interpret its meaning. [3]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=2.4+12.1=14.5$ hours [A1] $0.0172(t-80)=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $t=171$ (day 171) [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $D(t)=13$ [M1] $t=102.35$ and $t=240.30$ [A1] Number of days $=240.30-102.35=138$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $D'(t)=2.4(0.0172)\cos\big(0.0172(t-80)\big)$ [M1] $D'(100)=0.0389$ [A1] On day $100$ the hours of daylight are increasing at a rate of $0.0389$ hours per day [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The model uses radians, so check your GDC mode before every evaluation. For a rate of change, differentiate with the chain rule, or use the numerical derivative on your GDC, and always include units in the interpretation.

subtopic: Pendulum displacement and angular velocity
statement: The angular displacement, $\theta$ radians, of a pendulum from the vertical is modeled by $\theta(t)=0.3\cos(4\pi t)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after release and the argument of cosine is in radians. (a) Write down the amplitude of the motion and find its period. [2] (b) Find the first time at which $\theta=0.1$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the angular velocity $\theta'(t)$ at the time found in part (b), correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $=0.3$ radians [A1] Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{4\pi}=0.5$ seconds [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0.3\cos(4\pi t)=0.1$ gives $\cos(4\pi t)=\dfrac13$ [M1] $4\pi t=1.2310\ldots$ [M1] $t=0.0980$ seconds [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\theta'(t)=-1.2\pi\sin(4\pi t)$ [A1] At $4\pi t=\arccos\dfrac13$, $\sin(4\pi t)=\dfrac{\sqrt8}{3}$ [M1] $\theta'=-1.2\pi\times0.9428=-3.55$ radians per second [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The first positive solution of $\cos u=\tfrac13$ is $u=\arccos\tfrac13$ in radian mode. For part (c), use the identity $\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1$, or the GDC, to evaluate the sine.

subtopic: Closest approach of a drone to an antenna
statement: A drone flies along a straight path with position vector $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, where the components are in meters and $t$ is the time in seconds, $t\ge0$. An antenna is at the point $Q(10,9,2)$. (a) Find the speed of the drone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the value of $t$ for which the drone is closest to the antenna. [4] (c) Find the shortest distance between the drone and the antenna, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Speed $=\left|\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\right|=\sqrt{3^2+2^2+1^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{14}=3.74\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Vector from the drone to $Q$: $\begin{pmatrix}8-3t\\8-2t\\2-t\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $d^2=(8-3t)^2+(8-2t)^2+(2-t)^2=14t^2-84t+132$ [M1] Minimise, e.g. $\dfrac{d(d^2)}{dt}=28t-84=0$ (or use the GDC, or perpendicularity to the direction vector) [M1] $t=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $d^2=14(9)-84(3)+132=6$ [M1] $d=\sqrt6=2.45\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Minimising the squared distance avoids a square root and gives the same $t$. Alternatively the closest point occurs when the vector from the drone to the antenna is perpendicular to the direction of travel.

subtopic: Scalar product: perpendicular vectors and angle
statement: Let $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{c}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Given that $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ [M1] $2k-4+3=0$ [A1] $k=\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}=2-2+6=6$ [A1] $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{14}$ and $|\mathbf{c}|=3$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{6}{3\sqrt{14}}$ [M1] $\theta=57.7^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Perpendicular vectors have a zero scalar product. Compute the dot product and both magnitudes separately before substituting into $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{c}|}$.

subtopic: Ships on intersecting paths: do they collide?
statement: Two boats move with constant velocities. At time $t$ hours after noon, the position vector in kilometers of boat $A$ is $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and the position vector of boat $B$ is $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix}15\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-3\\3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the paths of the two boats cross at the point $(9,6)$. [3] (b) Show that the boats do not collide. [2] (c) After noon, find the minimum distance between the boats, correct to three significant figures, and the time at which it occurs. [4]
markscheme: (a) For boat $A$: $1+2t=9$ gives $t=4$ and $2+t=6$ is consistent, so $A$ passes $(9,6)$ [M1] For boat $B$ (using parameter $s$): $15-3s=9$ gives $s=2$ and $3s=6$ is consistent [M1] Both paths contain $(9,6)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $A$ is at $(9,6)$ when $t=4$, but $B$ is at $(9,6)$ when $t=2$ [M1] At $t=4$, $B$ is at $(3,12)\neq(9,6)$, so they are not at the same place at the same time [R1] [2 marks] (c) Displacement $\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix}14-5t\\-2+2t\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $d^2=(14-5t)^2+(2t-2)^2=29t^2-148t+200$ [M1] Minimum at $t=\dfrac{148}{58}=2.55$ hours [A1] $d=\sqrt{29(2.5517)^2-148(2.5517)+200}=3.34$ km [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Intersecting paths do not guarantee a collision: the boats must be at the intersection at the same time. Use a different parameter for each path when finding where the paths cross.

subtopic: Resultant of two forces and equilibrium
statement: Two forces act on a particle: $\mathbf{F}_1=\begin{pmatrix}12\\5\end{pmatrix}$ newtons and $\mathbf{F}_2=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ newtons, where the components are horizontal and vertical respectively. (a) Find the resultant force $\mathbf{F}$. [1] (b) Find the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the acute angle that $\mathbf{F}$ makes with the horizontal, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (d) A third force $\mathbf{F}_3$ is added so that the particle is in equilibrium. Write down $\mathbf{F}_3$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix}12-4\\5+9\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\14\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|\mathbf{F}|=\sqrt{8^2+14^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{260}=16.1\ \text{N}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{14}{8}$ [M1] $\theta=60.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{F}_3=-\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\-14\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Add the components separately to find a resultant, and use the right-angled triangle of its components for magnitude and direction. In equilibrium, the forces sum to the zero vector.

subtopic: Dividing a line segment in a given ratio
statement: The points $A$ and $B$ have position vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-4\\9\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [1] (b) Find the exact value of $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$. [2] (c) The point $P$ lies on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$. Find the position vector of $P$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-6\\6\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{36+36+36}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{108}=6\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AP}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a ratio $AP:PB=1:2$, the point is one-third of the way from $A$ to $B$, not one-half. Write $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}$ before doing anything else.

subtopic: Intersection and angle between two lines in 3D
statement: Two lines are given by $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\6\\-6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect, and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between $L_1$ and $L_2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Equating $x$ and $y$: $1+2s=t$ and $2+s=6-t$ [M1] Substituting: $2+s=6-1-2s$, so $s=1$ and $t=3$ [A1] Check $z$: $-1+s=0$ and $-6+2t=0$, equal, so the lines intersect [R1] Point of intersection $(3,3,0)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}=2-1+2=3$ [A1] $\left|\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\right|=\left|\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\right|=\sqrt6$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6\sqrt6}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $\theta=60^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Solve two of the three coordinate equations for the parameters and then test the third; if it fails, the lines are skew. The angle between lines uses only the direction vectors.

subtopic: Perpendicular bisector of a segment
statement: The points $A$ and $B$ have coordinates $(-2,5)$ and $(4,1)$. (a) Find the coordinates of the midpoint $M$ of $AB$. [1] (b) Find the gradient of $AB$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, giving your answer in the form $ax+by+d=0$, where $a,b,d\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $M=\left(\dfrac{-2+4}{2},\dfrac{5+1}{2}\right)=(1,3)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{1-5}{4-(-2)}$ [M1] $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Perpendicular gradient $=\dfrac32$ [A1] $y-3=\dfrac32(x-1)$ [M1] $3x-2y+3=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint with gradient equal to the negative reciprocal of the gradient of the segment. Check by substituting the midpoint into your final equation.

subtopic: Linear calibration model and inverse use
statement: A sensor reading $R$ is linearly related to temperature $T$ in degrees Celsius. When $T=20$, $R=3.4$, and when $T=65$, $R=9.7$. (a) Find the equation of the linear model in the form $R=mT+c$. [3] (b) Find the temperature when $R=5.0$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the value of $T$ for which the reading equals the temperature ($R=T$), correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Find the gradient first, then substitute one data point to find the intercept. To find where two lines meet, set the expressions equal and solve.

subtopic: Parallel and perpendicular lines and a distance
statement: The line $L_1$ has equation $2x-3y=12$. (a) Find the equation of the line $L_2$ that is parallel to $L_1$ and passes through $P(3,-4)$, giving your answer in the form $ax+by=c$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the line $L_3$ that is perpendicular to $L_1$ and passes through $P$, in the form $ax+by=c$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the point $Q$ where $L_1$ and $L_3$ intersect. [3] (d) Find the exact distance $PQ$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $L_2$ has the form $2x-3y=k$ [M1] $k=2(3)-3(-4)=18$, so $L_2:\ 2x-3y=18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The gradient of $L_1$ is $\dfrac23$, so the gradient of $L_3$ is $-\dfrac32$ [A1] $y+4=-\dfrac32(x-3)$ [M1] $3x+2y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $2x-3y=12$ and $3x+2y=1$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{27}{13}$ [A1] $y=-\dfrac{34}{13}$, so $Q=\left(\dfrac{27}{13},-\dfrac{34}{13}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $PQ=\sqrt{\left(3-\dfrac{27}{13}\right)^2+\left(-4+\dfrac{34}{13}\right)^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{12^2+18^2}}{13}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6\sqrt{13}}{13}$ (equivalently $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{13}}$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Lines parallel to $ax+by=c$ share the same $a$ and $b$; perpendicular lines swap them and change one sign. For an exact distance, keep fractions with a common denominator before taking the square root.

subtopic: Intercepts, area and intersection with y = x
statement: The line $L$ has equation $4x+5y=40$. (a) Find the coordinates of the points where $L$ meets the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. [2] (b) Find the area of the triangle bounded by $L$ and the two axes. [2] (c) The line $L$ meets the line $y=x$ at the point $P$. Find the coordinates of $P$. [2]
markscheme: (a) When $y=0$: $x=10$, so $(10,0)$ [A1] When $x=0$: $y=8$, so $(0,8)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12\times10\times8$ [M1] $=40$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4x+5x=40$ [M1] $P=\left(\dfrac{40}{9},\dfrac{40}{9}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Set one variable to zero to find each intercept. The triangle between a line and the axes is right-angled at the origin, so its legs are the intercept lengths.

subtopic: Two simultaneous equations from ticket sales
statement: At a theater, all adult tickets cost $\$a$ each and all child tickets cost $\$c$ each. A group buys $5$ adult tickets and $3$ child tickets for a total of $\$64$. A second group buys $2$ adult tickets and $4$ child tickets for a total of $\$41$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the equations to find the price of an adult ticket and of a child ticket. [2] (c) A third group buys $4$ adult tickets and $6$ child tickets. Find the total cost. [1] (d) The line $5a+3c=64$ is plotted with $a$ on the horizontal axis and $c$ on the vertical axis. Write down its gradient, and interpret it in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $5a+3c=64$ [A1] $2a+4c=41$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solving, e.g. by GDC [M1] $a=9.50$ and $c=5.50$ (adult \$9.50, child \$5.50) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4(9.5)+6(5.5)=38+33=\$71$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Gradient $=-\dfrac53$ [A1] Each \$1 increase in the adult price must be matched by a decrease of $\$\tfrac53$ in the child price to keep the first group's total at \$64 [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Define your variables clearly and write one equation per piece of information. For the gradient, rearrange to $c=-\tfrac53a+\tfrac{64}{3}$.

subtopic: Two tanks: intersecting linear models
statement: Tank $A$ contains $120$ liters of water and is being filled at a constant rate of $8$ liters per minute. Tank $B$ contains $450$ liters and is being emptied at a constant rate of $12$ liters per minute. Let $t$ be the time in minutes from the start. (a) Find the time at which the two tanks contain the same volume, and find this volume. [3] (b) Find the time at which tank $B$ becomes empty. [1] (c) Find the time at which tank $A$ contains twice as much water as tank $B$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V_A=120+8t$ and $V_B=450-12t$ [A1] Equating: $120+8t=450-12t$ [M1] $t=16.5$ minutes, and the volume is $120+8(16.5)=252$ liters [A1] [3 marks] (b) $450-12t=0$, so $t=37.5$ minutes [A1] [1 mark] (c) $120+8t=2(450-12t)$ [M1] $32t=780$ [A1] $t=24.4$ minutes (this is before $37.5$, so tank $B$ still contains water) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write each volume as a linear function of time, then set up an equation matching the condition. Check that your solution lies in the time interval where both models make sense.

subtopic: Separation of variables with initial condition
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xy$, where $y>0$. (a) Find the general solution, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [3] (b) Given that $y=3$ when $x=0$, find the value of $y$ when $x=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy=\int 2x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln y=x^2+C$ [A1] $y=Ae^{x^2}$, where $A=e^{C}>0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $3=Ae^{0}$, so $A=3$ [A1] $y=3e^{x^2}$, so when $x=1$, $y=3e$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate the variables first, then integrate each side; a single constant of integration is enough. Remember $y>0$ lets you write $\ln y$ without modulus signs.

subtopic: Euler's method and concavity
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y^2$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to find an approximation for $y$ when $x=0.2$. [3] (b) Continue the method to estimate $y$ when $x=0.3$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=1+2y(x+y^2)$, and hence explain why the Euler estimates are less than the true values of $y$ for $x\geq 0$. (Assume $y>0$.) [3]
markscheme: (a) $y_1=1+0.1(0+1^2)=1.1$ [M1] [A1] $y_2=1.1+0.1(0.1+1.1^2)=1.231$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y_3=1.231+0.1(0.2+1.231^2)$ [M1] $=1.4025\ldots\approx 1.40$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=1+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+2y(x+y^2)$ [A1] For $x\ge0$, $y>0$ this is positive, so the solution curve is concave up [R1] Each Euler step follows the tangent line, which lies below a concave-up curve, so each estimate is an underestimate [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write each Euler step as $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$ and keep full calculator accuracy until the last step. Link the sign of the second derivative to the geometry of tangent lines.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling
statement: A cup of tea is cooling in a room with constant temperature $20^\circ$C. Its temperature $T^\circ$C after $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $k>0$. Initially $T=90$, and after 10 minutes $T=60$. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $T=20+70e^{-kt}$. [4] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the tea to cool to $30^\circ$C, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the rate at which the temperature is changing when $T=50$. [2]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $k$ in later parts, or store it on your calculator. A negative rate of change means the temperature is falling.

subtopic: Coupled linear system: eigenvalues and saddle
statement: Consider the coupled system $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=x+2y,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=3x+2y$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=A\mathbf{x}$ and find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write down the general solution of the system. [2] (d) Classify the equilibrium point at the origin, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(2-\lambda)-6=\lambda^2-3\lambda-4=0$ [M1] $\lambda=4$ or $\lambda=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=4$: $-3a+2b=0$ [M1] eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=-1$: $a+b=0$, eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=c_1\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}e^{4t}$ [A1] $+\,c_2\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}e^{-t}$ [A1] (follow through from (b)) [2 marks] (d) Saddle point (unstable) [A1] because the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For a $2\times2$ system, solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ and then find each eigenvector from $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$. The signs of the eigenvalues classify the equilibrium.

subtopic: Predator-prey model: equilibrium, Euler and linearization
statement: The populations (in hundreds) of a prey species $x$ and its predator $y$ at time $t$ years are modelled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.4x-0.02xy,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.01xy-0.3y$, for $x,y\ge 0$. (a) Find the coordinates of the equilibrium point at which both populations are non-zero. [3] (b) Find $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ when $x=40$ and $y=15$. [2] (c) Given that $x=40$ and $y=15$ when $t=0$, use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate the populations when $t=1$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) Near the equilibrium point, let $u=x-30$ and $v=y-20$. The system can be approximated by $\dfrac{du}{dt}=-0.6v,\quad \dfrac{dv}{dt}=0.2u$. Find the eigenvalues of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-0.6\\0.2&0\end{pmatrix}$. [2] (e) Hence describe the long-term behavior of the populations near the equilibrium point, and find the approximate time between successive peaks of the prey population. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\frac{dx}{dt}=0$: $x(0.4-0.02y)=0$ [M1] $y=20$ [A1] $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$: $y(0.01x-0.3)=0$, so $x=30$; equilibrium $(30,20)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{dx}{dt}=16-12=4$ [A1] $\frac{dy}{dt}=6-4.5=1.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Step 1: $x_1=40+0.5(4)=42$, $y_1=15+0.5(1.5)=15.75$ [M1] [A1] Step 2: $\frac{dx}{dt}=0.4(42)-0.02(42)(15.75)=3.57$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=0.01(42)(15.75)-0.3(15.75)=1.89$ [M1] $x_2=43.785\approx 43.8$, $y_2=16.695\approx 16.7$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\lambda^2+0.12=0$ [M1] $\lambda=\pm i\sqrt{0.12}=\pm0.346i$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Purely imaginary eigenvalues, so the equilibrium is a center [A1] The populations follow closed orbits, oscillating periodically rather than converging or diverging [R1] Period $=\frac{2\pi}{0.3464}=18.1$ years [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In coupled-system questions, set both rates to zero to find equilibria. Purely imaginary eigenvalues give a center, and the period of oscillation is $2\pi$ divided by the imaginary part.

subtopic: Logistic growth: Euler's method and maximum growth rate
statement: A population $P$ of fish in a lake (measured in hundreds) is modelled by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{500}\right)$, where $t$ is in years and $P(0)=100$. (a) Use Euler's method with a step size of $1$ year to estimate $P$ at $t=1$, $t=2$ and $t=3$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the values of $P$ for which the population is in equilibrium. [2] (c) Find the value of $P$ at which the population grows fastest, and the maximum rate of growth. [3]
tips: Euler's method: $P_{n+1}=P_n+h\,\frac{dP}{dt}$ evaluated at $P_n$. For part (c) the growth rate is itself a quadratic in $P$, so no differentiation of the model is needed.

subtopic: Separation of variables with a nonlinear right-hand side
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2xy^2$, with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) Write down the maximum value of $y$ and the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the solution curve. [2] (c) Find the positive value of $x$ for which $y=\dfrac15$. [1]
tips: After integrating, use the initial condition immediately to find the constant, then rearrange to make $y$ the subject. Check your answer by testing it at $x=0$.

subtopic: Mixing problem: salt in a tank
statement: A tank contains 200 liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.5$ kg of salt per liter flows in at $4$ liters per minute. The well-mixed solution flows out at $4$ liters per minute, so the volume stays at 200 liters. Let $S$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=2-\dfrac{S}{50}$. [3] (b) Solve the differential equation with $S=0$ when $t=0$, giving $S$ in terms of $t$. [4] (c) Find the time taken for the tank to contain $60$ kg of salt, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Rate of salt in $=0.5\times4=2$ kg/min [A1] Concentration in the tank $=\frac{S}{200}$ kg/L [M1] Rate out $=4\times\frac{S}{200}=\frac{S}{50}$, so $\frac{dS}{dt}=2-\frac{S}{50}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{100-S}{50}$, so $\int\frac{50}{100-S}\,dS=\int dt$ [M1] $-50\ln(100-S)=t+c$ [A1] $t=0,S=0$: $c=-50\ln100$ [M1] $S=100\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $60=100(1-e^{-t/50})$, $e^{-t/50}=0.4$ [M1] $t=50\ln2.5=45.8$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Model inflow minus outflow, and remember that the outflow depends on the current concentration $S/V$. Factor the right-hand side before separating.

subtopic: Coupled system with complex eigenvalues: spiral
statement: Consider the coupled system $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-x+2y,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=-2x-y$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of the matrix of coefficients. [3] (b) Classify the equilibrium point at the origin. [2] (c) By considering the point $(1,0)$, determine whether trajectories rotate clockwise or anticlockwise about the origin. [2] (d) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$, starting at $(x,y)=(1,0)$ when $t=0$, to estimate $(x,y)$ when $t=0.2$. [3]
